title: Validation Pipeline: Expected-Cost Ordering (Bayes + Early Exit)
description:
## Goal
Minimize validation latency by ordering validators by expected cost and failure probability, while keeping deterministic behavior.

## Core Idea (Alien Artifact)
Model each validator i with cost c_i and failure probability p_i (posterior). Expected cost of an ordering pi is:
E[cost] = sum_k (c_{pi_k} * prod_{j<k} (1 - p_{pi_j}))
Choose ordering that minimizes expected cost. Update p_i online from observed failures with Beta priors.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Deterministic ordering under fixed seed + history.
- Latency improvement vs static ordering (documented).
- Explainable ranking with evidence ledger of p_i and c_i.

## Tests (REQUIRED)
- unit_expected_cost_formula: ordering matches brute-force for small n.
- unit_posterior_update: p_i updates with success/failure.
- perf_validation_latency: measure p50/p95 before/after; log.

## E2E (REQUIRED)
- Replay validation logs; verify ordering adjustments and deterministic output.
- Log: c_i, p_i, ordering, total latency.
close_reason: done

title: FrankenTUI: Complete Implementation Epic
description:
# FrankenTUI (ftui) - Master Epic

## Vision
FrankenTUI is a deliberately minimal, high-performance terminal UI kernel that fuses the best surviving abstractions from three Rust codebases (rich_rust, charmed_rust, opentui_rust) into one coherent system.

## Core Promise
ftui is designed so you can build a Claude Code / Codex-class agent harness UI without flicker, without cursor corruption, and without sacrificing native scrollback.

## Three-Library Synthesis (conceptual)
- opentui_rust: Cell grid, diff algorithm, alpha blending, scissor/opacity stacks, grapheme pool (cache-optimal 16-byte cells)
- rich_rust: Segment abstraction, markup parser, measurement protocol (Cow<str> for zero-copy)
- charmed_rust: LipGloss styling, CSS-like properties, theme system, Elm architecture (bitflags property tracking)

## Non-Negotiables (Engineering Contract)
1. One writer owns the terminal - serialized output
2. Untrusted bytes never executed - sanitize by default
3. Diffed + buffered UI only - no ad-hoc println
4. Inline-first is real - preserve scrollback
5. Safe by default, unsafe isolated (repo policy: unsafe forbidden)
6. Deterministic by design
7. Correctness continuously verified

## Performance Budgets (v1)
- Present (80x24, 5% changed): p50 < 1.0ms
- Cell comparison: < 1ns
- 16 bytes per cell (4 per cache line)

## Success Criteria (v1 = Done)
(Directly derived from plan Section 0.11.)

- [ ] Inline mode default is stable (streaming logs + UI does not corrupt scrollback/cursor).
- [ ] PTY tests confirm cleanup on normal exit and panic.
- [ ] Presenter/diff correctness validated by terminal-model tests.
- [ ] Unicode width correctness proven by corpus tests (ZWJ/emoji/combining).
- [ ] Style system is deterministic and documented (explicit masks + inheritance).
- [ ] Runtime supports update/view loop + ticks + batch/sequence cmds + deterministic simulator.
- [ ] Harness-essential widgets exist and are tested (viewport/log viewer, status/panel, prompt/text input, progress/spinner).
- [ ] Docs exist: agent harness tutorial, inline vs alt-screen trade-offs, one-writer rule guidance, windows limitations, compatibility matrix.

# Phase -1: Decision Spikes

## Purpose
Before building a big structure, run small spikes that de-risk the hardest unknowns. These are tiny experiments for fast learning.

## Why This Phase Exists
The plan is ambitious and certain decisions could cause multi-week churn if not resolved early. Decision spikes force us to confront reality before committing to architecture.

## Exit Criteria
One ADR (Architecture Decision Record) per spike capturing:
- Context: What problem are we solving?
- Decision: What did we choose?
- Alternatives considered
- Consequences: What are the tradeoffs?
- Test plan: How we'll know it worked

## Key Spikes Required
1. Inline mode spike: Implement both scroll-region and overlay strategies in tiny prototype
2. Presenter validation spike: Build terminal-model harness to validate output
3. Backend spike: Validate raw mode + resize + input reading across platforms

## Relationship to Other Phases
This phase BLOCKS Phase 0 (Contracts + Workspace Skeleton). We must not proceed with architecture until we've validated our assumptions through concrete experiments.

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Spikes are completed with runnable prototypes (even if throwaway) and notes.
- [ ] ADR-001/002/003 are unblocked and written based on spike outcomes.
- [ ] We have a clear go/no-go decision for:
  - inline mode strategy baseline
  - presenter emission baseline
  - backend selection

title: Spike: Inline Mode Strategies
description:
# Spike: Inline Mode Strategies

## Objective
Validate a **correctness-first** inline mode strategy for FrankenTUI: stable UI chrome + streaming logs without flicker, cursor drift, or scrollback corruption.

This spike is explicitly about **choosing and proving** the baseline policy before we harden API and implementation.

## Background: Why Inline Mode Is Hard
Inline mode + streaming logs is where most TUIs fail in practice:
- Logs write while UI is mid-draw (multiple writers, interleaving)
- Cursor position gets lost or restored incorrectly
- Full-screen clears destroy scrollback
- tmux/screen and terminal emulators differ in behavior for cursor save/restore, margins, and sync output

This project’s core promise depends on nailing the policy and cleanup invariants early.

## Strategies Under Test

### Strategy A: Scroll-Region Anchoring (DECSTBM / scroll margins)
Use CSI `t;b r` to set top/bottom margins:
- Constrains scrolling to a region (e.g., log region)
- UI region stays pinned while logs scroll within the region

Pros:
- Can reduce redraw work and cursor thrash
- More "native" scrolling behavior when it works

Cons:
- Muxes (tmux/screen) and some terminals may handle margins inconsistently
- Must be carefully reset on exit, panic, and when switching modes

### Strategy B: Overlay Redraw (universal fallback)
Before writing logs:
1. Save cursor position
2. Temporarily move cursor / clear UI region
3. Write logs (so they land in native scrollback)
4. Redraw UI region
5. Restore cursor

Pros:
- Works in the widest set of environments (baseline correctness)

Cons:
- More redraw work
- Requires an explicit “UI region” policy and predictable redraw sequence

### Strategy C: Hybrid (likely default)
- **Overlay redraw** is always available as the correctness baseline
- Scroll-region anchoring is an internal optimization **only** where proven safe
- Public API exposes policy (“inline mode”) not mechanism (“DECSTBM”) to avoid leaking terminal quirks into user code

## Environments / Compatibility Matrix To Validate
Minimum environments for this spike:
- Plain terminal (no mux)
- Kitty
- WezTerm
- Alacritty
- Ghostty
- tmux
- screen (if available)

Also record:
- Whether DEC 2026 synchronized output is supported and affects flicker
- Whether cursor save/restore should use DEC (`ESC7`/`ESC8`) vs ANSI (`CSI s`/`CSI u`) vs emulation

## Instrumentation Requirements
This spike must produce useful evidence, not vibes.

- Structured logs (via `tracing`) for:
  - enter/exit inline mode
  - log-write begin/end
  - UI redraw begin/end
  - cursor save/restore operations
  - any fallback taken (mux detected, feature probe disabled, etc.)
- In PTY tests, capture and store:
  - the raw byte stream written to the terminal
  - parsed “terminal model” invariants (cursor position, mode flags) where possible

## Deliverables
- A tiny prototype (~200 LOC is fine) that demonstrates both A and B, and the selection logic.
- A written decision (ADR-001) that records:
  - decision
  - fallback rules
  - observed incompatibilities
  - required cleanup invariants

## Tests Required
- PTY integration tests that assert:
  - cursor is restored after each frame present in inline mode
  - terminal modes are restored on normal exit and on panic
  - no full-screen clears are used in inline mode unless explicitly configured
- "Sustained output" scenario: continuous log stream + periodic UI redraw + resize events.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Both Strategy A and B can be exercised by a single prototype with an explicit switch.
- [ ] We have a documented default policy (likely Hybrid) with explicit fallback triggers.
- [ ] PTY test demonstrates no cursor drift and correct cleanup on both normal exit and panic.
- [ ] ADR-001 is unblocked with concrete observations (not just theoretical pros/cons).
close_reason: Spike complete: inline_mode.rs + ADR-001 created, all tests pass

title: Spike: Presenter Validation with Terminal Model
description:
# Spike: Presenter Validation with Terminal Model

## Objective
Build a minimal **terminal model** (a deliberately small emulator) to validate that a `present()` cycle produces the expected grid and cursor state.

This spike exists to turn presenter correctness from “looks right on my terminal” into something testable, repeatable, and CI-friendly.

## Why This Spike Matters
The Presenter is the inverse-function layer of the whole system:
- incorrect SGR sequencing leaks style across cells
- incorrect cursor moves corrupt subsequent renders or user input location
- incorrectly terminated OSC 8 hyperlinks cause "sticky" links
- missing resets break muxes and downstream output

If Presenter correctness isn’t proven, every later feature becomes suspect.

## Scope: Terminal Model (Not A Full Emulator)
The model only needs to understand the subset of sequences we emit.

It must track:
- a grid of cells (char/grapheme + style)
- cursor position
- current SGR state
- hyperlink state (OSC 8)
- mode flags relevant to correctness (cursor visibility, alt-screen if applicable, sync output nesting)

Out of scope:
- full VT parsing
- scrollback buffer modeling
- alternate character sets
- full mouse/keyboard decoding

## Sequences To Support (v1 model)
Minimum set (aligned to our planned Presenter behavior):
- CUP: `CSI r ; c H`
- relative cursor moves (CUU/CUD/CUF/CUB) if we emit them
- SGR: `CSI ... m` (at least reset + fg/bg + basic attrs)
- EL/ED: `CSI n K` / `CSI n J` (only the variants we emit)
- OSC 8 hyperlinks: start/end
- DEC 2026 synchronized output: begin/end (track nesting but can ignore visual effects)

## Test Strategy

### Deterministic unit tests
- Known buffers → Presenter output → Model apply → exact grid match
- Explicit cases for:
  - style reset boundaries
  - cursor position after present
  - hyperlink open/close correctness

### Property tests
- Generate random buffers (within constraints) and validate:
  - Presenter output is parseable by the model
  - Model grid equals desired buffer
  - No dangling style or hyperlink state after present

### Debuggability requirements
When a property test fails, we need:
- a small minimized failing case (proptest shrink)
- a readable diff of expected vs actual grid
- a dump of emitted escape sequences (escaped and annotated)

## Deliverables
- `TerminalModel` test harness
- A small “Presenter contract” suite that runs in CI and blocks regressions

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] TerminalModel supports the subset of sequences we emit (explicit list above).
- [ ] Unit tests cover representative edge cases (style/link/cursor correctness).
- [ ] Property tests run in CI and have actionable failure output (diff + byte dump).
- [ ] The model is used as a gate for presenter changes (documented in the operational playbook).
close_reason: Completed: TerminalModel with 27 tests (19 unit + 8 property)

title: Spike: Terminal Backend Validation
description:
# Spike: Terminal Backend Validation

## Objective
Validate raw mode + resize + input reading across platforms with the candidate backend.

This spike exists to produce a confident, written backend decision (ADR-003) before we commit to API surfaces and cleanup invariants.

## Why This Spike Matters
The terminal backend is foundational and extremely hard to swap later:
- raw mode enter/exit must be reliable
- resize delivery must be accurate
- input reading must be robust under high throughput (pastes, mouse)
- panic cleanup must restore the user’s terminal

If we get this wrong, the project becomes permanently flaky.

## Candidate Backend(s)
Primary candidate to evaluate first:
- Crossterm

Explicit alternatives (only if Crossterm is insufficient):
- termwiz
- termion (Unix-only)
- minimal custom termios (last resort; highest control, highest maintenance)

## Evaluation Matrix

### Functionality
- raw mode
- alternate screen (optional)
- cursor show/hide
- mouse mode enable/disable (SGR)
- bracketed paste enable/disable + correct parsing
- focus events enable/disable (if supported)
- resize events

### Robustness
- bounded-time input reads (avoid deadlocks)
- handles partial / malformed sequences without panics
- does not allocate unbounded memory on adversarial inputs

### Cleanup Discipline
For both normal exit and panic:
- raw mode restored
- cursor shown
- bracketed paste disabled
- mouse mode disabled
- scroll region reset if used
- alt-screen exited if used

### Platform coverage (v1 reality)
- Linux: required
- macOS: required
- Windows: “best effort” acceptable, but must not corrupt terminal

## Test Approach
- Minimal wrapper that exercises:
  - enter raw mode
  - read events
  - resize notifications
  - exit/cleanup
- PTY tests for Linux/macOS to assert cleanup invariants (where applicable)
- Manual validation notes where automation is not possible

## Deliverables
- A written backend decision (ADR-003) with:
  - decision
  - rationale
  - limitations
  - fallback strategy (if backend lacks a feature)
- A small compatibility note to feed into the terminal compatibility matrix

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Backend choice is backed by evidence (tests + notes), not assumptions.
- [ ] Cleanup invariants are validated (PTY where possible) for normal exit and panic.
- [ ] ADR-003 is completed and blocks downstream implementation appropriately.
close_reason: Spike complete: Crossterm validated, ADR-003 written, TerminalSession implemented with cleanup

title: ADRs: Architecture Decision Records
description:
# ADRs: Architecture Decision Records

## Purpose
Lock the 'churn-magnets' - decisions that most often cause multi-week churn if not resolved early. Each ADR follows the format:
- Context
- Decision
- Alternatives considered
- Consequences
- Test plan

## Why ADRs Matter
These are not bureaucratic paperwork. They are the decisions that:
- Could cause weeks of refactoring if changed later
- Have non-obvious tradeoffs
- Need documented rationale for future contributors
- Serve as the 'why' behind the code

## ADRs Required for v1

### ADR-001: Inline Mode Strategy
Hybrid anchoring: overlay redraw baseline + scroll-region optimization
- Most impactful decision for agent harness behavior

### ADR-002: Presenter Emission Strategy
Reset+apply for v1 correctness; incremental behind feature flag
- Affects output size and correctness guarantees

### ADR-003: Terminal Backend Selection
Crossterm as v1 default
- Affects portability and maintenance burden

### ADR-004: Windows v1 Scope
What's supported vs best-effort
- Sets user expectations and testing requirements

### ADR-005: One-Writer Rule Enforcement
Type-level ownership model
- Core correctness invariant for inline mode

### ADR-006: Untrusted Output Policy
Sanitize-by-default for security
- Prevents escape sequence injection attacks

## ADR Discipline Rules
- Every controversial design choice gets an ADR
- ADRs are short and opinionated
- Once written and reviewed, ADRs are locked
- Changes require new ADR or amendment with rationale

## Success Criteria
- [ ] ADR-001..ADR-006 are each written with: Context / Decision / Alternatives / Consequences / Test Plan.
- [ ] Each ADR includes explicit stop-ship tests (PTY/terminal-model/property tests as appropriate).
- [ ] Any future changes to a locked decision require a new ADR (no silent drift).
close_reason: All 6 ADRs completed: ADR-001 through ADR-006

title: ADR-001: Inline Mode Strategy
description:
# ADR-001: Inline Mode Strategy

## Status
PROPOSED

## Context
We need stable UI chrome + scrollback-native logs, with no flicker or cursor corruption, across terminals and multiplexers.

Inline mode plus streaming output is the hardest real-world requirement. Most flicker/corruption bugs come from broken assumptions about terminal ownership and write interleaving.

## Options Considered

### Option A: Scroll-Region Anchoring (DECSTBM)
- Pros: UI truly pinned, logs scroll naturally, fewer UI redraws
- Cons: Tricky interactions (cursor save/restore, origin mode), mux quirks, needs serious PTY coverage

### Option B: Overlay Redraw
- Pros: Portable baseline, correctness-first, simplest mental model
- Cons: Needs careful 'clear only UI region', buffered output to avoid flicker

### Option C: Hybrid (RECOMMENDED)
- Pros: Best of both; baseline works everywhere, optimization where safe
- Cons: Complexity; requires capability policy and more tests

## Decision
**Hybrid approach**:
1. Overlay redraw is always available and is the correctness baseline
2. Scroll-region anchoring is an internal optimization enabled only when proven safe
3. Public API exposes policy, not mechanism

## Implementation Notes (Baseline Overlay)
1. Begin synchronized output if supported
2. Save cursor position (prefer robust option)
3. Move cursor to UI anchor
4. Clear only the UI region (localized EL/ED)
5. Present diffed UI frame
6. Restore cursor position
7. End synchronized output; flush

## Implementation Notes (Scroll-Region Optimization)
When enabled:
- Set scroll region to log area: top..(h-ui_height)
- Ensure UI writes land outside scroll region
- Restore scroll region on exit and mode switches
- Disable by default in tmux/screen

## Consequences
- More complex than pure overlay or pure scroll-region
- Requires capability detection and policy logic
- Requires PTY tests for both strategies
- Better user experience when optimization is safe

## Test Plan
- PTY test: log spam + UI tick does not corrupt scrollback
- Cursor contract test: cursor restored after every present
- Resize test: changing ui_height and terminal height re-anchors correctly
- Mux tests: verify tmux/screen behavior and fallback
close_reason: ADR-001 created at docs/adr/ADR-001-inline-mode.md as part of spike bd-10i.1.1

title: ADR-002: Presenter Emission Strategy
description:
# ADR-002: Presenter Emission Strategy

## Status
PROPOSED

## Context
SGR and link state tracking can either be simple and correct or minimal-bytes and complex. The Presenter must emit ANSI sequences that transform the terminal from current state to desired state.

## Options Considered

### Option A: Reset+Apply Always
Emit SGR 0 then re-apply all attributes for each style change.
- Pros: Simplest, correctness is trivial
- Cons: More bytes emitted

### Option B: Incremental SGR Diffs
Track previous style, emit only changed attributes.
- Pros: Fewer bytes, faster on slow terminals
- Cons: Complex, risk of 'dangling attributes' bugs

### Option C: Hybrid (RECOMMENDED for future)
Reset on hard cases, incremental on small diffs.
- Pros: Best of both
- Cons: Needs heuristics and benchmarks

## Decision
**v1 default: Reset+Apply** for correctness.
**Add incremental/hybrid behind feature flag** until benchmarks + PTY coverage justify enabling by default.

## Rationale
Correctness beats optimization at this stage. Reset+apply is:
- Trivially correct
- Easy to test and verify
- Good enough for most workloads
- Foundation for future optimization

Incremental emission can be added later when:
- We have comprehensive terminal-model tests
- Benchmarks show meaningful benefit
- PTY tests cover edge cases

## Consequences
- Higher byte output than theoretically minimal
- Simpler implementation and maintenance
- Clear path to optimization via feature flag
- No 'dangling attribute' bugs possible

## Test Plan
- Terminal-model tests: style state cannot leak across runs
- PTY tests: links (OSC 8) cannot remain open after present/exit
- Benchmark: measure bytes/frame for representative workloads
- Regression: track byte output in CI
close_reason: Created ADR-002-presenter-emission.md with reset+apply strategy

title: ADR-003: Terminal Backend Selection
description:
# ADR-003: Terminal Backend Selection

## Status
PROPOSED

## Context
We must support raw mode, key/mouse input, resize, and reliable cleanup on Unix and Windows.

## Options Considered

### Option A: Crossterm
- Pros: Widely used, cross-platform, avoids bespoke termios/Windows plumbing
- Cons: Another dependency, abstractions may not fit perfectly

### Option B: termion
- Pros: Pure Rust, simpler
- Cons: Unix-only, no Windows support

### Option C: Raw termios + Windows Console API
- Pros: Maximum control
- Cons: Significant implementation effort, platform-specific code

### Option D: termwiz
- Pros: Feature-rich, from wezterm project
- Cons: Heavier dependency, may include more than we need

## Decision
**v1 default: Crossterm**

Kernel remains backend-agnostic at the conceptual level, but v1 does NOT over-abstract. Ship one backend 'batteries included'; treat alternatives as experimental.

## Rationale
- Crossterm is widely used and tested
- Cross-platform without custom code
- Fits our Event model reasonably well
- Community support and maintenance
- We can switch later if needed (abstraction in place)

## Consequences
- Dependency on crossterm crate
- Must work within crossterm's event model
- Windows support comes 'for free' (with caveats)
- Path to alternatives via feature flags

## Test Plan
- Spike validates Crossterm functionality (bd-10i.1.3)
- PTY tests verify raw mode + cleanup
- Multi-platform CI (Linux, macOS, Windows)
- Document any Crossterm limitations in Windows ADR
close_reason: ADR-003 written at docs/adr/ADR-003-terminal-backend.md - Crossterm accepted as v1 backend

title: ADR-004: Windows v1 Scope
description:
# ADR-004: Windows v1 Scope

## Status
PROPOSED

## Context
Windows terminal support varies significantly from Unix. We need to decide what's fully supported vs best-effort for v1.

## Supported in v1
- Raw mode enter/exit and cleanup on panic
- Key input and resize events
- Basic mouse (where Crossterm supports it)
- Color where available (16/256/truecolor when exposed)

## Best-Effort / May Be Missing in v1
- DEC synchronized output (mode 2026) - not widely supported
- OSC 8 hyperlinks - limited Windows Terminal support
- Bracketed paste differences across terminals
- Focus events differences
- Kitty keyboard protocol - not supported

## Decision
Accept Windows as 'supported with documented limitations' for v1.

## Rationale
- Primary target is agent harness UIs (likely Unix/macOS)
- Windows Terminal is improving but not at feature parity
- Full Windows feature parity would delay v1 significantly
- Honest documentation is better than broken promises

## Consequences
- Windows users may have reduced functionality
- Must clearly document limitations
- Future versions can improve Windows support
- CI must include Windows builds (even if tests are limited)

## Documentation Requirement
A 'Windows Limitations' section must exist and be honest about:
- Which features work fully
- Which features are degraded
- Which features are missing
- Workarounds if any

## Test Plan
- Windows CI build must pass
- Core functionality tests on Windows (raw mode, basic input)
- Document behavior differences

title: ADR-005: One-Writer Rule Enforcement
description:
# ADR-005: One-Writer Rule Enforcement

## Status
PROPOSED

## Context
Inline mode guarantees break if other code writes to stdout/stderr concurrently. The terminal is a shared mutable resource that doesn't support concurrent access safely.

## Problem
If multiple sources write to the terminal simultaneously:
- Cursor position becomes undefined
- Partial escape sequences corrupt output
- UI and logs interleave unpredictably
- Scrollback gets corrupted

## Decision
Enforce the one-writer rule through type-level ownership:
- TerminalOwner / TerminalSession owns raw mode and output handle
- TerminalWriter is the only way to write logs and present UI
- Provide routing helpers for subprocess and in-process logs

## Type-Level Enforcement
TerminalSession takes ownership of stdout:
- Only TerminalWriter can produce output
- Cannot accidentally println! while ftui is active
- Drop returns terminal to normal state

## Supported Routing Patterns

### Pattern A: LogSink (In-Process Logs)
Provide a LogSink: Write that application code uses instead of println!
- Discourage raw println! during inline mode
- Route through TerminalWriter with sanitization

### Pattern B: PTY Capture (Subprocess Output)
Spawn tool subprocesses under PTY:
- Read their stdout/stderr streams
- Write as log stream through ftui
- Preserves scrollback and UI stability
- Feature-gated (adds dependency on PTY crate)

### Pattern C: Stdio Capture (Optional)
Pipe + reader thread that forwards through ftui:
- Captures accidental println! from libraries
- Best-effort, may miss some output
- Feature-gated

## Consequences
- Application code must use ftui APIs for output
- Libraries that write directly may cause issues
- Subprocess output requires explicit handling
- More disciplined but more work for users

## What Happens If Violated
If external code writes to stdout during inline mode:
- Behavior is undefined
- Cursor may drift
- UI may corrupt
- This is documented as unsupported

## Test Plan
- PTY tests with concurrent log writes via supported mux path
- Assert stability under parallel output
- Document undefined behavior for unsupported patterns

title: ADR-006: Untrusted Output Policy (Sanitize-by-Default)
description:
# ADR-006: Untrusted Output Policy (Sanitize-by-Default)

## Status
PROPOSED

## Context
Agent harnesses display tool output, LLM streams, and logs. Malicious or buggy content can smuggle ANSI/OSC sequences that:
- Manipulate terminal state
- Deceive users (fake prompts, hidden commands)
- Persist changes after the app exits
- Exfiltrate data via terminal queries

This is a real security concern for AI agent UIs.

## Decision
**Sanitize by default**: Any text flowing through write_log() or rendered as user-provided content has control sequences stripped or escaped.

**Explicit opt-in for raw passthrough**: An API like write_raw() or Text::raw() allows trusted content to include ANSI.

## What Gets Sanitized
- ESC (0x1B) and all CSI/OSC/DCS/APC sequences
- C0 controls except: TAB (0x09), LF (0x0A), CR (0x0D)
- Option for semi-trusted mode: allow SGR styling only

## Sanitization Strategies
1. **Strip**: Remove escape sequences entirely
2. **Escape**: Convert to visible representation (e.g., ^[ for ESC)
3. **Replace**: Substitute with placeholder character

Default: Strip (cleanest output)

## API Design
// Sanitized by default
harness.write_log('User provided text with \x1b[31mattack\x1b[0m');
// -> 'User provided text with attack'

// Explicit opt-in for trusted content
harness.write_raw(trusted_ansi_bytes);

// Text with explicit trust level
Text::sanitized(user_input);
Text::raw(trusted_source);

## Consequences
- User content is safe by default
- Trusted content must be explicitly marked
- Some legitimate ANSI in logs will be stripped
- Security posture matches threat model

## Test Plan
- PTY tests feeding adversarial sequences into logs
- Assert terminal invariants remain intact
- Fuzz tests with random byte streams in log paths
- Verify no state leakage after malicious input

title: Testing + QA: Verification Suite
description:
# Testing + QA: Verification Suite

## Purpose
Kernel must be 'boringly correct'. Testing is not optional - it's how we prove our claims and prevent regressions.

## Test Categories

### Unit Tests (Kernel)
- Cell packing/equality
- Buffer bounds + scissor/opacity invariants
- GraphemePool refcount correctness
- LinkRegistry correctness
- Width measurement accuracy

### Property Tests (Randomized)
- Diff correctness: applying changes reproduces target buffer
- Presenter state tracking never emits malformed sequences
- Width correctness: rendering never writes beyond frame bounds

### Snapshot Tests (Widgets/Apps)
- Frame buffers across themes and widths
- Segment streams for export pipelines
- Deterministic outputs in simulator mode

title: Implement input parser fuzzing
description:
# Implement input parser fuzzing

## Objective
Fuzz the InputParser to ensure it handles all possible byte sequences without panicking or excessive resource usage.

## Why Fuzzing?
- Terminal input is untrusted
- Malformed sequences are common
- DoS via crafted input is possible
- Parser must be robust

## Fuzz Targets

### Target 1: Raw Byte Parsing
fuzz_target\!(|data: &[u8]| {
    let mut parser = InputParser::new();
    let _ = parser.parse(data);
    // Must not panic
    // Must not hang
    // Must not exceed memory limits
});

### Target 2: Structured Fuzzing
// Generate semi-valid sequences
#[derive(Arbitrary)]
enum FuzzSequence {
    Char(u8),
    Escape,
    Csi(Vec<u8>),
    Osc(Vec<u8>),
    Mouse { button: u8, x: u16, y: u16 },
    Paste(Vec<u8>),
}

### Target 3: Long Sequences
// Specifically test DoS limits
fuzz_target\!(|len: u16| {
    let data = vec\![0x1b, b'[']  // CSI
        .into_iter()
        .chain(std::iter::repeat(b'0').take(len as usize))
        .chain(std::iter::once(b'm'))
        .collect::<Vec<_>>();

    let mut parser = InputParser::new();
    let _ = parser.parse(&data);
    // Should not allocate unbounded memory
});

## Properties to Verify
1. No panics on any input
2. Memory bounded (no OOM from crafted input)
3. Time bounded (no quadratic behavior)
4. Always returns to Ground state eventually
5. DoS limits enforced

## Corpus Seeds
- Valid key sequences
- Valid mouse sequences
- Bracketed paste boundaries
- OSC 8 links
- Malformed UTF-8
- Truncated sequences

## Running Fuzzer
cargo +nightly fuzz run input_parser -- -max_len=4096

## Integration with CI
- Run fuzzer for limited time on each PR
- Maintain corpus in repo
- Report new crashes immediately

## Tests Required
- [ ] Fuzz harness builds
- [ ] Initial corpus covers major cases
- [ ] No crashes in 1-hour fuzz session
- [ ] Memory limits enforced

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Fuzzer integrated in CI
- [ ] No panics found
- [ ] Corpus maintained
- [ ] Coverage tracked

# Write Glossary (Appendix B)

## Background
The plan includes a short glossary of terms that recur throughout the kernel design. This needs to be in-repo so future contributors don't need the plan doc to understand terminology.

## Deliverable
Create `docs/glossary.md` containing (at minimum) the glossary table below, plus any additional terms introduced by implementation.

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| **Cell** | Single grid position (content + fg + bg + attrs) |
| **Buffer** | 2D array of Cells representing display state |
| **Frame** | Buffer + metadata for a render pass |
| **Diff** | Set of (x, y) positions that changed between buffers |
| **Presenter** | State-tracked ANSI emitter |
| **Grapheme** | User-perceived character (may be multiple codepoints) |
| **GraphemePool** | Interned storage for complex grapheme clusters |
| **LinkRegistry** | URL storage for OSC 8 hyperlinks |
| **Scissor** | Clipping rectangle for rendering |
| **SGR** | Select Graphic Rendition (style codes) |
| **OSC** | Operating System Command (escape sequence) |
| **CSI** | Control Sequence Introducer (`\x1b[`) |
| **DEC** | Digital Equipment Corporation (terminal standard) |
| **ZWJ** | Zero Width Joiner (connects graphemes into compound) |
| **Porter-Duff** | Compositing algebra for alpha blending |

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `docs/glossary.md` exists.
- [ ] Table is present and correct.
- [ ] Any additional ftui-specific terms (e.g., TerminalWriter, ScreenMode, UiAnchor) are added with concise definitions.

title: Write Risk Register + Mitigation Links (Appendix C)
description:
# Write Risk Register + Mitigation Links (Appendix C)

## Background
The plan includes a small Risk Register to keep engineering effort focused on the failure modes that destroy trust in a terminal UI kernel (cursor corruption, escape injection, width bugs, capability mismatches, unsafe creep, byte bloat, interleaved writes).

We want this risk list in-repo so:
- mitigations stay attached to code and tests
- adding features doesn't silently reintroduce known risks

## Deliverable
Create `docs/risk-register.md` that includes the plan's risks and extends them with:
- the *actual* Beads issue IDs that mitigate the risk
- the *actual* test suites / scripts that enforce the mitigation

## Required risks (from plan)
1) Inline mode cursor corruption
- Mitigation: PTY tests + strict cursor policy + centralized writer API for logs/UI.

1b) ANSI / OSC injection via untrusted log content
- Mitigation: sanitize-by-default + explicit opt-in raw passthrough + adversarial PTY tests.

2) Unicode width bugs
- Mitigation: curated test corpus + snapshot tests + ASCII fast path only when proven.

3) Terminal capability mismatches
- Mitigation: conservative defaults + feature detection + robust fallbacks.

4) Unsafe creep
- Mitigation: forbid unsafe by default; isolate any perf tricks; require tests + benches.

5) Presenter byte bloat
- Mitigation: run grouping + style-run coalescing + output-length benchmarks in CI.

6) Interleaved stdout writes from user code
- Mitigation: one-writer rule; TerminalSession/TerminalWriter; routing/capture patterns.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `docs/risk-register.md` exists and contains the risks above.
- [ ] Each mitigation links to specific Beads issues and/or specific test suites (unit/property/pty/e2e).
- [ ] The risk register includes a short section "How to add a new risk" and "When to revisit".

description:
# Add Executable Invariant Tests (Chapter 2.3)

## Background
Plan 2.3 lists explicit invariants for Buffer, scissor/opacity stacks, and GraphemePool validity.

We want these invariants to be enforced by tests so regressions are caught immediately.

## Invariants to encode (from plan)
- Buffer dimensions: width/height immutable; cells length == width*height
- Cell access bounds: safe get/set reject out-of-bounds
- Scissor stack intersection monotonically decreases on push
- Opacity stack product stays in [0,1]
- GraphemePool: slot.refcount > 0 implies slot is valid
- CellContent with GraphemeId implies id is valid in associated pool

## Test Strategy
- Unit tests for the deterministic invariants (stack behaviors, bounds)
- Property tests for randomized sequences of push/pop (scissor/opacity)

title: Define public Buffer API contract
description:
# Define public Buffer API contract

## Objective
Document and lock the Buffer type's public API. Buffer is the 2D grid that holds Cells.

## Buffer Contract

### Core Structure
pub struct Buffer {
    width: u16,
    height: u16,
    cells: Vec<Cell>,
    scissor_stack: Vec<Rect>,
    opacity_stack: Vec<f32>,
}

### Invariants (MUST ALWAYS HOLD)
1. cells.len() == width * height
2. width/height never change after creation
3. Scissor stack intersection monotonically decreases on push
4. Opacity stack product stays in [0, 1]
5. Scissor/opacity stacks always have at least one element

### Constructor
fn new(width: u16, height: u16) -> Self
- Initializes cells to Cell::default()
- Scissor stack starts with full buffer rect
- Opacity stack starts with 1.0

### Cell Access
fn get(&self, x: u16, y: u16) -> Option<&Cell>
- Returns None if out of bounds

fn get_unchecked(&self, x: u16, y: u16) -> &Cell
- No bounds check, panics on OOB (debug) or UB (release)
- Only use when bounds verified

fn set(&mut self, x: u16, y: u16, cell: Cell)
- Respects scissor (skips if outside)
- Applies opacity stack to cell colors
- Applies alpha compositing if bg has transparency
- Handles wide character continuation cells

### Scissor Stack
fn push_scissor(&mut self, rect: Rect)
- Computes intersection with current scissor
- Pushes intersected rect

fn pop_scissor(&mut self)
- Pops if stack.len() > 1 (preserves base)

fn current_scissor(&self) -> Rect
- Returns top of stack

### Opacity Stack
fn push_opacity(&mut self, opacity: f32)
- Clamps to [0, 1]
- Pushes current * new

fn pop_opacity(&mut self)
- Pops if stack.len() > 1

fn current_opacity(&self) -> f32
- Returns top of stack

### Utilities
fn clear(&mut self)
- Fills all cells with Cell::default()

fn cells(&self) -> &[Cell]
- Raw slice for diffing

fn width(&self) -> u16
fn height(&self) -> u16

## Frame Contract
Frame = Buffer + render pass metadata

pub struct Frame {
    pub buffer: Buffer,
    pub hit_grid: Option<HitGrid>,
    pub cursor_position: Option<(u16, u16)>,
    pub cursor_visible: bool,
}

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All methods documented
- [ ] Invariants stated in code comments
- [ ] Test for each invariant
- [ ] No UB in safe API
close_reason: Buffer API contract defined and implemented with 22 passing tests. Public API includes get/set, scissor stack, opacity stack, fill, clear, copy_from.

# Define TerminalCapabilities contract

## Objective
Document the capability detection model that informs how ftui behaves on different terminals.

## TerminalCapabilities Structure
pub struct TerminalCapabilities {
    // Color support
    pub true_color: bool,
    pub colors_256: bool,

    // Advanced features
    pub sync_output: bool,       // DEC mode 2026
    pub osc8_hyperlinks: bool,
    pub scroll_region: bool,     // DECSTBM

    // Multiplexer detection
    pub in_tmux: bool,
    pub in_screen: bool,
    pub in_zellij: bool,

    // Input features
    pub kitty_keyboard: bool,
    pub focus_events: bool,
    pub bracketed_paste: bool,
    pub mouse_sgr: bool,

    // Optional features
    pub osc52_clipboard: bool,   // Best-effort output
}

## Detection Logic

### Environment Variables
- COLORTERM: truecolor, 24bit
- TERM: terminal type (kitty, xterm-256color, etc.)
- TERM_PROGRAM: iTerm.app, WezTerm, Alacritty, Ghostty
- NO_COLOR: disable color (de-facto standard)
- TMUX, STY, ZELLIJ: multiplexer detection
- KITTY_WINDOW_ID: Kitty detection

### Detection Rules
true_color = \!NO_COLOR && (COLORTERM contains truecolor/24bit
             || TERM_PROGRAM in modern terminals)

sync_output = TERM_PROGRAM in [WezTerm, Alacritty, Ghostty]
              || TERM contains kitty

osc8_hyperlinks = \!NO_COLOR && TERM_PROGRAM in modern terminals

scroll_region = TERM \!= dumb (broadly supported)

osc52_clipboard = \!in_any_mux && TERM \!= dumb (security restricted)

## Methods
impl TerminalCapabilities {
    fn detect() -> Self;      // From environment
    fn basic() -> Self;       // Minimal fallback
    fn in_any_mux(&self) -> bool;  // Any multiplexer?
}

## Multiplexer Notes
- TMUX/screen/zellij sit between us and terminal
- May need passthrough for some features
- Some features disabled in mux by default
- WezTerm/Kitty built-in mux doesn't need special handling

## Future: Runtime Probing
Optional feature-gated probing:
- Device attribute queries (DA)
- OSC queries for capabilities
- Must be bounded with timeouts

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All fields documented with detection logic
- [ ] detect() works on common terminals
- [ ] basic() provides safe fallback
- [ ] in_any_mux() helper available
close_reason: Contract fully implemented in crates/ftui-core/src/ with tests

title: Define TerminalSession lifecycle contract
description:
# Define TerminalSession lifecycle contract

## Objective
Document the RAII-based terminal lifecycle management that ensures cleanup even on panic.

## TerminalSession Structure
pub struct TerminalSession<W: Write> {
    writer: W,
    raw_mode_active: bool,
    alt_screen_active: bool,
    mouse_active: bool,
    bracketed_paste_active: bool,
    capabilities: TerminalCapabilities,
}

## Lifecycle Guarantees
1. All terminal state changes tracked
2. Drop restores previous state
3. Panic hook ensures cleanup
4. No leaked state on any exit path

## Constructor
fn new(writer: W) -> io::Result<Self>
- Detects capabilities
- Installs panic hook for cleanup
- Does NOT enter raw mode automatically

## Terminal Modes
fn enter_raw_mode(&mut self) -> io::Result<()>
- Enables raw mode (no echo, no line buffering)
- Tracks state for cleanup

fn enter_alt_screen(&mut self) -> io::Result<()>
- Switches to alternate screen buffer
- Emits CSI ? 1049 h

fn enable_mouse(&mut self) -> io::Result<()>
- Enables SGR mouse mode (1000, 1002, 1006)
- Tracks for cleanup

fn enable_bracketed_paste(&mut self) -> io::Result<()>
- Enables bracketed paste mode
- Emits CSI ? 2004 h

fn enable_focus_events(&mut self) -> io::Result<()>
- Enables focus tracking
- Emits CSI ? 1004 h

## Cleanup (Drop)
impl<W: Write> Drop for TerminalSession<W> {
    fn drop(&mut self) {
        // Disable mouse modes
        // Disable bracketed paste
        // Exit alt screen
        // Reset style (SGR 0)
        // Show cursor
        // Restore raw mode (via backend)
        // Flush
    }
}

## Panic Hook
On panic, best-effort cleanup:
- Exit alt screen
- Show cursor
- Reset style
- Disable mouse
- Disable bracketed paste
- Flush

## Escape Sequences Reference
- Alt screen: CSI ? 1049 h/l
- Mouse: CSI ? 1000/1002/1006 h/l
- Bracketed paste: CSI ? 2004 h/l
- Focus events: CSI ? 1004 h/l
- Show cursor: CSI ? 25 h
- Reset style: CSI 0 m

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All state changes tracked
- [ ] Drop cleans up all active modes
- [ ] Panic hook installed and tested
- [ ] PTY test verifies cleanup
close_reason: TerminalSession lifecycle implemented with RAII cleanup, Drop guarantee, and feature tracking

title: Phase 1: Core Render Kernel
description:
# Phase 1: Core Render Kernel

## Purpose
Implement the sacred kernel types that everything else builds upon. This is the most critical phase - these types must be correct, fast, and stable.

## Core Types to Implement
1. Cell (16 bytes exactly): content + fg + bg + attrs
2. CellContent: char or GraphemeId encoding
3. CellAttrs: flags (8 bits) + link_id (24 bits)
4. PackedRgba: RGBA as u32 with Porter-Duff blending
5. GraphemeId + GraphemePool: reference-counted interned complex strings
6. Buffer: 2D grid with scissor/opacity stacks
7. Rect, Sides, Measurement primitives

## Technical Constraints

### Cell Layout (The 16-Byte Sweet Spot)
- 16 bytes = exactly 4 cells per 64-byte cache line
- Layout: content(4B) + fg(4B) + bg(4B) + attrs(4B)
- Must use repr(C, align(16)) if needed to preserve layout

### Why NOT 24 or 32 bytes?
- 24 bytes: 2.67 cells/line, wastes 16 bytes per line
- 32 bytes: 2 cells/line, doubles memory bandwidth
- 16 bytes: Perfect fit, minimal cache misses

### CellContent Encoding
- Bit 31 == 0: char (Unicode scalar value)
- Bit 31 == 1: GraphemeId (pool slot in bits 0-23, width in bits 24-30)

### GraphemePool
- Reference-counted slots for memory efficiency
- Intern on first use, reuse existing ID if present
- Free list for slot reuse
- Refcount management via incref/decref

## Exit Criteria
- Unit tests pass for all types
- Scalar bits_eq is correct
- Buffer invariants enforced (bounds, scissor monotonicity, opacity in [0,1])
- No unsafe code in this phase

## Success Criteria
- [ ] `Cell` is 16 bytes and equality/compare is fast and correct.
- [ ] `Buffer` is correct-by-construction with enforced scissor/opacity invariants.
- [ ] Grapheme pooling works (no leaks, correct refcounts, stable IDs).
- [ ] Unit tests exist for every invariant (plus property tests where appropriate).

title: Phase 2: Diff + Presenter (Near-minimal ANSI)
description:
# Phase 2: Diff + Presenter (Near-minimal ANSI)

## Purpose
Implement the diff engine and ANSI presenter that transform buffer changes into minimal terminal output. This is where the 'zero-flicker' promise is delivered.

## Components

### BufferDiff
- Compute diff between old and new buffers
- Row-major scan for cache efficiency
- Output as list of changed positions
- Convert to ChangeRuns for efficient emission

### ChangeRun
- Contiguous run of changed cells on a single row
- Allows single cursor move per run instead of per-cell

### Presenter (State-Tracked ANSI Writer)
- Tracks current style, link, cursor position
- Only emits changes from tracked state
- Uses BufWriter with 64KB buffer
- Supports synchronized output (DEC mode 2026)

## Key Decisions (from ADRs)

### Style Emission Strategy
- v1 default: Reset+apply (SGR 0 then re-apply)
- Simple and correct, though more bytes
- Incremental/hybrid behind feature flag until benchmarks justify

### Synchronized Output
- Use CSI ? 2026 h/l when available
- Reduces flicker by batching updates
- Must work without it (graceful degradation)

### Run Grouping
- Emit changes in row-major runs
- Single cursor move per run
- Sequential character emission within runs (cursor advances naturally)

## Exit Criteria
- Single buffered write per frame achieved
- Run grouping works correctly
- Style state cannot leak across runs (terminal-model tests)
- Links (OSC 8) cannot remain open after present/exit

## Success Criteria
- [ ] BufferDiff is correct and fast (row-major; scratch reuse; property tests where possible).
- [ ] Presenter emits correct ANSI (terminal-model validated) and never leaves dangling state (SGR/link).
- [ ] Bytes emitted for small changes are O(changes), not O(screen), and are tracked in benches.

title: Phase 3: Input System
description:
# Phase 3: Input System

## Purpose
Implement robust input parsing that handles terminal input sequences while protecting against DoS attacks.

## Event Types
- Key(KeyEvent): code, modifiers, kind (Press/Repeat/Release)
- Mouse(MouseEvent): kind, x, y, modifiers
- Resize { width, height }
- Paste(PasteEvent): text, bracketed flag
- Focus(bool): gained/lost

## Parser State Machine
States: Ground, Escape, Csi, CsiParam, Osc, Dcs, Ss3

### DoS Protection (CRITICAL)
- max_csi_len: 256 bytes (prevents CSI bomb)
- max_osc_len: 4096 bytes
- max_dcs_len: 4096 bytes
- max_paste_len: 1MB (configurable)
- Parser must remain linear time for worst-case inputs
- No panics on malformed sequences

## Protocols to Support
1. Standard ASCII + UTF-8
2. CSI sequences (arrows, function keys, modifiers)
3. SS3 sequences (alternate function keys)
4. SGR mouse protocol (1006) for precise coordinates
5. Bracketed paste mode (200~/201~)
6. Focus events (CSI I / CSI O)
7. Optional: Kitty keyboard protocol (feature-gated)

## Event Coalescing (Recommended)
- Mouse move: keep latest position per frame
- Resize: keep latest size per tick
- Key repeat: optionally surface KeyEventKind::Repeat if kitty protocol enabled

## Exit Criteria
- Parser passes fuzzing with random byte streams
- Deterministic tests for all key/mouse/paste/resize sequences
- Hard bounds on sequence lengths enforced
- No panics on any input

## Success Criteria
- [ ] All supported protocols decode into canonical Events (lossless for supported sequences).
- [ ] Hard caps prevent unbounded memory/time (DoS resistance).
- [ ] Fuzzing runs continuously in CI (or as a separate job) and remains green.
- [ ] PTY tests prove bracketed paste/mouse/focus modes are enabled/disabled correctly via RAII.

title: Implement InputParser state machine
description:
# Implement InputParser state machine

## Objective
Implement robust terminal input parsing with DoS protection.

## Parser States
enum ParserState {
    Ground,    // Normal character input
    Escape,    // After ESC
    Csi,       // After ESC [
    CsiParam,  // Collecting CSI parameters
    Osc,       // After ESC ]
    Dcs,       // After ESC P
    Ss3,       // After ESC O
}

## Transitions
Ground:
  ESC (0x1B) -> Escape
  0x00 -> Key(Null, Ctrl)
  0x01-0x1A -> Key(Ctrl+A..Z)
  0x7F -> Key(Backspace)
  0x80+ -> UTF-8 sequence
  other -> Key(Char)

Escape:
  [ -> Csi
  O -> Ss3
  ] -> Osc
  P -> Dcs
  other -> Key(Alt+char) + Ground

Csi:
  0-9;:<=>? -> CsiParam
  A-Za-z~ -> parse + Ground

CsiParam:
  0-9;: -> stay
  A-Za-z~Mm -> parse + Ground

Ss3:
  A-S -> function key + Ground

Osc:
  BEL (0x07) -> complete + Ground
  ESC \\ -> complete + Ground

## DoS Protection Limits
const MAX_CSI_LEN: usize = 256;   // Prevent CSI bomb
const MAX_OSC_LEN: usize = 4096;
const MAX_DCS_LEN: usize = 4096;
const MAX_PASTE_LEN: usize = 1024 * 1024;  // 1MB

If limit exceeded: abandon sequence, return to Ground.

## Special Sequences

### Bracketed Paste
CSI 200 ~ -> start paste mode
CSI 201 ~ -> end paste mode, emit Paste event

### Focus Events
CSI I -> Focus(true)
CSI O -> Focus(false)

### SGR Mouse (1006)
CSI < params M -> mouse down
CSI < params m -> mouse up
params: button ; x ; y

### Arrow Keys
CSI A -> Up
CSI B -> Down
CSI C -> Right
CSI D -> Left

### Function Keys
Ss3 P -> F1
Ss3 Q -> F2
etc.

CSI 15 ~ -> F5
CSI 17 ~ -> F6
etc.

## Implementation
pub struct InputParser {
    state: ParserState,
    buffer: Vec<u8>,
    paste_buffer: Vec<u8>,
    in_paste: bool,
    // Limits
    max_csi_len: usize,
    max_osc_len: usize,
    max_paste_len: usize,
}

impl InputParser {
    pub fn new() -> Self { ... }

    pub fn parse(&mut self, input: &[u8]) -> Vec<Event> {
        let mut events = Vec::new();
        for &byte in input {
            if let Some(event) = self.process_byte(byte) {
                events.push(event);
            }
        }
        events
    }
}

## Tests Required
- [ ] ASCII characters parsed correctly
- [ ] Arrow keys produce correct events
- [ ] Function keys F1-F12
- [ ] Modifiers (Ctrl, Alt, Shift)
- [ ] Mouse events decoded correctly
- [ ] Bracketed paste collected
- [ ] Focus events detected
- [ ] DoS limits enforced
- [ ] Invalid sequences don't panic

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All tests pass
- [ ] Fuzz testing passes
- [ ] No panics on any input
- [ ] Linear time complexity
close_reason: InputParser state machine fully implemented with 14 passing tests. DoS protection, UTF-8, CSI, SS3, OSC sequences, mouse SGR, bracketed paste, focus events all working.

title: Phase 4: Styling (Split Responsibilities)
description:
# Phase 4: Styling (Split Responsibilities)

## Purpose
Implement a style system that separates concerns: renderer-facing CellStyle is tiny and fast, while higher-level style (theme/semantic colors) resolves into CellStyle before drawing.

## Architecture Decision
Style is split by responsibility:
- CellStyle: tiny, renderer-facing (packed fg/bg/attrs/link-id)
- FullStyle: higher-level with all properties + explicit tracking via bitflags
- Theme: semantic color slots + presets

## Components

### StyleFlags (8 bits)
BOLD, DIM, ITALIC, UNDERLINE, BLINK, REVERSE, STRIKETHROUGH, HIDDEN

### Props Bitflags (explicit property tracking)
Tracks which properties are explicitly set for proper inheritance.
Unset properties inherit from parent style.

### Color System
- AdaptiveColor: can resolve differently for light/dark themes
- ColorProfile detection: Ascii, Ansi (16), Ansi256 (256), TrueColor (24-bit)
- Color downgrade: TrueColor -> 256 -> 16 -> ASCII
- NO_COLOR environment variable respected

### Border System
- Presets: Rounded, Square, Double, Heavy, Ascii, Hidden
- Custom borders supported
- All corner and edge characters defined

### Markup Parser (Optional Layer)
- Regex-based parser for Rich-style markup: [bold red]text[/]
- Escape sequences: \[ becomes literal [
- Style stack for proper nesting
- Feature-gated, not part of kernel

## Exit Criteria
- Deterministic style merge with explicit masks
- Theme resolution documented and tested
- Markup parsing correct under tests (feature-gated)
- Color downgrade works for all profile levels

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Style merge semantics are deterministic and documented (no hidden precedence).
- [ ] Color downgrade is correct and tested across profiles.
- [ ] Border presets are defined and used consistently by widgets.
- [ ] Markup parsing is optional and cannot destabilize the kernel.
close_reason: Fully implemented: Style with explicit flags, ColorProfile with downgrade pipeline (TrueColor→256→16→Mono), ColorCache, StyleSheet, Theme with light/dark, border presets in ftui-style crate. Markup feature-gated.

# Phase 5: Layout + Components (Widgets Ring)

## Purpose
Implement the widget layer that builds on kernel primitives. Widgets are ring-2 concepts - they depend on the kernel but the kernel does not depend on them.

## Renderable Trait
The core abstraction for components:
- measure(&self, ctx: &RenderContext) -> Measurement / TextMeasurement
- render(&self, ctx: &RenderContext, rect: Rect, buffer: &mut Buffer)

## Measurement Protocol
- minimum: tightest compression width
- maximum: ideal unconstrained width
- union(): for side-by-side layout (max of both)
- stack(): for vertical stacking (sum of both)

## v1 Essential Widgets (Agent Harness Needs)

### Viewport / Log Viewer
- Scrollable text area for streaming logs
- Essential for agent harness UIs

### Panel
- Bordered container with optional title
- Border presets: Rounded, Square, Double, Heavy, Ascii, Hidden
- Title alignment: Left, Center, Right

### Spinner
- Animated progress indicator
- Styles: Dots, Line, Braille, Bounce, Custom
- Frame advancement via tick()

### Progress Bar
- Value 0.0-1.0 with optional percentage display

### Text Input / Prompt

- Cursor management (selection/history can be future)

### Status Line

- Hit testing works where applicable

# Phase 6: Runtime + Agent Harness Reference App

## Purpose
Implement the optional-but-recommended Bubbletea/Elm-style runtime and build a reference agent harness app that proves the architecture works for its primary use case.

## Runtime Model (Bubbletea/Elm Lineage)

### Model Trait
- init() -> Cmd: initialization commands
- update(msg) -> Cmd: state transitions
- view(&self, frame: &mut Frame): render current state

### Cmd Enum
- None: no-op
- Quit: exit application
- Batch(Vec<Cmd>): parallel commands
- Sequence(Vec<Cmd>): sequential commands
- Msg(M): send message to self
- Tick(Duration): schedule tick
- Async integration (feature-gated): threadpool or tokio

### Program Responsibilities
- Own terminal lifecycle (raw mode, mouse, paste, focus, alt screen)
- Poll input -> Event -> Message
- Run update loop, schedule ticks/commands
- Render frames only when dirty
- Enforce screen mode policy (Inline/AltScreen)
- FPS cap and frame coalescing

## Deterministic Simulator (Stop regressions forever)
ProgramSimulator that:
- Injects sequence of Events/Messages
- Captures produced Frames
- Enables snapshot tests for widgets and full apps
- Runs without real terminal (no flakiness)

## Agent Harness Reference App
The design forcing function - not 'just an example':
- Inline scrollback log stream + UI region
- Tool indicators, status line, input area
- Streaming render updates
- No flicker, no corruption
- Survives resize
- Exits cleanly on panic

## What 'Agent-Ergonomic' Means in Practice
- Hello world harness in <200 LOC
- Tool output streaming is one function call
- Pinned bottom UI is one config option
- Temporary full-screen modal supported without rewriting app

## Exit Criteria
- Harness demo passes PTY tests
- Inline mode stable under sustained output
- Simulator enables deterministic testing

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Runtime enables the "pit of success" (easy inline harness with strong defaults).
- [ ] One-writer routing is practical (LogSink + PTY capture paths exist).
- [ ] Sanitization is enforced by default for untrusted output.
- [ ] Simulator produces stable snapshots and prevents regressions.

description:
# Implement LogSink for in-process output routing

## Background
Plan 0.9.4 and ADR-005 call out the need for in-process log routing so application code and libraries can write output without violating the one-writer rule.

In real harnesses, we want:
- a `Write` implementation (or similar) that forwards to `TerminalWriter::write_log`
- sanitization by default (ADR-006)
- newline-aware behavior (avoid breaking prompt/UI)

## Deliverable
Provide a type like:
- `LogSink` implementing `std::io::Write`
- plus an ergonomic constructor from `TerminalWriter` / `TerminalSession`

## Behavior
- Buffers partial lines until newline (or flush)
- On newline:
  - forward the complete line through `TerminalWriter::write_log`
  - trigger any required UI redraw coordination
- Applies sanitizer by default

## Tests
- Unit tests:
  - partial writes are buffered
  - newline flushes
  - explicit flush flushes
  - sanitizer applied
- Integration tests:
  - interleave log writes and UI presents and assert UI remains stable (terminal-model + PTY)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] LogSink exists and is documented as the preferred pattern for in-process output.
- [ ] Line buffering + flush semantics are correct.
- [ ] Sanitization is enforced by default.
- [ ] No deadlocks / re-entrancy issues when used from multiple producers (single-writer enforcement preserved).
close_reason: LogSink already implemented in log_sink.rs with tests for line buffering, flushing, and sanitization

title: Implement PTY capture for subprocess output (one-writer routing)
description:
# Implement PTY capture for subprocess output (one-writer routing)

## Background
Plan 0.9.4 and ADR-005: For agent harness realism, the most robust way to capture tool subprocess output is to spawn under a PTY and route output through ftui's writer.

PTY capture helps enforce the one-writer rule because:
- subprocess output cannot directly write to the user's terminal
- ftui controls how output is displayed (sanitize, chunking, redraw)

## Scope
Feature-gated PTY capture utilities usable by `ftui-harness`:
- spawn child process attached to PTY
- read PTY output asynchronously
- forward output through `TerminalWriter::write_log` (sanitized by default)

## Design notes
- This is *not* the same as `ftui-pty` test harness crate.
  - `ftui-pty` is test-only.
  - This task is runtime capture functionality (likely in `ftui-extras` or `ftui-harness`).
- Handle:
  - stdout/stderr merge semantics (PTY typically merges)
  - exit status propagation
  - backpressure / chunking to avoid UI starvation

## Tests
- Integration tests (PTY):
  - run a small child process that prints mixed output + escape sequences
  - assert sanitizer prevents terminal mutation
  - assert UI redraw remains stable during capture

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Feature-gated PTY capture API exists.
- [ ] Output is routed through TerminalWriter/LogSink (no direct terminal writes).
- [ ] Sanitization is applied by default.
- [ ] Harness demo uses this path for tool execution.
close_reason: Implemented PTY capture utility + harness helper

title: Optional: stdio capture/forwarding for accidental println! (best-effort)
description:
# Optional: stdio capture/forwarding for accidental println! (best-effort)

## Background
ADR-005 mentions an optional pattern: capturing stdout/stderr in-process to reduce the chance that third-party libs corrupt inline mode by writing directly.

This is inherently best-effort and platform-sensitive, so it must be feature-gated and clearly documented.

## Scope
- Feature-gated utility to capture and forward selected streams through `TerminalWriter::write_log`.
- Explicitly not a hard guarantee (some output may still escape capture).

## Design constraints
- Must not deadlock.
- Must not break normal non-ftui stdout usage.
- Must be easy to disable.

## Tests
- Integration tests where feasible (may be limited in CI environments).
- At minimum, unit tests around forwarding/buffering behavior.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Feature-gated capture utility exists.
- [ ] Documentation clearly explains limitations and when to use PTY capture instead.

title: Migrate input widgets with cursor control (Category C)
description:
## Scope

Migrate Category C widgets - input widgets that need cursor positioning.

## Frame Features Used

- `frame.cursor_position` - Set where the cursor should appear
- `frame.cursor_visible` - Control cursor visibility

## Migration Pattern

1. Change signature to use Frame
2. Set cursor position for text inputs:
   ```rust
   fn render(&self, area: Rect, frame: &mut Frame) {
       let buf = &mut frame.buffer;
       
       // ... draw the input widget ...
       
       // Position cursor at current input position
       if self.focused {
           let cursor_x = area.x + self.cursor_offset as u16;
           let cursor_y = area.y;
           frame.cursor_position = Some((cursor_x, cursor_y));
           frame.cursor_visible = true;
       }
   }
   ```

## Widgets Expected in This Category

Based on functionality (to be confirmed by audit):
- TextInput
- MultilineInput (if exists)
- SearchBox (if exists)
- Any editable text field

## Critical Considerations

1. **Focus state**: Only set cursor when widget is focused
2. **Cursor position math**: Must account for:
   - Area offset (area.x, area.y)
   - Text scroll offset
   - Unicode character widths
3. **Cursor visibility**: May need to hide cursor for password fields or inactive states

## Important

This is the most critical category - broken cursor positioning makes inputs unusable.
Test thoroughly with real terminal interaction.

## Verification

- `cargo check -p ftui-widgets` must pass
- All existing tests must pass
- Manual verification of cursor behavior in terminal
close_reason: Added frame cursor position support to TextInput. After rendering, the widget now calls frame.set_cursor() to position the hardware/terminal cursor at the text input position. This is important for accessibility and IME input. Added 2 tests. All 35 input tests pass.

title: Demo Showcase: Action Timeline / Event Stream Viewer
description:
## Background

FrankenTUI is intentionally "kernel-like": deterministic rendering, explicit diffs, and a disciplined runtime loop. That makes it uniquely suited to *teach itself*.

This screen is an observability + pedagogy tool:
- show what the runtime is doing (messages, commands, subscriptions)
- show what the renderer is doing (diff size, ANSI bytes, frame timings)
- make fallbacks visible (capabilities, degradation decisions)

Done right, this becomes a jaw-dropping "X-ray view" of the engine.

## UX / Core Interactions

- Live scrollable timeline of events.
  - newest at bottom (with follow mode)
  - pause/follow toggle
- Filter bar:
  - by component (core/runtime/render/widgets)
  - by severity
  - by event type (input, cmd, subscription, render, present)
- Detail pane:
  - selecting an event shows structured fields and (when available) the reasoning ledger.

Suggested keybindings:
- F: toggle follow
- /: filter/search events
- Enter: toggle expanded detail
- Ctrl+T: theme cycle (coherent with the rest of the showcase)

## Architecture Notes

- Event source:
  - Integrate with ftui-runtime and/or tracing spans.
  - Prefer structured events (typed) over ad-hoc strings.

- Storage:
  - Keep an in-memory ring buffer for recent events.
  - Optional: record to JSONL for replay in bd-3sa7 (time travel).

- Rendering:
  - Use theme::intent/status styles for severity.
  - Keep allocations bounded (ring buffer + virtualization).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Timeline updates live during normal demo usage (inputs, commands, renders).
- Filtering is responsive and deterministic.
- Selecting an event shows structured fields (not just a formatted string).
- Provides at least one "galaxy brain" style card for a non-trivial decision (e.g., a fallback), showing:
  - the rule/evidence
  - the chosen action
  - a one-line intuition

Additionally (project-wide standards):
- Alien Artifact: define invariants + failure modes; if heuristics exist, specify an explainable decision rule (evidence ledger / Bayes factors where applicable)
- Extreme Optimization: baseline -> profile -> opportunity matrix; for each perf change include an isomorphism proof + golden output checksums
- Unit tests: happy path + edge cases + regression fixtures; add property tests for core invariants where applicable
- E2E: scripts with verbose JSONL logging (env, capabilities, timings, seed, checksums) + deterministic mode
- Baseline: record p50/p95/p99 with `hyperfine` and store command lines + raw outputs
- Profile: capture CPU flamegraph and (if relevant) allocation profile; include top-5 hotspots + opportunity matrix scores
- Regression gate: add a microbench/perf test with a documented budget and a JSONL perf log schema

## Alien Artifact Upgrades (Concrete)

- Sketch-based aggregation (bd-11ck.7):
  - summarize high-volume event types without losing correctness for the full stream
  - define error budgets and surface them in the UI
- Change-point alerts:
  - detect regime shifts (frame time spikes, diff byte spikes) and annotate the timeline
- Threshold calibration (bd-1rzr):
  - use conformal/e-process methods so alerts remain valid under optional stopping

## Extreme Optimization

- Keep the timeline view overhead small:
  - event ingestion should be O(1)
  - rendering should be virtualized and incremental
  - budgets measured and enforced (bd-11ck.2)

title: e2e/pty_run: ensure controlling TTY + faster drain/optional capture for high-output TUIs
description:
Problem
- `tests/e2e/lib/pty.sh` `pty_run` currently spawns the child via `subprocess.Popen(... start_new_session=True ...)` with inherited slave stdio. In some cases (notably `ftui-demo-showcase --vfx-harness`), the child fails with `os error 6 (ENXIO)` when opening `/dev/tty`, implying it has no controlling TTY.
- When capturing high-throughput ANSI output, the current reader loop (`read_poll` + 4k chunks) can backpressure the PTY and inflate `present_ms_*`, polluting perf measurements (root cause for bd-t153k).

Scope
- Fix `pty_run` so the child process reliably has a controlling TTY bound to the slave PTY (so `/dev/tty` works).
- Improve drain performance (drain-until-EAGAIN, larger reads) and add an opt-in mode to *discard* capture while still draining (to avoid perf backpressure).
- Default behavior must remain unchanged for existing e2e scripts unless the opt-in env var is set.

Acceptance Criteria
1) `pty_run` can run `ftui-demo-showcase --vfx-harness --vfx-perf` without `/dev/tty` ENXIO failures.
2) New opt-in env (e.g. `PTY_CAPTURE_MODE=none` or `PTY_CAPTURE_MAX_BYTES`) prevents perf backpressure while still draining output.
3) Existing e2e scripts using `pty_run` continue to pass.

Validation
- Run at least one existing e2e script that uses `pty_run` (or a representative `pty_run` invocation) and confirm exit 0.
- Add/extend a minimal deterministic check path proving `/dev/tty` is openable inside the child session.
close_reason: Completed (pty_run controlling TTY + drain-only capture + /dev/tty E2E check landed)

- incremental redraw without flicker

This screen exists to prove FrankenTUI can support *real* interactive editing primitives (ftui-text + widgets) with deterministic rendering, strong invariants, and performance that scales.

## UX / Demo Flow

- Main pane: multi-line editor with line numbers, selection highlights, and a visible caret.
- Secondary pane: search/replace UI (query input, match count, next/prev match).
- Status bar: cursor position (line/col), selection length, mode, and performance counters (optional).

Suggested keybindings (exact mapping can be adjusted to project conventions):
- Arrow keys / Home / End: navigation
- Shift+Arrow: selection
- Ctrl+F: focus search
- Enter: next match
- Ctrl+H: toggle replace UI
- Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y: undo/redo (ties into bd-1nac)

The goal is to feel "surprisingly close to a real editor" while still being a demo.

## Architecture Notes

- Data model: use ftui-text rope/editor types as the single source of truth for content.
- Rendering:
  - Use theme-aware styles from ftui-extras::theme (syntax::* and alpha::* where appropriate).
  - Avoid per-frame allocations for layout/render of large buffers.
- Search:
  - Provide a fast path for ASCII queries.
  - Ensure determinism and stable tie-breaking for match ordering.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Editor supports:
  - multi-line input + deletion
  - selection
  - search with next/prev match
  - replace (single + replace-all) with a clear confirmation step
- Rendering is deterministic under fixed inputs and terminal size.
- The UI remains usable in inline mode (no scrollback corruption).

Additionally (project-wide standards):

## Alien Artifact Upgrades (Concrete)

  - add property tests for round-trip edits and cursor movement
- Search/replace optimization (bd-12o8.8):

## Extreme Optimization

- Define perf targets:
  - large buffer navigation remains sub-millisecond per keypress at 80x24

title: Responsive Layout Breakpoints System
description:
## Background

Terminals vary wildly in size:
- Phone SSH client: 40x20
- Standard terminal: 80x24
- Modern laptop: 120x40
- 4K monitor: 200x60+

Currently, widgets either overflow or waste space. Dashboard could show 1 column on small, 3 columns on large.

## Solution: Responsive Layout System

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum Breakpoint {
    XSmall,  // < 60 cols
    Small,   // 60-79 cols
    Medium,  // 80-119 cols
    Large,   // 120-159 cols
    XLarge,  // 160+ cols
}

impl Breakpoint {
    pub fn from_width(width: u16) -> Self {
        match width {
            0..60 => Self::XSmall,
            60..80 => Self::Small,
            80..120 => Self::Medium,
            120..160 => Self::Large,
            _ => Self::XLarge,
        }
    }
    
    pub fn is_at_least(&self, other: Self) -> bool;
    pub fn is_at_most(&self, other: Self) -> bool;
}

/// Responsive value that changes with breakpoint
pub struct Responsive<T> {
    xsmall: T,
    small: Option<T>,
    medium: Option<T>,
    large: Option<T>,
    xlarge: Option<T>,
}

impl<T: Clone> Responsive<T> {
    pub fn get(&self, bp: Breakpoint) -> &T;
}

// Usage
let columns = Responsive::new(1)  // XSmall: 1 column
    .medium(2)                     // Medium: 2 columns
    .large(3);                     // Large: 3 columns

let layout = ResponsiveLayout::new()
    .xsmall(|area| Layout::vertical([...]))
    .medium(|area| Layout::horizontal([...]));
```

## Integration with Layout Crate

```rust
// In ftui-layout
pub struct Layout {
    // ... existing fields
    responsive: Option<Box<dyn Fn(Breakpoint, Rect) -> Layout>>,
}

impl Layout {
    pub fn responsive<F>(f: F) -> Self
    where
        F: Fn(Breakpoint, Rect) -> Layout + 'static;
}
```

## Benefits

- Optimal UX on any terminal size
- CSS-like mental model
- Progressive enhancement

## Files to Create

- crates/ftui-layout/src/responsive.rs
- crates/ftui-layout/src/breakpoint.rs

## Success Criteria
- Epic delivers a cohesive user-visible capability: Responsive Layout Breakpoints System
- Child tasks are not just implemented; each has unit tests + E2E scripts with verbose JSONL logs and deterministic fixtures
- Graceful degradation tiers are specified (capabilities, fallbacks, safety) and validated in tests
- Formal invariants documented + enforced via property tests; any dynamic decisions have an evidence ledger and debug UI


## Alien Artifact Upgrades
- Model the core decision(s) with explicit state, priors/assumptions, and invariants; write down failure modes as first-class artifacts.
- Explainability: add an evidence ledger for any non-trivial decision (why this branch, why this fallback). Prefer Bayes factors / log-likelihood contributions over ad-hoc scoring.
- Guarantees: where prediction/thresholding exists, prefer distribution-free calibration (conformal prediction) or anytime-valid testing (e-process) so we can stop early without invalid inference.
- Graceful degradation: define capability tiers + deterministic fallbacks; never fail closed without a traceable reason.
- Layout: formulate constraints explicitly; consider LP/dual sensitivity for responsive variants; enforce stable tie-breaking for determinism.


## Extreme Optimization
- Baseline first: capture p50/p95/p99 for relevant command(s) with `hyperfine` (store raw output).
- Profile next: CPU flamegraph + allocation profile; identify top-5 hotspots.
- Opportunity matrix: implement only Score ≥ 2.0 (Impact×Confidence/Effort).
- Isomorphism proof per change: ordering, tie-breaking, RNG seeds, and golden checksums must match.
- Regression gates: add microbench + budgets; failures must print actionable deltas and include log artifacts.


## Testing Plan
- Unit tests: happy path + edge cases + regression fixtures.
- Property tests: invariants (idempotence, monotonicity, determinism) where applicable.
- Fuzz tests: parsers/state machines and any input-facing logic.
- Determinism: fixed seeds/time-freeze; snapshot fixtures must be stable.
- Metamorphic tests: shrink/grow, reorder non-semantic inputs, and ensure invariants still hold.

- scheduling policies that are explainable and testable

The point is not "toy concurrency"; it is to prove the runtime + UI can represent and control a realistic workload.

## UX / Core Interactions

- A table/list of jobs with:
  - name
  - state (queued/running/succeeded/failed/canceled)
  - progress
  - runtime
  - priority
- Controls:
  - spawn job
  - cancel selected
  - cancel all
  - change scheduler mode

Suggested keybindings:
- N: spawn a new job
- C: cancel selected job
- S: cycle scheduler policy
- R: retry failed job

## Architecture Notes

- Determinism is mandatory for tests:
  - jobs should be driven by a deterministic clock/stepper in test mode
  - avoid wall-clock coupling in core scheduling logic

- Scheduling policies (bd-13pq.7):
  - implement as pure functions over job state + metrics
  - explicitly define objective (latency, fairness, throughput)
  - stable tie-breaking

- Cancellation (bd-13pq.8):
  - model cancellation as a state transition with audit events
  - ensure no resource leaks

## Acceptance Criteria

- Jobs progress and complete with visible updates.
- Cancellation is immediate and leaves the system consistent.
- Scheduler policies are user-visible and explainable (why this job ran next).

Additionally (project-wide standards):
- Alien Artifact: define invariants + failure modes; if heuristics exist, specify an explainable decision rule (evidence ledger / Bayes factors where applicable)
- Extreme Optimization: baseline -> profile -> opportunity matrix; for each perf change include an isomorphism proof + golden output checksums
- Unit tests: happy path + edge cases + regression fixtures; add property tests for core invariants where applicable
- E2E: scripts with verbose JSONL logging (env, capabilities, timings, seed, checksums) + deterministic mode

## Alien Artifact Upgrades (Concrete)

- Queueing theory scheduler (bd-13pq.7):
  - define a small model (e.g., weighted fair scheduling vs shortest-remaining-time)
  - provide a comparison harness with deterministic traces
- Hazard-based cancellation (bd-13pq.8):
  - treat "should we cancel?" as expected-loss minimization with explicit costs
  - document assumptions and emit an evidence ledger entry when a policy triggers

## Extreme Optimization

- Budget the per-tick update overhead.
- Provide a stress test with many jobs and verify the UI remains responsive.
