title: task(galaxy-brain): Implement drift-triggered fallback visualization
description:
## Summary

Visualize the automatic fallback mechanism when the Bayesian diff strategy selector detects regime drift. Show the confidence dropping, the fallback trigger point, and the transition to the deterministic safety policy. Includes live posterior sparkline showing posterior probability evolution over last N frames for each decision domain.

## Detail

### Live Posterior Sparkline
Real-time sparkline showing posterior probability evolution over last N frames for each decision domain. Color-coded: green=confident, yellow=uncertain, red=fallback zone. Click to expand into full decision card.

### Drift Visualization Flow
1. Normal operation: posterior is concentrated, confidence is high (green)
2. Drift onset: anomalous observations arrive, posterior broadens (yellow)
3. Confidence threshold: confidence drops below 0.7, border turns red
4. Fallback trigger: automatic switch to deterministic policy, flash animation
5. Recovery: new observations stabilize posterior, return to normal (green fade-in)

### Visual Elements
- Confidence sparkline: last 60 frames of confidence values
- Drift indicator: vertical line on sparkline at fallback trigger point
- Regime banner: current regime displayed prominently during transition
- Strategy transition: animated swap from Bayesian -> deterministic and back
- Evidence burst: rapid log entries during drift shown as accelerated scroll

### Interactive Drift Injection
- Button/hotkey to inject anomalous observations (simulated scroll burst, resize, etc.)
- Slider to control drift intensity (0 = no drift, 1 = maximum anomaly)
- Timeline scrubber to replay past drift events from EvidenceLedger

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Live posterior sparkline renders per-domain color-coded probability evolution
2. Drift visualization correctly shows confidence decline and recovery
3. Fallback trigger is visually prominent (animation, color change)
4. Interactive drift injection works with configurable intensity
5. Timeline scrubber replays past events accurately
6. 60fps maintained during drift visualization (no ironic frame drops during perf demo)
7. Golden frame checksums for drift sequence checkpoints
8. Click-to-expand from sparkline to full decision card
close_reason: done

title: task(galaxy-brain): Create FrankenLab scenario file for demo
description:
## Summary

Create a FrankenLab scenario file that scripts the entire galaxy-brain transparency demo for automated CI execution. The scenario defines the input sequence, checkpoint frames, and expected golden frame hashes.

## Detail

FrankenLab scenario structure:
```toml
[scenario]
name = "galaxy-brain-transparency-demo"
description = "Demonstrates Bayesian diff strategy transparency with drift injection"
terminal_size = { width = 120, height = 40 }
duration_frames = 600  # 10 seconds at 60fps

[[checkpoints]]
frame = 0
description = "Initial state: L0 disclosure, stable regime"
golden_hash = "..."

[[checkpoints]]
frame = 60
description = "Expand to L1: posterior bars visible"
golden_hash = "..."

[[events]]
frame = 0
type = "keypress"
key = "Enter"  # Open demo

[[events]]
frame = 30
type = "keypress"
key = "Right"  # Expand to L1

[[events]]
frame = 120
type = "inject_drift"
intensity = 0.8  # Trigger drift

# ... etc.
```

Scenario phases:
1. Frames 0-60: Show L0, expand to L1
2. Frames 60-120: Expand to L2, show loss matrix
3. Frames 120-240: Inject drift, watch confidence decline, fallback trigger
4. Frames 240-360: Recovery, posterior re-concentrates
5. Frames 360-480: Expand to L3, show full evidence
6. Frames 480-600: Return to L0, final state verification

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Scenario file defines complete demo sequence
2. All checkpoints have golden frame hashes
3. CI runs scenario headlessly and verifies all checkpoints
4. Scenario completes in <30 seconds on CI runner
5. Failure output shows which checkpoint failed with visual diff
6. Scenario can be run interactively for manual demo

title: Focus Graph Data Structure
description:
Implement directed graph for focus navigation relationships.

## Requirements
- Nodes represent focusable widgets with unique IDs
- Edges encode navigation direction (up/down/left/right/next/prev)
- Support dynamic insertion and removal
- Cycle detection for focus trapping regions

## Proposed API

```rust
pub type FocusId = u64;

#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub enum NavDirection {
    Up, Down, Left, Right,
    Next, Prev,  // Tab order
}

pub struct FocusNode {
    pub id: FocusId,
    pub bounds: Rect,
    pub tab_index: i32,      // -1 = skip
    pub is_focusable: bool,
    pub group_id: Option<u32>,
}

pub struct FocusGraph {
    nodes: HashMap<FocusId, FocusNode>,
    edges: HashMap<(FocusId, NavDirection), FocusId>,
}

impl FocusGraph {
    pub fn insert(&mut self, node: FocusNode) -> FocusId;
    pub fn remove(&mut self, id: FocusId) -> Option<FocusNode>;
    pub fn connect(&mut self, from: FocusId, dir: NavDirection, to: FocusId);
    pub fn navigate(&self, from: FocusId, dir: NavDirection) -> Option<FocusId>;
    pub fn find_cycle(&self, start: FocusId) -> Option<Vec<FocusId>>;
}
```

- Custom adjacency list (smaller than petgraph)
- O(1) neighbor lookup via HashMap

title: epic: Predictive Screen Tick Management
description:
## Predictive Screen Tick Management for FrankenTUI

### Problem Statement

In multi-screen TUI applications built on ftui, ALL screens are ticked every frame—even screens the user isn't looking at. Each screen's tick() method typically does I/O (DB queries, file reads, lock acquisitions, network polls). With 15 screens at 10fps, this creates ~150 blocking I/O operations per second from invisible screens, causing visible stuttering and frame drops.

The immediate trigger was mcp-agent-mail-rust's `am` TUI, where the analytics screen's tick() opened a new SQLite connection, ran CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS + SELECT COUNT(*), iterated all tool metrics, and grabbed multiple locks—all happening 10x/second even when viewing the Dashboard. Multiply by 14 other screens doing similar I/O, and the main thread was spending more time on invisible work than rendering the visible screen.

### Current Stopgap (in mcp-agent-mail-rust)

A simple `INACTIVE_SCREEN_TICK_DIVISOR = 5` constant throttles inactive screens to tick every 5th frame (~500ms). This is hardcoded in the app, not in ftui. It works but is:
- Not reusable across ftui apps
- Not adaptive (fixed divisor regardless of screen importance)
- Not predictive (doesn't know which screen the user is likely to switch to next)

### Vision: Framework-Level Tick Strategy

ftui should own screen tick lifecycle decisions via a composable TickStrategy system:

1. **ActiveOnly** — Only tick the visible screen (zero background I/O)
2. **Uniform(divisor)** — All inactive screens tick at reduced rate (what am does now)
3. **ActivePlusAdjacent** — Tick visible + neighbor tabs at full rate, others throttled
4. **Predictive** — Learn screen transition patterns via Markov chain, pre-warm likely next screens at higher rates, aggressively throttle unlikely ones
5. **Custom** — User provides a function `(screen_id, tick_count, is_active) -> bool`

The Predictive strategy is the crown jewel: a lightweight Markov chain learns which screens the user tends to visit after which, and allocates tick budget proportionally. Screen A→B happens 60% of the time? B ticks at near-full rate when A is active. Screen A→C happens 2%? C barely ticks. The matrix can be persisted across sessions for cold-start accuracy.

### Benefits

- **Immediate**: Eliminate 80-98% of background I/O without user-visible staleness
- **Progressive**: Start with Uniform, graduate to Predictive as usage data accumulates
- **Reusable**: Every ftui app gets this for free—demo-showcase, am, any future app
- **Principled**: The framework owns tick decisions, not ad-hoc app code

### Architecture Notes

- TickStrategy lives in ftui-runtime alongside Program/Model
- The tick dispatch loop in program.rs consults the strategy before calling screen.tick()
- Force-tick on screen activation is always applied (wrapped in catch_unwind for error boundary safety)
- Transition data collector hooks into screen activation events
- Persistence uses a simple JSON file in the app's data directory
- The strategy is set at Program::new() time and can be changed at runtime via Cmd

### Key Design Decisions

- Strategies are composable: Predictive wraps Uniform as its fallback for cold-start
- Force-tick on activation is NOT part of the strategy—it's a runtime guarantee
- The Markov chain uses Laplace smoothing so unseen transitions still get some budget
- Temporal decay ensures the model adapts as user habits change
- Screen IDs are generic (the strategy works with any Eq+Hash+Clone type)

Framework side (ftui-runtime tick_strategy: TransitionCounter, MarkovPredictor, TickAllocation, ActiveOnly/Uniform/ActivePlusAdjacent/Predictive, persistence, tracing, debug stats, runtime integration, 170+ tests) landed in prior sessions; this session landed the real-app proof in mcp_agent_mail_rust (9c30e5f8): app-driven strategy-in-the-loop migration preserving housekeeping ownership + staleness clamps, AM_TUI_TICK_* config, robot-health tui_tick operator surface, and a 24/24 E2E suite. The original hardcoded INACTIVE_SCREEN_TICK_DIVISOR stopgap is gone; tick cadence is framework-decided, configurable, learned, persisted, and observable

title: Track A: Screen Transition Data Collection
description:
## Track A: Screen Transition Data Collection

### Purpose

Before we can predict which screen the user will visit next, we need to observe and record screen transitions. This track builds the data collection infrastructure that feeds the Markov chain prediction engine (Track B).

### What "Transition Data" Means

A transition is a pair (from_screen, to_screen) recorded each time the user switches screens. Over time, this builds a frequency matrix:

```
         Dashboard  Messages  Threads  Analytics  ...
Dashboard    -        42        18       5
Messages    30         -        25       2
Threads     12        20         -       8
Analytics    3         1          4       -
```

From this matrix, we derive transition probabilities (Track B). The collection layer doesn't interpret the data—it just counts.

### Design Constraints

- Must be generic over screen ID type (not coupled to any specific app's enum)
- Must be lightweight (incrementing a counter on screen switch, not I/O)
- Must support both session-scoped (in-memory) and cross-session (persisted) accumulation
- Must handle screen IDs that appear/disappear (lazy init, not pre-allocated matrix)
- Must be thread-safe (transition may be recorded from any context)

### Subtasks

- A.1: TransitionCounter struct (in-memory frequency matrix)
- A.2: Emit transition events from Program tick dispatch
- A.3: Session history ring buffer for recent transition sequence

title: A.1: TransitionCounter — in-memory frequency matrix
description:
## A.1: TransitionCounter — In-Memory Frequency Matrix

### What To Build

A generic `TransitionCounter<S>` struct that maintains a HashMap<(S, S), f64> counting how many times each (from, to) screen transition has occurred. This is the raw data that feeds the Markov chain (Track B).

### Location

`crates/ftui-runtime/src/tick_strategy/transition_counter.rs` (new file within new module)

### API

```rust
pub struct TransitionCounter<S: Eq + Hash + Clone> {
    counts: HashMap<(S, S), f64>,
    total_from: HashMap<S, f64>,  // row totals for fast probability computation
    total_transitions: f64,
}

impl<S: Eq + Hash + Clone> TransitionCounter<S> {
    pub fn new() -> Self;
    pub fn record(&mut self, from: S, to: S);            // increments by 1.0
    pub fn count(&self, from: &S, to: &S) -> f64;
    pub fn total_from(&self, from: &S) -> f64;
    pub fn total(&self) -> f64;
    pub fn probability(&self, from: &S, to: &S) -> f64;  // count / total_from, with Laplace smoothing
    pub fn all_targets_ranked(&self, from: &S) -> Vec<(S, f64)>;  // sorted desc by probability
    pub fn merge(&mut self, other: &TransitionCounter<S>);  // combine two counters
    pub fn decay(&mut self, factor: f64);  // multiply all counts by factor (0.0..1.0)
    pub fn screen_ids(&self) -> HashSet<S>;  // all known screen IDs
}
```

### Why f64 Counts (Not u64)

Counts must be f64 because temporal decay multiplies all counts by a factor like 0.85. With u64 counts, entries with count=1 truncate to 0 on the first decay (1 * 0.85 = 0 in integer math), causing premature pruning. With f64:
- Count 1.0 → 0.85 → 0.72 → 0.61 → ... → prune at 0.5 (after ~3 decay cycles)
- Much more gradual degradation of low-count transitions
- Floating-point arithmetic preserves relative ordering for probability computations

record() increments by 1.0. probability() divides counts normally. All operations are natural on f64.

### Key Design Details

- **Laplace smoothing**: `probability()` uses additive smoothing: `(count + alpha) / (total_from + alpha * N)` where N = number of known target screens from this source screen. This gives unseen-but-known screens a small non-zero probability. Note: truly unknown screens (never seen anywhere) aren't handled here — that's the MarkovPredictor's job (B.1).

- **Temporal decay**: `decay(0.85)` multiplies all counts by 0.85, effectively down-weighting old transitions. Entries below prune_threshold (default 0.5) after decay are removed to prevent unbounded map growth.

- **Merge**: Combines two counters additively. Used when loading persisted data on startup and merging with the current session's observations.

- **total_from cache**: Maintain a separate HashMap for row totals to avoid iterating all entries on every probability query. Update incrementally in `record()` and recompute in `merge()` / `decay()`.

### Testing

- record() increments counts correctly

title: A.3: Session history ring buffer for transition sequence
description:
## A.3: Session History Ring Buffer for Transition Sequence

### What To Build

A fixed-capacity ring buffer that stores the last N screen transitions as an ordered sequence (not just counts). This enables higher-order Markov analysis (e.g., "after visiting Dashboard→Messages→Threads, user usually goes to Search") and debugging/introspection.

### Location

`crates/ftui-runtime/src/tick_strategy/transition_history.rs`

### API

```rust
pub struct TransitionHistory<S: Clone> {
    entries: VecDeque<TransitionEntry<S>>,
    capacity: usize,
}

pub struct TransitionEntry<S: Clone> {
    pub from: S,
    pub to: S,
    pub timestamp: Instant,
    pub tick_count: u64,
}

impl<S: Clone> TransitionHistory<S> {
    pub fn with_capacity(n: usize) -> Self;
    pub fn record(&mut self, from: S, to: S, tick_count: u64);
    pub fn recent(&self, n: usize) -> &[TransitionEntry<S>];
    pub fn last_n_screens(&self, n: usize) -> Vec<S>;  // ordered sequence of most recent screens visited
    pub fn len(&self) -> usize;
    pub fn is_empty(&self) -> bool;
}
```

### Design Notes

- Default capacity: 256 transitions (enough for a full work session)
- VecDeque for O(1) push_back + automatic eviction from front
- Timestamps use std::time::Instant (not wall clock) for monotonic ordering
- This is supplementary to TransitionCounter—the counter stores aggregates, the history stores the raw sequence
- Future enhancement: higher-order Markov chains (bigram/trigram transition analysis) can read from this buffer

### Priority

P2 because this is an enhancement beyond the core Markov chain (which only needs pairwise counts from A.1). The history buffer enables:
- Debug introspection ("show me the last 20 screen switches")
- Higher-order prediction models (future work)
- Session analytics (time spent on each screen)

### Dependencies

- No hard dependencies (standalone data structure)
- Useful for B.4 (temporal weighting) but not strictly required

title: Track B: Markov Chain Prediction Engine
description:
## Track B: Markov Chain Prediction Engine

### Purpose

Transform raw transition counts (Track A) into actionable predictions: given the current screen, which screens should receive higher tick rates because the user is likely to switch to them soon?

### Why a Markov Chain?

A first-order Markov chain is the simplest model that captures the core pattern: "what screen do users go to AFTER this screen?" It requires minimal memory (NxN matrix for N screens), minimal computation (normalize row to get probabilities), and is trivially interpretable.

More sophisticated models (HMMs, neural, n-gram) are overkill: screen count is small (5-20), transitions are infrequent (user-initiated), and the primary consumer just needs a ranked list of screens with weights.

### How It Works

1. User is on screen A
2. Engine queries TransitionCounter: "given A, what's the probability of going to each other screen?"
3. Returns ranked list: [(B, 0.45), (C, 0.25), (D, 0.15), (E, 0.10), (F, 0.05)]
4. TickStrategy uses these weights to set per-screen tick rates:
   - B: tick every frame (likely next)
   - C: tick every 2nd frame
   - D: tick every 4th frame
   - E: tick every 8th frame
   - F: tick every 16th frame

### Subtasks

- B.1: MarkovPredictor struct (wraps TransitionCounter, adds prediction API)
- B.2: Tick rate allocation from probabilities (probability → divisor mapping)
- B.3: Cold-start handling (what to do before enough data is collected)
- B.4: Temporal decay integration (recent transitions weighted more)

title: B.1: MarkovPredictor — prediction API wrapping TransitionCounter
description:
## B.1: MarkovPredictor — Prediction API

### What To Build

A `MarkovPredictor<S>` that wraps a `TransitionCounter<S>` and provides a clean prediction API. This is the interface that TickStrategy::Predictive (C.5) queries to get transition probabilities.

### Location

`crates/ftui-runtime/src/tick_strategy/markov_predictor.rs`

### API

```rust
pub struct MarkovPredictor<S: Eq + Hash + Clone> {
    counter: TransitionCounter<S>,
    min_observations: u64,     // minimum transitions before predictions are trusted
    smoothing_alpha: f64,      // Laplace smoothing parameter (default 1.0)
}

pub struct ScreenPrediction<S> {
    pub screen: S,
    pub probability: f64,      // 0.0..1.0
    pub confidence: f64,       // 0.0..1.0, based on observation count
}

impl<S: Eq + Hash + Clone> MarkovPredictor<S> {
    pub fn new() -> Self;
    pub fn with_min_observations(n: u64) -> Self;
    pub fn record_transition(&mut self, from: S, to: S);
    pub fn predict(&self, current_screen: &S) -> Vec<ScreenPrediction<S>>;
    pub fn is_cold_start(&self, screen: &S) -> bool;  // fewer than min_observations from this screen
    pub fn confidence(&self, screen: &S) -> f64;       // overall confidence for predictions from this screen
    pub fn counter(&self) -> &TransitionCounter<S>;
    pub fn counter_mut(&mut self) -> &mut TransitionCounter<S>;
}
```

### Why No suggested_divisor

ScreenPrediction returns probability and confidence ONLY. The conversion from probability to tick divisor is the responsibility of TickAllocation (B.2), and is owned by the Predictive strategy (C.5). This separation of concerns means:
- B.1 is purely about prediction (probability, confidence)
- B.2 is purely about allocation (probability → divisor mapping)
- C.5 combines them: query B.1 for predictions, apply B.2 for divisors
- B.1 can be tested without B.2

### Prediction Logic

1. Query `counter.all_targets_ranked(current_screen)` for probability distribution
2. For each target, compute confidence = `min(1.0, total_from / min_observations as f64)`
3. Return sorted by probability descending

### Confidence Model

Confidence starts at 0 and grows linearly to 1.0 as observations accumulate. Before reaching min_observations (default: 20 transitions from a given screen), predictions are blended with a uniform distribution. This means:

- Cold start: all screens get equal probability (equivalent to Uniform strategy)
- Warm: predictions are fully trusted
- In between: gradual transition from uniform to predicted

Formula: `effective_prob = confidence * predicted_prob + (1 - confidence) * uniform_prob`

### Testing

- Predictions match expected probabilities after recording known transitions
- Cold-start returns near-uniform distribution
- Confidence increases with observations
- Laplace smoothing gives non-zero probability to unseen transitions
- Probabilities sum to 1.0 for any given source screen

### Dependencies

- Depends on A.1 (TransitionCounter)
- Does NOT depend on B.2 (allocation is C.5's concern)
close_reason: Implemented MarkovPredictor with prediction/confidence API, cold-start blending, 13 tests. Also fixed wasm_runner Cmd::SetTickStrategy arm.

title: B.2: Probability-to-divisor tick rate allocation
description:
## B.2: Probability-to-Divisor Tick Rate Allocation

### What To Build

A function that maps a transition probability (0.0..1.0) to a tick divisor (1..max_divisor). This is the bridge between 'how likely is the user to switch to screen X?' and 'how often should we tick screen X?'

### Location

`crates/ftui-runtime/src/tick_strategy/tick_allocation.rs`

### API

```rust
pub struct TickAllocation {
    pub max_divisor: u64,      // ceiling: least-likely screens tick at most every max_divisor frames
    pub min_divisor: u64,      // floor: most-likely screens tick at least every min_divisor frames (usually 1)
    pub curve: AllocationCurve, // how probability maps to divisor
}

pub enum AllocationCurve {
    /// Linear: divisor = max - (max - min) * probability
    Linear,
    /// Exponential: divisor = max * (1 - probability)^exponent
    /// Gives more budget to high-probability screens, sharper falloff for unlikely ones
    Exponential { exponent: f64 },
    /// Stepped: bucket probabilities into tiers, checked in descending threshold order.
    /// First matching threshold wins. E.g.:
    ///   [(0.3, 1), (0.1, 2), (0.03, 5), (0.0, 20)]
    /// means: >0.3 -> every frame, 0.1-0.3 -> every 2nd, 0.03-0.1 -> every 5th, <0.03 -> every 20th
    /// INVARIANT: thresholds must be sorted descending. Validated at construction time.
    Stepped { thresholds: Vec<(f64, u64)> },
}

impl TickAllocation {
    pub fn default() -> Self;  // Exponential { exponent: 2.0 }, max=20, min=1
    pub fn divisor_for(&self, probability: f64) -> u64;
}
```

### Stepped Threshold Ordering

Stepped thresholds are checked in order (first match wins). They MUST be sorted by threshold descending. The constructor validates this and panics on invalid ordering. Example:

```rust
AllocationCurve::Stepped {
    thresholds: vec![
        (0.30, 1),   // p > 0.30: every frame
        (0.10, 2),   // 0.10 < p <= 0.30: every 2nd frame
        (0.03, 5),   // 0.03 < p <= 0.10: every 5th frame
        (0.00, 20),  // p <= 0.03: every 20th frame (max)
    ]
}
```

### Recommended Defaults

The exponential curve with exponent=2.0 gives a good balance:

| Probability | Divisor | Tick Rate (at 10fps) |
|-------------|---------|---------------------|
| 0.50        | 1       | Every frame (100ms) |
| 0.30        | 2       | Every 200ms         |
| 0.15        | 5       | Every 500ms         |
| 0.05        | 12      | Every 1.2s          |
| 0.02        | 18      | Every 1.8s          |
| 0.01        | 20      | Every 2.0s (max)    |

### Design Rationale

- **Max divisor capped at 20** (2 seconds at 10fps): Even the least-likely screen should refresh within 2 seconds to avoid visibly stale data when the user does switch to it. Combined with force-tick-on-activation (D.3), this is a safety net, not the primary freshness mechanism.

- **Exponential over linear**: Linear distributes tick budget too evenly — a screen with 5% probability gets too many ticks relative to its likelihood. Exponential concentrates budget on high-probability screens where it matters most.

- **Stepped alternative**: For apps that want explicit control ('these 3 screens get full rate, those 5 get half, rest get slow'), the stepped curve is simpler to reason about.

### Testing

- divisor_for(1.0) returns min_divisor
- divisor_for(0.0) returns max_divisor
- divisor_for() is monotonically decreasing as probability increases
- All three curves produce valid results in [min_divisor, max_divisor]
- Default allocation matches the table above (within rounding)
- Stepped: thresholds validated at construction (panic on unsorted)
- Stepped: first matching threshold wins

### Dependencies

- No code dependencies (pure function)
- Used by C.5 (Predictive strategy owns a TickAllocation instance)
close_reason: Implemented TickAllocation with Linear, Exponential, Stepped curves. 15 tests, all passing. Monotonicity verified.

title: B.3: Cold-start handling — uniform fallback before sufficient data
description:
## B.3: Cold-Start Handling — Uniform Fallback

### What To Build

Logic within MarkovPredictor that gracefully handles the cold-start problem: when we don't have enough transition data to make meaningful predictions, fall back to a uniform probability distribution (all screens get equal predicted probability).

### The Problem

On first launch (or after clearing persisted data), the Markov chain has zero observations. Blindly using an empty model would assign uniform probabilities via Laplace smoothing alone, which works mathematically but provides no learning benefit. B.3 adds confidence-weighted blending so that as data accumulates, the model smoothly transitions from uniform to data-driven predictions.

### Solution: Confidence-Weighted Blending

```rust
fn effective_predictions(&self, current: &S) -> Vec<ScreenPrediction<S>> {
    let confidence = self.confidence(current);  // 0.0 to 1.0
    let markov_preds = self.raw_predictions(current);
    let uniform_prob = 1.0 / num_screens as f64;

    markov_preds.iter().map(|p| {
        let blended = confidence * p.probability + (1.0 - confidence) * uniform_prob;
        ScreenPrediction { screen: p.screen.clone(), probability: blended, confidence }
    }).collect()
}
```

### Confidence Thresholds

- **< 5 transitions**: Zero confidence -> pure uniform probability (all screens equal)
- **5-20 transitions**: Partial confidence -> blended (Markov signal starts contributing)
- **> 20 transitions**: Full confidence -> pure Markov probabilities

These thresholds are configurable via `MarkovPredictor::with_min_observations()`.

### Optional: Default Priors

For apps that know their screen layout, allow injecting prior probabilities:
```rust
predictor.set_prior(ScreenId::Dashboard, 0.3);
predictor.set_prior(ScreenId::Messages, 0.25);
```
These priors are used as the 'uniform' baseline instead of 1/N, giving better cold-start behavior for apps with known screen importance hierarchies. This is an optional enhancement -- vanilla uniform works fine.

### Separation of Concerns

B.3 operates ENTIRELY in probability space. It blends probabilities, not divisors. The downstream conversion from blended probabilities to tick divisors is handled by:
- B.2 (TickAllocation) defines the probability-to-divisor mapping
- C.5 (Predictive strategy) applies B.2 to B.3's blended output

This means B.3 does NOT depend on B.2.

### Testing

- Zero observations -> all screens get equal probability (1/N)
- Few observations -> predictions are heavily blended toward uniform
- Many observations -> predictions closely match raw Markov probabilities
- Confidence transitions smoothly from 0 to 1
- With priors: cold-start uses prior weights instead of 1/N uniform
- Sum of blended probabilities == 1.0 (normalization preserved)

### Dependencies

- Depends on B.1 (MarkovPredictor -- confidence-weighted blending lives inside predict())
- Does NOT depend on B.2 (probability-to-divisor is C.5's concern)

title: C.2: ActiveOnly strategy — zero background ticks
description:
## C.2: ActiveOnly Strategy

### What To Build

The simplest strategy: only the active screen gets ticked. All inactive screens are completely skipped. This is the most aggressive I/O reduction (100% background elimination) but means screens may show stale data when switched to (mitigated by force-tick-on-activation).

### Implementation

```rust
pub struct ActiveOnly;

impl TickStrategy for ActiveOnly {
    fn should_tick(&mut self, _screen_id: &str, _tick_count: u64, _active: &str) -> TickDecision {
        TickDecision::Skip  // always skip inactive screens
    }

    fn name(&self) -> &str { "ActiveOnly" }
}
```

### When To Use

- Apps with very expensive screen tick() methods (heavy DB queries, network calls)
- Apps where force-tick-on-activation provides sufficient freshness
- Battery-constrained environments
- Testing/debugging (isolate active screen behavior)

### Testing

- should_tick() always returns Skip for any screen_id and tick_count
- on_screen_transition() is a no-op (default)
- name() returns "ActiveOnly"

### Dependencies

- Depends on C.1 (TickStrategy trait)

title: Track D: ftui Runtime Integration
description:
## Track D: ftui Runtime Integration

### Purpose

Wire the TickStrategy framework into ftui's Program runtime so that tick dispatch automatically consults the configured strategy. This is where the framework changes happen—modifying program.rs and related runtime code.

### Current Architecture (pre-change)

In ftui's runtime, the Program drives the Elm architecture loop:
1. Event arrives (keyboard, mouse, tick, etc.)
2. Model::update() is called, returns Cmd
3. Cmd is dispatched (tick scheduling, mouse capture, etc.)
4. Model::view() is called to render the frame

The tick dispatch currently just calls Model::update(Tick) unconditionally. There's no concept of "screens" at the framework level—that's entirely in the Model.

### Challenge

ftui doesn't know about screens. The Model owns all screen management internally. So how does the runtime decide which screens to tick?

### Solution: ScreenTickDispatch trait

Add an optional trait that Models with multiple screens can implement:

```rust
pub trait ScreenTickDispatch {
    fn screen_ids(&self) -> Vec<String>;
    fn active_screen_id(&self) -> String;
    fn tick_screen(&mut self, screen_id: &str, tick_count: u64);
}
```

If the Model implements this trait (detected via a method on Model), the runtime uses the TickStrategy to selectively call tick_screen() instead of a monolithic update(Tick).

If the Model doesn't implement it, behavior is unchanged: the full update(Tick) is called as before.

### Subtasks

- D.1: Add TickStrategy configuration to Program builder
- D.2: Modify tick dispatch loop to consult strategy
- D.3: Force-tick on screen activation (runtime guarantee)
- D.4: ScreenTickDispatch trait definition

title: D.1: Add TickStrategy configuration to Program builder
description:
## D.1: Add TickStrategy Configuration to Program Builder

### What To Build

Extend ftui's Program (or ProgramBuilder if one exists) to accept a TickStrategy at construction time. This is how apps configure which strategy to use.

### Current API

```rust
// Current (simplified)
Program::new(model)
    .tick_interval(Duration::from_millis(100))
    .run()
```

### New API

```rust
Program::new(model)
    .tick_interval(Duration::from_millis(100))
    .tick_strategy(TickStrategyKind::Predictive {
        config: PredictiveConfig::default(),
    })
    .run()
```

### Implementation

Add a `tick_strategy: Option<Box<dyn TickStrategy + Send>>` field to Program. If None, all screens tick every frame (backwards-compatible default = current behavior).

### Storage

The TickStrategy is stored as `Option<Box<dyn TickStrategy + Send>>` in Program. It's mutable because strategies like Predictive need to update internal state (record transitions, run decay).

### Default Behavior

If no tick_strategy is configured:
- All screens tick every frame (current behavior, fully backwards compatible)
- No transition recording, no prediction, no throttling
- Zero overhead: the strategy check is a single Option::is_none() branch

### Runtime Changeable

Add `Cmd::SetTickStrategy(Box<dyn TickStrategy + Send>)` so apps can switch strategies at runtime. Use case: start with Uniform, switch to Predictive after loading persisted data.

Note: Takes `Box<dyn TickStrategy + Send>` (not TickStrategyKind) because strategies are stateful and not cloneable. The Cmd variant takes ownership of the boxed strategy.

### Shutdown Integration

When the Program exits (clean shutdown), it calls:
```rust
if let Some(strategy) = &mut self.tick_strategy {
    strategy.shutdown();
}
```

This gives strategies a chance to persist state (e.g., Predictive saves transitions).

### Testing

- Program without tick_strategy behaves identically to current behavior
- Program with tick_strategy stores and uses it correctly
- Cmd::SetTickStrategy updates the strategy at runtime
- Builder method is ergonomic and type-safe
- shutdown() is called on Program exit

### Dependencies

- Depends on C.1 (TickStrategy trait, TickStrategyKind enum)

title: D.2: Modify tick dispatch loop to consult TickStrategy
description:
## D.2: Modify Tick Dispatch Loop to Consult TickStrategy

### What To Build

The core runtime change: when a Tick event arrives and the Model implements ScreenTickDispatch, the runtime uses the TickStrategy to selectively tick screens AFTER calling update(Tick) for app-level work.

### Current Flow (program.rs)

```
Event::Tick → model.update(MailMsg::Terminal(Event::Tick)) → Cmd
  (inside update: iterate all screens, tick them all)
```

The Model's update() handler iterates all screens internally and ticks them all.

### New Flow (when ScreenTickDispatch + TickStrategy are configured)

```
Event::Tick →
  1. model.update(Tick) → Cmd           // App handles GLOBAL tick work only (clocks, timers, animations)
                                         // App must NOT iterate/tick individual screens here
  2. dispatch = model.as_screen_tick_dispatch()
  3. active = dispatch.active_screen_id()
  4. dispatch.tick_screen(active, tick_count)    // Active screen always ticks
  5. For each other screen:
     if strategy.should_tick(screen, tick_count, active) == Tick:
       dispatch.tick_screen(screen, tick_count)
  6. strategy.maintenance_tick(tick_count)
  7. Return Cmd::tick(interval) as usual
```

### CRITICAL: update(Tick) Is Still Called

The runtime DOES still call model.update(Tick). This is essential because apps do non-screen work in their tick handler: updating clocks, refreshing status bars, polling background tasks, managing timers, etc. The split is:

- **update(Tick)**: App handles global/cross-screen tick work. Does NOT iterate or tick individual screens.
- **ScreenTickDispatch**: Runtime handles per-screen tick dispatch via the strategy.

The app must be migrated to remove per-screen ticking from update(Tick) and rely on tick_screen() calls from the runtime.

### Backwards Compatibility

```rust
trait Model {
    fn as_screen_tick_dispatch(&mut self) -> Option<&mut dyn ScreenTickDispatch> { None }
}
```

If as_screen_tick_dispatch() returns None, the runtime calls model.update(Tick) as it does today (the app handles everything internally). Zero behavior change for existing apps.

If it returns Some, the runtime splits responsibility as described above.

### tick_screen() Does Not Return Cmds

ScreenTickDispatch::tick_screen() returns () because the trait is message-agnostic (doesn't know the app's Msg type). Any periodic work that needs to produce Cmds should be done in the app's update(Tick) handler, which still returns Cmd<Msg>.

### Performance

The strategy check adds at most O(N) calls to should_tick() per frame where N = number of screens. Each should_tick() is a trivial comparison (Uniform: single modulo; Predictive: HashMap lookup). Negligible compared to I/O saved.

### Testing

- Model without ScreenTickDispatch: full update(Tick) called as before, no strategy involvement
- Model with ScreenTickDispatch + ActiveOnly: update(Tick) called for global work + only active screen ticked via dispatch
- Model with ScreenTickDispatch + Uniform(5): update(Tick) called + screens tick at correct intervals
- maintenance_tick called at correct intervals
- Active screen always ticked regardless of strategy
- tick_screen() is NOT called inside update(Tick) — only the runtime calls it

### Dependencies

- Depends on C.1 (TickStrategy trait)
- Depends on D.1 (strategy stored in Program)
- Depends on D.4 (ScreenTickDispatch trait)
close_reason: Implemented per-screen tick dispatch in run_event_loop: active screen always ticks, inactive screens go through strategy.should_tick(), maintenance_tick() called. 84 tests pass.

title: D.4: ScreenTickDispatch trait for selective screen ticking
description:
## D.4: ScreenTickDispatch Trait for Selective Screen Ticking

### What To Build

A trait that Models with multiple screens implement to allow the runtime to tick screens individually instead of monolithically.

### Location

`crates/ftui-runtime/src/tick_strategy/mod.rs` (alongside TickStrategy trait)

### API

```rust
/// Implemented by Models that manage multiple screens and want
/// per-screen tick control via TickStrategy.
pub trait ScreenTickDispatch {
    /// Returns IDs of all currently registered screens.
    fn screen_ids(&self) -> Vec<String>;

    /// Returns the ID of the currently active/visible screen.
    fn active_screen_id(&self) -> String;

    /// Tick a specific screen by ID.
    fn tick_screen(&mut self, screen_id: &str, tick_count: u64);
}
```

### Why Owned Strings (Not &str)

screen_ids() and active_screen_id() return owned Strings rather than borrowed &str because:
- Screen IDs are typically derived from enum formatting (e.g. `format!("{:?}", MailScreenId::Dashboard)`) which produces temporary Strings
- Returning &str would require the Model to store pre-computed String representations, adding complexity
- The runtime clones the active_screen_id() anyway (stored in `last_active_screen: Option<String>` for transition detection)
- The overhead of String allocation is negligible (called once per tick, ~15 short strings)

### Integration with Model Trait

The Model trait gets an optional downcasting method:
```rust
pub trait Model {
    // ... existing methods ...
    fn as_screen_tick_dispatch(&mut self) -> Option<&mut dyn ScreenTickDispatch> { None }
}
```

### Runtime Behavior

The runtime calls `model.as_screen_tick_dispatch()` on each tick. If it returns Some, the runtime:
1. Calls `active_screen_id()` to determine the visible screen
2. Always ticks the active screen
3. For each inactive screen, consults the TickStrategy via `should_tick()`
4. Calls `tick_screen()` only for screens the strategy approves

If it returns None, the runtime calls `model.update(Tick)` as it does today. Fully backwards compatible.

The runtime also checks `active_screen_id()` after every update() call to detect transitions. When a transition is detected, it force-ticks the new screen (D.3) and calls `strategy.on_screen_transition()` (A.2). This is purely runtime-driven -- apps don't need to emit any Cmds for transition detection.

### Design Rationale

- **Separate trait, not on Model**: Most Models aren't multi-screen. Default None keeps existing apps unaffected.
- **Owned String screen IDs**: Avoids lifetime complexity while keeping the trait simple. See rationale above.
- **tick_screen() is fire-and-forget**: Returns (). The app handles error boundaries internally (catch_unwind). Any Cmd-producing work goes through update(Tick).

### Testing

- Model returning None: full update(Tick) behavior, unchanged
- Model returning Some: per-screen dispatch via TickStrategy
- screen_ids() returns all registered screens
- active_screen_id() matches current active
- tick_screen() panicking screen: error caught by implementation
- Unknown screen_id in tick_screen(): no-op

### Dependencies

- Depends on C.1 (TickStrategy trait)
- Blocks D.2 (tick dispatch loop needs this)
- Blocks F.1 (MailAppModel implements this)

title: Track E: Transition Data Persistence

## Track E: Transition Data Persistence

### Purpose

Save learned transition data across sessions so the Predictive strategy doesn't cold-start every time the app launches. After a few sessions, the model has enough data to make accurate predictions from the first frame.

### Why Persistence Matters

Without persistence, every app launch starts with zero observations. The cold-start handler (B.3) falls back to uniform distribution until enough transitions are recorded. This means the first 2-5 minutes of every session get no prediction benefit. With persistence, accumulated data from all previous sessions is loaded on startup.

### Subtasks

- E.1: Serialize TransitionCounter to JSON file
- E.2: Load persisted data on startup, merge with defaults
- E.3: Periodic auto-save during session

title: E.1: Serialize TransitionCounter to JSON file
description:
## E.1: Serialize TransitionCounter to JSON File

### What To Build

Serde serialization for TransitionCounter so it can be saved to and loaded from a JSON file. The file format should be human-readable for debugging.

### Location

`crates/ftui-runtime/src/tick_strategy/persistence.rs`

### File Format

```json
{
  "version": 1,
  "total_transitions": 1247,
  "last_saved": "2026-02-24T02:30:00Z",
  "transitions": [
    { "from": "Dashboard", "to": "Messages", "count": 142 },
    { "from": "Dashboard", "to": "Threads", "count": 87 },
    { "from": "Messages", "to": "Dashboard", "count": 98 },
    { "from": "Messages", "to": "Threads", "count": 115 },
    ...
  ]
}
```

### API

```rust
pub fn save_transitions<S: Eq + Hash + Clone + Serialize>(
    counter: &TransitionCounter<S>,
    path: &Path,
) -> io::Result<()>;

pub fn load_transitions<S: Eq + Hash + Clone + DeserializeOwned>(
    path: &Path,
) -> io::Result<TransitionCounter<S>>;
```

### File Location Convention

Apps provide the path. Recommended convention:
- `~/.config/<app-name>/tick_transitions.json`
- For mcp-agent-mail: `~/.mcp_agent_mail/tick_transitions.json`

### Atomic Writes

Use write-to-temp-then-rename pattern to avoid corruption on crash:
```rust
let temp = path.with_extension("json.tmp");
fs::write(&temp, json)?;
fs::rename(&temp, path)?;
```

### Testing

- Round-trip: save then load produces identical TransitionCounter
- Missing file: load returns empty counter (not an error)
- Corrupted file: load returns error (don't silently use empty data)
- Version mismatch: load returns error with message about version
- Atomic write: temp file is cleaned up on success

### Dependencies

- Depends on A.1 (TransitionCounter must derive Serialize/Deserialize)

## F.2: Configure Predictive Strategy and Remove Stopgap Code

### What To Build

Wire up the Predictive TickStrategy in mcp-agent-mail-rust's Program construction and remove all ad-hoc tick throttling code.

### Code to Remove

In tui_app.rs:
1. Delete `const INACTIVE_SCREEN_TICK_DIVISOR: u64 = 5;`
2. Delete the `active_id` / `is_background_tick` logic in the tick handler
3. Delete the manual force-tick block in `activate_screen()` — the runtime now handles this (D.3)
4. Delete the `id != active_id && !is_background_tick` continue guard
5. Remove per-screen iteration from the tick handler — the runtime does this via ScreenTickDispatch

### Code to Add

In the Program construction:
```rust
let tick_strategy = TickStrategyKind::Predictive {
    config: PredictiveConfig {
        fallback_divisor: 5,    // matches current INACTIVE_SCREEN_TICK_DIVISOR
        min_observations: 20,
        persistence_path: Some(config.storage_root().join("tick_transitions.json")),
        ..PredictiveConfig::default()
    },
};

Program::new(model)
    .tick_interval(TICK_INTERVAL)
    .tick_strategy(tick_strategy)
    .run()
```

Strategy selection is controlled by env vars (H.3):
```rust
let strategy = build_tick_strategy_from_config(&config);
Program::new(model)
    .tick_interval(TICK_INTERVAL)
    .tick_strategy(strategy)
    .run()
```

### Simplified activate_screen()

```rust
fn activate_screen(&mut self, id: MailScreenId) {
    let from = self.screen_manager.active_screen();
    if from == id { return; }
    // ... existing focus/transition logic ...
    self.screen_manager.set_active(id);
    // NO manual force-tick needed — the runtime detects the change
    // via active_screen_id() diff and force-ticks automatically (D.3)
}
```

### Simplified update(Tick) handler

```rust
MailMsg::Terminal(Event::Tick(_)) => {
    // Only handle GLOBAL tick work here:
    // - Update status bar clock
    // - Poll background tasks
    // - Refresh any cross-screen state
    // Do NOT iterate/tick individual screens — the runtime handles that
    self.update_global_tick_state();
    Cmd::none()
}
```

title: G.3: Property tests — Markov chain invariants
description:
## G.3: Property Tests — Markov Chain Invariants

### What To Build

Property-based tests (proptest/quickcheck) that verify mathematical invariants of the Markov chain and probability system.

### Invariants to Test

1. **Probability normalization**: For any screen, sum of all outgoing probabilities = 1.0 (within floating-point epsilon)

2. **Monotonicity**: If count(A→B) > count(A→C), then probability(A→B) > probability(A→C)

3. **Divisor monotonicity**: Higher probability → lower divisor (more frequent ticking)

4. **Decay idempotency**: decay(1.0) is identity (no change)

5. **Decay monotonicity**: decay(0.5) produces strictly smaller counts than decay(0.9) on the same data

6. **Merge commutativity**: merge(A, B) produces same result as merge(B, A)

7. **Merge associativity**: merge(merge(A, B), C) = merge(A, merge(B, C))

8. **Round-trip serialization**: save(load(save(counter))) = save(counter)

9. **Confidence bounds**: 0.0 <= confidence <= 1.0 for any input

10. **Divisor bounds**: min_divisor <= divisor_for(p) <= max_divisor for any 0 <= p <= 1

### Property Test Strategy

Use proptest with:
- Random screen IDs (strings of length 1-20)
- Random transition sequences (1-1000 transitions)
- Random decay factors (0.01-0.99)
- Random probability values (0.0-1.0)

### Dependencies

- Depends on A.1 (TransitionCounter)
- Depends on B.1 (MarkovPredictor)
- Depends on B.2 (TickAllocation)
- Depends on E.1 (serialization)

title: H.1: Structured tracing for tick strategy decisions
description:
## H.1: Structured Tracing for Tick Strategy Decisions

### What To Build

Add tracing spans and events to the tick strategy system so operators can see exactly what the strategy is doing via RUST_LOG or similar.

### Tracing Points

1. **Strategy initialization** (INFO):
   `tick_strategy.init: name="Predictive" fallback_divisor=5 min_observations=20`

2. **Screen transition detected** (DEBUG):
   `tick_strategy.transition: from="Dashboard" to="Messages" total_transitions=247`

3. **Divisor cache refresh** (DEBUG):
   `tick_strategy.cache_refresh: active="Messages" screens=15 predictions=[{"Dashboard": 2}, {"Threads": 3}, ...]`

4. **Tick decision summary** (TRACE, per-frame):
   `tick_strategy.frame: tick=1234 active="Messages" ticked=["Dashboard","Threads"] skipped=["Analytics","Contacts",...]`
   Note: TRACE level only -- this fires every frame and would be overwhelming at DEBUG.

5. **Decay event** (DEBUG):
   `tick_strategy.decay: factor=0.85 entries_before=45 entries_after=42 pruned=3`

6. **Persistence save** (INFO):
   `tick_strategy.save: path="/home/user/.mcp_agent_mail/tick_transitions.json" transitions=247`

7. **Persistence load** (INFO):
   `tick_strategy.load: path="..." loaded_transitions=189 confidence=0.87`

8. **Cold start detected** (INFO):
   `tick_strategy.cold_start: screen="Analytics" observations=3 min_required=20 using_fallback=true`

### Implementation

Use the `tracing` crate with structured fields. Note: since ScreenPrediction no longer has suggested_divisor (B.1 only returns probability+confidence), the divisor is computed by C.5 via TickAllocation:

```rust
use tracing::{debug, info, trace};

impl Predictive {
    fn refresh_cache(&mut self, active: &str) {
        let predictions = self.predictor.predict(active);
        self.cached_divisors = predictions.iter()
            .map(|p| {
                let divisor = self.allocation.divisor_for(p.probability);
                trace!(screen = %p.screen, divisor, prob = %p.probability, conf = %p.confidence, "screen divisor");
                (p.screen.clone(), divisor)
            })
            .collect();
        self.cached_for_screen = Some(active.to_string());
        debug!(
            strategy = self.name(),
            active_screen = active,
            num_screens = predictions.len(),
            "tick strategy cache refreshed"
        );
    }
}
```

### Log Level Policy

| Level | What | When |
|-------|------|------|
| INFO | Strategy init, persist save/load, cold start | Startup, periodic |
| DEBUG | Transitions, cache refresh, decay | Per-transition, periodic |
| TRACE | Per-frame decisions, per-screen divisors | Every frame (high volume) |

### Testing

- Tracing events fire at correct levels
- Structured fields contain expected values
- No tracing at INFO level on every frame (would be too noisy)
- Cold start message appears when confidence < threshold
- Divisors logged during cache refresh match TickAllocation output

### Dependencies

- Depends on C.1 (TickStrategy trait -- name() and debug_stats() methods)
- Depends on C.5 (Predictive strategy -- tracing integration)
- Should be implemented alongside C.5, not after

## H.2: Debug Stats Surface for Runtime Introspection

### What To Build

A way for apps to query the current state of the tick strategy at runtime. This enables debug screens, inspector overlays, and \`am robot\` commands to show tick strategy behavior.

### Per-Strategy Stats

**ActiveOnly:**
\`\`\`
[("strategy", "ActiveOnly"), ("background_ticks", "0")]
\`\`\`

**Uniform:**
\`\`\`
[("strategy", "Uniform"), ("divisor", "5"), ("effective_fps_bg", "2.0")]
\`\`\`

**Predictive:**
\`\`\`
[("strategy", "Predictive"),

title: H.3: Environment variable configuration for mcp-agent-mail tick strategy
description:
## H.3: Environment Variable Configuration for Tick Strategy

### What To Build

Add env vars to mcp-agent-mail-core/src/config.rs so operators can configure the tick strategy without code changes. Consistent with the project's 100+ env var configuration pattern.

### New Environment Variables

| Variable | Default | Description |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| \`AM_TUI_TICK_STRATEGY\` | \`predictive\` | Strategy: \`active_only\`, \`uniform\`, \`adjacent\`, \`predictive\` |
| \`AM_TUI_TICK_DIVISOR\` | \`5\` | Divisor for Uniform strategy; fallback divisor for Predictive |
| \`AM_TUI_TICK_PERSIST\` | \`true\` | Enable transition data persistence across sessions |
| \`AM_TUI_TICK_MIN_OBSERVATIONS\` | \`20\` | Minimum transitions before Predictive predictions are trusted |
| \`AM_TUI_TICK_DECAY_FACTOR\` | \`0.85\` | Temporal decay factor (0.0-1.0) |

### Config Struct Addition

In Config:
\`\`\`rust
pub tui_tick_strategy: String,        // "predictive", "uniform", "adjacent", "active_only"
pub tui_tick_divisor: u64,            // fallback/uniform divisor
pub tui_tick_persist: bool,           // persist transition data
pub tui_tick_min_observations: u64,   // cold-start threshold
pub tui_tick_decay_factor: f64,       // temporal decay
\`\`\`

### Strategy Construction

In the TUI initialization code:
\`\`\`rust
let strategy = match config.tui_tick_strategy.as_str() {
    "active_only" => TickStrategyKind::ActiveOnly,
    "uniform" => TickStrategyKind::Uniform { divisor: config.tui_tick_divisor },
    "adjacent" => TickStrategyKind::ActivePlusAdjacent {
        screens: ALL_SCREEN_IDS.iter().map(|id| format!("{id:?}")).collect(),
        background_divisor: config.tui_tick_divisor,
    },
    "predictive" | _ => TickStrategyKind::Predictive {
        config: PredictiveConfig {
            fallback_divisor: config.tui_tick_divisor,
            min_observations: config.tui_tick_min_observations,
            decay_factor: config.tui_tick_decay_factor,
            ..PredictiveConfig::default()
        },
    },
};
\`\`\`

### Testing

- Default config selects Predictive strategy
- Each strategy string maps to correct TickStrategyKind
- Invalid strategy string falls back to Predictive
- Divisor=0 clamped to 1
- Decay factor outside 0.0-1.0 clamped
- Persist=false skips persistence path setup
- Test: env var override works (set AM_TUI_TICK_STRATEGY=uniform, verify Uniform selected)

### Dependencies

- Depends on C.1 (TickStrategyKind enum)
- Used by F.2 (strategy configuration in mcp-agent-mail)

title: I.1: Unit tests for TransitionCounter
description:
## I.1: Unit Tests for TransitionCounter

### Test Cases (minimum 15 tests)

**Basic recording:**
1. record() increments count for (from, to) pair
2. record() same pair multiple times: count grows correctly
3. count() for unrecorded pair returns 0
4. total_from() returns sum of all outgoing from a screen
5. total() returns sum of all transitions

**Probability:**
6. probability() with one transition: returns 1.0 (before smoothing)
7. probability() with multiple targets: sums to 1.0 (within epsilon)
8. probability() with Laplace smoothing: unseen transitions get small non-zero value
9. probability() for unknown screen: returns uniform (via smoothing)
10. all_targets_ranked(): sorted descending by probability

**Decay:**
11. decay(0.5) halves all counts
12. decay(1.0) is identity (no change)
13. decay(0.0) zeroes all counts
14. decay prunes entries below threshold
15. total_from cache consistent after decay

**Merge:**
16. merge() combines two counters additively
17. merge() with disjoint screens: union of all entries
18. merge() is commutative: merge(A,B) == merge(B,A) (verify counts)
19. merge() empty counter: identity

**Edge cases:**
20. screen_ids() on empty counter: empty set
21. screen_ids() returns all seen screens
22. record() with same from and to (self-loop): counted correctly

### Logging in Tests

Each test should use \`eprintln!\` for key intermediate values:
\`\`\`rust
#[test]
fn probability_sums_to_one() {
    let mut counter = TransitionCounter::new();
    counter.record("A", "B");
    counter.record("A", "C");
    counter.record("A", "B");
    let targets = counter.all_targets_ranked("A");
    let sum: f64 = targets.iter().map(|(_, p)| p).sum();
    eprintln!("targets: {targets:?}, sum: {sum}");
    assert!((sum - 1.0).abs() < 1e-10, "probabilities must sum to 1.0, got {sum}");
}
\`\`\`

### Dependencies

- Depends on A.1 (TransitionCounter implementation)

title: I.7: E2E test script for mcp-agent-mail tick strategy
description:
## I.7: E2E Test Script for mcp-agent-mail Tick Strategy

### What To Build

A bash E2E test script `tests/e2e/test_tick_strategy.sh` that validates tick strategy behavior in the actual `am` binary. Focuses on configuration and strategy selection (testable without a TUI session).

### Script Structure

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
SCRIPT_DIR="\$(cd \"\$(dirname \"\${BASH_SOURCE[0]}\")\"\$(pwd)"
source \"\${SCRIPT_DIR}/e2e_lib.sh\"

section "Tick Strategy E2E Tests"

# --- Test 1: Default strategy is Predictive ---
test_default_strategy() {
    log "Testing default tick strategy selection"
    local output
    output=\$(am robot health --format json 2>&1)
    assert_contains \"\$output\" "tick_strategy" "health output should include tick strategy info"
    assert_contains \"\$output\" "Predictive" "default should be Predictive"
    pass "default strategy is Predictive"
}

# --- Test 2: Uniform strategy via env var ---
test_uniform_strategy() {
    log "Testing AM_TUI_TICK_STRATEGY=uniform"
    local output
    output=\$(AM_TUI_TICK_STRATEGY=uniform AM_TUI_TICK_DIVISOR=10 am robot health --format json 2>&1)
    assert_contains \"\$output\" "Uniform" "should report Uniform strategy"
    assert_contains \"\$output\" "10" "should report divisor 10"
    pass "uniform strategy configurable via env var"
}

# --- Test 3: ActiveOnly strategy ---
test_active_only_strategy() {
    log "Testing AM_TUI_TICK_STRATEGY=active_only"
    local output
    output=\$(AM_TUI_TICK_STRATEGY=active_only am robot health --format json 2>&1)
    assert_contains \"\$output\" "ActiveOnly" "should report ActiveOnly strategy"
    pass "active_only strategy works"
}

# --- Test 4: Adjacent strategy with tab order ---
test_adjacent_strategy() {
    log "Testing AM_TUI_TICK_STRATEGY=adjacent"
    local output
    output=\$(AM_TUI_TICK_STRATEGY=adjacent AM_TUI_TICK_DIVISOR=8 am robot health --format json 2>&1)
    assert_contains \"\$output\" "ActivePlusAdjacent" "should report ActivePlusAdjacent strategy"
    pass "adjacent strategy works"
}

# --- Test 5: Invalid strategy falls back to Predictive ---
test_invalid_strategy_fallback() {
    log "Testing invalid strategy name falls back to Predictive"
    local output
    output=\$(AM_TUI_TICK_STRATEGY=nonsense am robot health --format json 2>&1)
    assert_contains \"\$output\" "Predictive" "invalid should fall back to Predictive"
    pass "invalid strategy falls back gracefully"
}

# --- Test 6: Divisor clamping ---
test_divisor_clamping() {
    log "Testing AM_TUI_TICK_DIVISOR=0 clamps to 1"
    AM_TUI_TICK_STRATEGY=uniform AM_TUI_TICK_DIVISOR=0 am robot health --format json >/dev/null 2>&1
    assert_exit_code 0 "am with divisor=0 should not crash"
    pass "divisor=0 clamped to 1"
}

# --- Test 7: Persistence disabled via env var ---
test_persistence_disabled() {
    log "Testing AM_TUI_TICK_PERSIST=false disables persistence"
    local tmp_storage
    tmp_storage=\$(mktemp -d)
    AM_TUI_TICK_PERSIST=false am --storage-root \"\$tmp_storage\" robot health --format json >/dev/null 2>&1
    if [[ ! -f \"\$tmp_storage/tick_transitions.json\" ]]; then
        pass "persistence correctly disabled"
    else
        fail "persistence file should not exist when disabled"
    fi
    rm -rf \"\$tmp_storage\"
}

# --- Test 8: Decay factor clamping ---
test_decay_clamping() {
    log "Testing decay factor out-of-range clamped"
    AM_TUI_TICK_DECAY_FACTOR=5.0 am robot health --format json >/dev/null 2>&1
    assert_exit_code 0 "am with decay=5.0 should not crash"
    AM_TUI_TICK_DECAY_FACTOR=-0.5 am robot health --format json >/dev/null 2>&1
    assert_exit_code 0 "am with decay=-0.5 should not crash"
    pass "out-of-range decay factors clamped safely"
}

# --- Test 9: Debug stats accessible ---
test_debug_stats() {
    log "Testing tick strategy debug stats in health output"
    local output
    output=\$(am robot health --format json 2>&1)
    assert_contains \"\$output\" "total_transitions" "should report transition count"
    pass "debug stats accessible via robot health"
}

run_tests test_default_strategy test_uniform_strategy test_active_only_strategy \
          test_adjacent_strategy test_invalid_strategy_fallback test_divisor_clamping \
          test_persistence_disabled test_decay_clamping test_debug_stats

summary
```

### Why No TUI Session Test

Tick strategy persistence requires an actual TUI session with user interactions to generate transitions. This is difficult to automate in a headless E2E test. Instead:
- **Unit tests** (I.5) verify persistence round-trip correctness
- **Integration tests** (I.6) verify persistence with MockMultiScreenModel
- **E2E tests** (this script) verify configuration, strategy selection, and env var handling

### Expected Assertions: 9+

### Dependencies

- Depends on F.2 (mcp-agent-mail migration to framework strategy)
- Depends on H.3 (env var configuration)

title: Parser: DA/DSR device queries + character set designation (G0/G1) + single shifts
description:
## Background
The VT parser handles 56 action variants covering most core terminal sequences, but lacks several important features needed for application compatibility.

## Gaps to Fill

### Device Attribute / Status Reports (Tier 1 — critical handshake)
- DA1 (CSI c / CSI 0 c): Primary device attributes — many CLI programs send this as a startup handshake
- DA2 (CSI > c / CSI > 0 c): Secondary device attributes (terminal type/version)
- DSR (CSI 5 n): Device status report — "are you OK?" query
- CPR (CSI 6 n): Cursor position report request

### Character Set Designation (Tier 1 — affects rendering)
- G0 designate (ESC ( B / ESC ( 0): ASCII / DEC Special Graphics
- G1 designate (ESC ) B / ESC ) 0): ASCII / DEC Special Graphics
- These are used by ncurses, vim, tmux for box-drawing characters

### Single Shift (Tier 2 — completeness)
- SS2 (ESC N): Single shift to G2
- SS3 (ESC O): Single shift to G3

## Deliverables
- New Action variants for DA1, DA2, DSR, CPR, DesignateCharset, SingleShift
- Parser dispatch for all new sequences
- Unit tests for each new sequence
- Conformance fixtures for key sequences
- Wire new actions in test harnesses (no-op in harness is fine)

## Testing
- cargo fmt --check
- cargo check --all-targets
- cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
- cargo test -p frankenterm-core

title: Async Task Manager E2E: Anytime-Valid Flake Detector (e-process)
description:
## Goal
Detect flaky timing regressions in E2E tests without inflating false positives, using anytime-valid statistics.

## Core Idea (Alien Artifact)
Compute an e-value for latency/outcome deviations during E2E runs. For sub-Gaussian residuals r_t (mean 0 under null), use:
- e_t = exp(lambda * r_t - (lambda^2 * sigma^2) / 2)
- E_t = product_{i=1..t} e_i
Fail early only when E_t > 1/alpha, preserving validity under optional stopping.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Early fail only with strong evidence; no false alarms in stable runs.
- Works with variable-length test runs.
- Logs e-value trajectory and decision point.

## Tests (REQUIRED)
- unit_eprocess_threshold: failure at E_t > 1/alpha.
- unit_eprocess_nonnegative: e-values never negative.
- unit_optional_stopping: stopping early preserves decision validity (simulated).

## E2E (REQUIRED)
- Inject synthetic latency spikes; verify early failure and log evidence.
- No spike: no failure; log shows stable e-values.

## Alien Artifact Upgrades
- Model the core decision(s) with explicit state, priors/assumptions, and invariants; write down failure modes as first-class artifacts.
- Explainability: add an evidence ledger for any non-trivial decision (why this branch, why this fallback). Prefer Bayes factors / log-likelihood contributions over ad-hoc scoring.
- Guarantees: where prediction/thresholding exists, prefer distribution-free calibration (conformal prediction) or anytime-valid testing (e-process) so we can stop early without invalid inference.
- Graceful degradation: define capability tiers + deterministic fallbacks; never fail closed without a traceable reason.


## Extreme Optimization
- Baseline first: capture p50/p95/p99 for relevant command(s) with `hyperfine` (store raw output).
- Profile next: CPU flamegraph + allocation profile; identify top-5 hotspots.
- Opportunity matrix: implement only Score ≥ 2.0 (Impact×Confidence/Effort).
- Isomorphism proof per change: ordering, tie-breaking, RNG seeds, and golden checksums must match.
- Regression gates: add microbench + budgets; failures must print actionable deltas and include log artifacts.


## Testing Plan
- Unit tests: happy path + edge cases + regression fixtures.
- Property tests: invariants (idempotence, monotonicity, determinism) where applicable.
- Fuzz tests: parsers/state machines and any input-facing logic.
- Determinism: fixed seeds/time-freeze; snapshot fixtures must be stable.
close_reason: Implemented anytime-valid flake detector with e-process statistics. Features: FlakeConfig, FlakeDetector, sub-Gaussian e-value formula, batch observation, variance estimation, evidence logging, 12 unit tests, E2E script. All tests pass.

title: epic(graveyard): Testing & Fault Injection — Resilience Under Adversarial Conditions
description:
## Summary

Comprehensive fault injection and end-to-end testing framework to validate FrankenTUI's resilience under adversarial conditions. Covers bursty input storms, resize thrash, terminal capability mismatches, forced frame drops, and sustained performance under load.

## Graveyard Methodology

Every graveyard optimization must be tested under fault conditions, not just happy-path scenarios. A 2x speedup that causes flicker under resize is a net negative. This epic ensures every optimization is stress-tested before merge.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Fault injection framework for bursty inputs, resize thrash, capability mismatch, frame drops
2. No-flicker invariant verified under all fault scenarios
3. Deterministic frame hash parity across 100+ scenarios
4. 60fps sustained on 1000-widget tree for 60 seconds
5. All faults produce graceful degradation, not crashes or corruption
close_reason: done

title: task(fault-injection): Bursty input storms
description:
## Summary

Implement fault injection for bursty input events — rapid keyboard/mouse events that arrive faster than the frame rate. Verify that FrankenTUI handles input coalescing, event queue backpressure, and frame-time stability.

## Detail

Bursty input scenarios:
1. **Keyboard storm**: 1000 keypress events in 100ms (10K events/sec)
2. **Mouse flood**: Rapid mouse-move events at 1000Hz
3. **Mixed burst**: Interleaved keyboard + mouse + paste at maximum rate
4. **Long paste**: 100KB paste event in a single burst
5. **Repeated resize**: 100 resize events in 1 second (see separate bead for resize thrash)

Expected behavior under burst:
- Input queue does not grow unboundedly (backpressure or coalescing)
- Frame rate remains >30fps (degraded but not frozen)
- No event loss for keyboard input (coalescing only for mouse-move)
- Paste events are processed correctly even if split across frames
- Memory usage stays bounded (no accumulation in input buffers)

Instrumentation:
- Log queue depth at each frame
- Log events coalesced per frame
- Log frame time distribution during burst
- Record peak memory usage during burst

## Acceptance Criteria

1. All 5 burst scenarios implemented as test cases
2. Queue depth never exceeds configured limit (default: 1000 events)
3. Frame rate stays >30fps during sustained burst
4. No event loss (except mouse-move coalescing, which is intentional)
5. Memory stays bounded (< baseline + 10MB during burst)
6. Results recorded in structured JSONL for evidence
close_reason: Complete: input_storm module (5 burst patterns, xorshift64 PRNG, JSONL logging, 10 unit tests) + 8 E2E tests via ProgramSimulator. All quality gates pass (fmt, clippy, 18 total tests).

title: task(fault-injection): Resize thrash (rapid resize events)
description:
## Summary

Implement fault injection for rapid terminal resize events. Resize is the most disruptive event in a TUI — it invalidates all layout, requires full reflow, and can expose race conditions between input processing and rendering.

## Detail

Resize thrash scenarios:
1. **Rapid oscillation**: Toggle between 80x24 and 120x40 every 16ms (60Hz)
2. **Progressive shrink**: Decrease terminal size by 1 column/row every 16ms until 10x5
3. **Progressive grow**: Increase terminal size by 1 column/row every 16ms until 300x100
4. **Random sizes**: Random terminal size every 16ms for 10 seconds
5. **Extreme sizes**: Resize to 1x1, then to 1000x1000, then to 10x10000

Expected behavior:
- No panic or crash at any terminal size
- Layout recomputes correctly at every size (verified by golden frame checksums)
- Frame render time stays bounded (no quadratic blowup on extreme sizes)
- Widget content is clipped correctly, not rendered out of bounds
- Scroll state is preserved across resizes (proportional scrolling)
- No ANSI escape sequence corruption (complete sequences emitted per resize)

Critical invariant: After resize thrash, returning to original size produces identical output to never having resized. This is the "resize round-trip" property.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. All 5 resize scenarios implemented
2. No panics or crashes at any terminal size
3. Resize round-trip property verified (return to original size = identical output)
4. Frame time bounded by O(W*H) — no quadratic behavior
5. ANSI escape sequences never corrupted (validated by terminal emulator parser)
6. Results recorded in structured JSONL for evidence
close_reason: Completed resize-thrash fault-injection implementation and validation

title: task(fault-injection): Terminal capability mismatch
description:
## Summary

Implement fault injection for terminal capability mismatches — situations where FrankenTUI assumes capabilities the terminal doesn't support (e.g., 256-color on a 16-color terminal, mouse capture on a terminal without mouse support).

## Detail

Capability mismatch scenarios:
1. **Color downgrade**: Request 24-bit color on 16-color terminal
2. **No mouse**: Enable mouse capture on terminal that ignores mouse escapes
3. **No alternate screen**: Enter alternate screen on terminal that doesn't support it
4. **No Unicode**: Emit wide characters on terminal with ASCII-only support
5. **Slow terminal**: Terminal that takes 50ms+ to process each escape sequence
6. **Broken bracketed paste**: Terminal that sends paste content without bracketing

Expected behavior:
- Graceful degradation: fall back to closest supported capability
- Color quantization: 24-bit → 256 → 16 → 8 automatically
- Feature detection: probe terminal capabilities at startup
- No garbled output: if a feature isn't supported, don't emit its escape sequences
- Warning log: record capability mismatches for debugging

## Acceptance Criteria

1. All 6 mismatch scenarios implemented as test cases
2. Graceful degradation verified (output is usable, not garbled)
3. Color quantization produces visually acceptable results
4. No escape sequence pollution (unsupported escapes not emitted)
5. Capability detection documented and tested
notes: Claimed by FoggyPeak; implementing terminal capability mismatch fault-injection scenarios and evidence checks.
close_reason: Implemented and validated terminal capability mismatch fault-injection matrix

title: task(fault-injection): Forced frame drops
description:
## Summary

Implement fault injection for forced frame drops — simulate situations where frames are skipped due to computation taking longer than the frame budget. Verify that FrankenTUI recovers gracefully and the next frame is correct.

## Detail

Frame drop scenarios:
1. **Single frame drop**: Skip one frame, verify next frame is correct
2. **Burst frame drops**: Drop 5 consecutive frames, verify recovery
3. **Periodic frame drops**: Drop every 3rd frame for 10 seconds
4. **Layout timeout**: Inject 50ms delay in layout computation, causing frame budget overrun
5. **Diff timeout**: Inject 50ms delay in diff computation

Expected behavior:
- After frame drop, the next rendered frame is fully correct (not a partial update)
- No accumulated visual artifacts from dropped frames
- Input events during dropped frames are not lost (queued and processed)
- Frame counter accounts for dropped frames (telemetry shows gap)
- The diff engine does not assume the previous frame is the one that was displayed (it may have been dropped)

Critical invariant: Frame N+2 after dropping frame N+1 must be identical to what frame N+2 would have been WITHOUT the drop. Frame drops are invisible to the visual output — only frame timing is affected.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. All 5 frame drop scenarios implemented
2. Post-drop frames are pixel-identical to no-drop baseline (verified by checksum)
3. No accumulated visual artifacts
4. Input events preserved during drops
5. Telemetry correctly records dropped frames
notes: Claimed by FoggyPeak; starting forced frame-drop fault-injection harness work from PTY layer.
close_reason: done

All pass, clippy clean. Key invariant verified: frame N+2 after dropping N+1 produces identical buffer checksums as presenting N, N+2 directly.

title: task(e2e): No-flicker invariant under all fault scenarios
description:
## Summary

End-to-end test that verifies the no-flicker invariant: under ALL fault injection scenarios, the user never sees a partially-rendered or corrupted frame. This is the ultimate quality gate.

## Detail

No-flicker definition:
- Every ANSI escape sequence sent to the terminal is complete and valid
- No cursor jump to a position and then jump away without writing (visible cursor flicker)
- No cell is written twice in a single frame (double-render flicker)
- The diff engine never emits a diff that would cause visible flicker (e.g., clear-then-redraw)
- Hidden cursor during render, restored after

Test methodology:
1. Wrap the terminal output in a capture layer that records all bytes written
2. Parse the capture as ANSI escape sequences
3. Verify invariants:
   a. Every CSI sequence is complete (no truncation)
   b. Cursor is hidden at start of render, shown at end
   c. No cell is written more than once per frame
   d. No clear-screen followed by full redraw (should be incremental)
   e. Cursor position is restored to expected location after render

Run this verification under each fault scenario:
- Bursty input storms
- Resize thrash
- Capability mismatch
- Forced frame drops
- Combined: multiple faults simultaneously

## Acceptance Criteria

1. No-flicker invariant holds under all individual fault scenarios
2. No-flicker invariant holds under combined fault scenarios
3. ANSI sequence validation catches all truncation/corruption
4. Test produces clear failure output showing the exact flicker event
5. CI-gated: any flicker detection fails the build
close_reason: done

comments.text: TanLion: Implemented 30 test scenarios covering no-flicker invariant under all fault injection scenarios: frame drops (5 tests), resize thrash (4 tests), bursty input (5 tests), capability mismatch (4 tests), combined faults (4 tests), stress (2 tests), edge cases (5 tests), determinism (1 test). All pass, clippy clean. Key invariant: sync brackets are always complete and no visible content outside brackets under any fault condition.

title: task(e2e): Deterministic frame hash parity across 100 scenarios
description:
## Summary

End-to-end test verifying that frame hashes are deterministic and reproducible across 100+ test scenarios. Given the same input sequence, the same frame buffer must be produced every time, regardless of timing, system load, or environmental factors.

## Detail

Determinism sources to control:
- Random number generators: must be seeded deterministically
- Timing: frame timestamps must be injectable (not wall-clock dependent)
- System state: terminal size, capabilities must be mocked
- Input order: events must be processed in a defined order

Test methodology:
1. Define 100+ test scenarios with explicit:
   - Initial terminal size
   - Widget tree definition
   - Input event sequence with logical timestamps
   - Expected frame hashes at each checkpoint
2. Run each scenario in the deterministic simulator (Ring 2)
3. Compare frame hashes against golden values
4. Any mismatch = test failure with detailed diff

Scenario categories (aim for 100+ total):
- Simple widgets: text, input, button, list (20 scenarios)
- Complex layouts: flex, grid, split, tabs (20 scenarios)
- Interaction sequences: typing, scrolling, focus, resize (30 scenarios)
- Edge cases: empty, oversized, Unicode, RTL (20 scenarios)
- Regression scenarios: previously-found bugs (10+ scenarios)

## Acceptance Criteria

1. 100+ scenarios defined and passing
2. All frame hashes reproducible across CI runs
3. Scenario definitions are human-readable (TOML or similar)
4. Adding a new scenario is straightforward (template provided)
5. Failures produce visual diffs showing frame difference
close_reason: Implemented 103 test scenarios across 5 categories: simple widgets (20), complex layouts (20), interaction sequences (30), edge cases (20), regression scenarios (12+1 summary). All pass deterministically.

title: task(e2e): 60fps sustained on 1000-widget tree for 60 seconds
description:
## Summary

Soak test: verify that FrankenTUI sustains 60fps rendering on a 1000-widget tree for 60 continuous seconds with active interaction (scrolling, typing, focus changes). This validates that there are no slow leaks, GC-like pauses, or progressive degradation.

## Detail

Test setup:
- Widget tree: 1000 widgets (mix of text, list, input, flex containers)
- Interaction: automated input sequence simulating active user (typing + scrolling + tab)
- Frame budget: 16.67ms (60fps)
- Duration: 60 seconds (3600 frames)

Pass criteria:
- p50 frame time < 8ms (50% headroom)
- p95 frame time < 14ms (16% headroom)
- p99 frame time < 16ms (4% headroom)
- MAX frame time < 33ms (never drop below 30fps)
- Zero frames with visual corruption (verified by checksum stability)
- Memory usage: stable or decreasing over time (no leaks)
- Allocation count: stable per frame (no accumulation)

Measurements:
- Frame time histogram (1ms buckets)
- Memory RSS sampled every second
- Allocation count per frame (via custom allocator)
- Frame checksum per frame (for corruption detection)
- Event queue depth per frame (for backpressure detection)

Failure analysis (if soak fails):
- Identify the frame where regression starts
- Capture flamegraph of that frame
- Diff against early-session flamegraph
- Report: memory growth rate, allocation accumulation rate

## Acceptance Criteria

1. 60fps sustained for full 60 seconds (pass criteria above)
2. Memory stable: RSS at end - RSS at start < 1MB
3. Allocations stable: per-frame allocation count variance < 10%
4. No visual corruption: all frame checksums consistent with expected output
5. Results stored as CI artifacts (frame time histogram, memory trace, flamegraph)
6. Regression gate: any SLA violation fails CI
close_reason: done

title: Implement Image widget with protocol detection
description:
PHASE 7 - EXTRAS: IMAGE WIDGET

## Background
Image widget displays images in terminal using Kitty Graphics Protocol, iTerm2 inline images, or Sixel fallback. Requires protocol detection and graceful degradation.

## Technical Requirements
- Protocol detection:
  - Kitty Graphics Protocol (XTGETTCAP query)
  - iTerm2 inline images (TERM_PROGRAM check)
  - Sixel (DA2 response parsing)
  - Fallback: ASCII/Braille representation
- Image loading via image crate
- Resize/fit modes: Contain, Cover, Stretch, None
- Aspect ratio preservation
- Partial update for animated GIFs
- Memory management for large images

## Design Rationale
Image support is a premium feature gated behind 'image' flag. Protocol detection happens once at startup and caches result. Fallback ensures graceful degradation.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Protocol detection and caching
- [ ] Kitty Graphics Protocol implementation
- [ ] iTerm2 inline image implementation
- [ ] Sixel fallback (optional sub-feature)
- [ ] ASCII fallback when no protocol available
- [ ] Resize mode configuration
- [ ] Aspect ratio handling
- [ ] Feature gate: image

## Performance Budget
- Protocol detection: < 50ms (one-time)
- Image encode/transmit: proportional to size

## Location: ftui-extras crate (feature = "image")
