title: Diagram Color Themes & Style Presets
description:
## Goal
Add named color palettes for diagram rendering (e.g., "default", "corporate", "neon", "monochrome", "pastel", "high-contrast") that remap node fills, edge colors, cluster backgrounds, and text colors.

## Why
- Visual polish with minimal effort. Color is the cheapest way to make diagrams look professional.
- Different contexts need different palettes: documentation (corporate), presentations (neon), accessibility (high-contrast), printing (monochrome).
- The IR already carries style_refs; this adds a palette layer on top.
- Users can cycle themes in the demo showcase with a keybinding.

## Palette Definitions
Each palette defines:
- node_fill: [Color; 8] — one per NodeShape or cycling through nodes
- node_border: Color
- node_text: Color
- edge_color: Color
- edge_label_color: Color
- cluster_fill: Color (low opacity)
- cluster_border: Color
- background: Color
- accent: Color (for selection/highlighting)

## Preset Palettes
1. Default: blue nodes, gray edges (current behavior)
2. Corporate: navy/teal/gray, professional look
3. Neon: cyan/magenta/green on dark background, high contrast
4. Monochrome: white/gray/black only, works on any terminal
5. Pastel: soft muted colors, easy on eyes
6. High-contrast: WCAG AAA compliant, bold primary colors

## Files
- crates/ftui-extras/src/mermaid_render.rs (add DiagramPalette struct + preset palettes)
- crates/ftui-extras/src/mermaid.rs (add palette selection to MermaidConfig)
- crates/ftui-demo-showcase/src/screens/mermaid_showcase.rs (keybinding to cycle themes)

## Tests
- Unit: each palette has valid contrast ratios
- Snapshot: same diagram in each palette

title: Migrate interactive widgets with hit testing (Category B)
description:
## Scope

Migrate Category B widgets - those that need mouse interaction via hit testing.

## Frame Features Used

- `frame.hit_grid` - Register clickable regions for mouse events

## Migration Pattern

1. Change signature to use Frame
2. For clickable regions, add hit grid registration:
   ```rust
   fn render(&self, area: Rect, frame: &mut Frame) {
       let buf = &mut frame.buffer;
       
       // ... draw the widget ...
       
       // Register clickable region
       if let Some(hit_grid) = &mut frame.hit_grid {
           hit_grid.register(area, HitId::Widget(self.id));
       }
   }
   ```

## Widgets Expected in This Category

Based on functionality (to be confirmed by audit):
- List (selectable items)
- Table (clickable rows/cells)
- Buttons (if any)
- Links (if any)

## Design Consideration

Some widgets may have multiple clickable regions (e.g., table cells).
These need careful hit ID assignment for disambiguation.

## Important

- Preserve existing behavior for non-mouse interaction
- Hit testing is ADDITIVE - widgets must still work without hit_grid
- Check `if let Some(hit_grid)` - don't assume it's always present

## Verification

- `cargo check -p ftui-widgets` must pass
- All existing tests must pass
- Manual verification of mouse interaction (if test harness supports it)
close_reason: Added hit testing to List and Table widgets. Each widget now has a .hit_id() method that enables mouse interaction. When enabled, each item/row registers a hit region with the frame's hit grid, storing the item index as hit data. Added 6 tests. All 273 ftui-widgets tests pass.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Alien Artifact Math Notes (MANDATORY)

Purpose
- Provide a mathematically principled resize scheduler with anytime validity, explicit loss tradeoffs, and provable bounds on worst‑case behavior.

Core Model
- Treat resize events as a non‑stationary time series with regime shifts.
- Objective: minimize expected loss L(action, state) with asymmetric costs.

Loss Matrix (example)
- keep_reflow | skip_frame
  - smooth (true)  : 0   |  30
  - storm (burst)  : 10  |  1
- Intent: during bursts, skipping a frame is cheap; during steady state, skipping is costly.

Decision Rule (Bayes)
- Maintain posterior over regimes:
  P(storm|data_t) ∝ P(storm) × Π P(x_i|storm)
- Action a* = argmin_a Σ_c L(a,c) × P(c|data_t)

Anytime Validity (e‑process)
- Define e‑value e_t such that E[e_t] ≤ 1 under null (no regime shift).
- Trigger “storm mode” when e_t ≥ 1/α (optional stopping safe).
- This lets the scheduler switch modes without invalidating guarantees.

Output Guarantees
- Bound expected latency under steady state.
- Bound average render cost under storms by throttling to max_fps.
- Explicitly log when bounds are violated.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
BOCPD Details (Change‑Point Detection)

Model
- Observations: inter‑resize intervals Δt and magnitude |Δsize|.
- Assume piecewise‑stationary hazard λ (probability of regime change).
- Run length r_t tracks time since last change.

Recurrence
- p(r_t, x_t) = Σ_{r_{t-1}} p(r_{t-1}, x_{t-1}) × p(r_t|r_{t-1}) × p(x_t|r_{t-1})
- p(r_t=0|r_{t-1}) = λ (change)
- p(r_t=r_{t-1}+1|r_{t-1}) = 1-λ (no change)

Outputs
- Posterior P(r_t=0|x_1:t) gives change‑point probability.
- Use threshold τ_cp to enter storm mode.

Parameters
- λ chosen from empirical resize patterns (configurable, safe default).
- Likelihood modeled with exponential/gamma on Δt, mixture for |Δsize|.

Guarantees
- Sensitivity to burst onset; bounded false positives via λ and τ_cp.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Control‑Theoretic Frame Pacing (PID/PI)

Goal
- Maintain target frame latency T (e.g., 16–33ms) under resize storms.

Signals
- error e_t = T - render_latency_t
- output u_t = throttle level (max FPS / skip ratio)

PID (or PI) Update
- u_t = Kp*e_t + Ki*Σ e + Kd*(e_t - e_{t-1})
- Clamp u_t to safe bounds [u_min, u_max]

Stability Notes
- Choose Kp, Ki from Ziegler‑Nichols‑style sweep on representative resize storms.
- Prefer PI (Kd=0) to avoid jitter from noisy latency measurements.

Fallback
- If measurements missing, default to conservative throttle.

Guarantee
- Bounded overshoot and monotone convergence to target latency (empirical).

title: Resize Scheduler: Anytime-Valid Decision Rule (e-process)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Anytime‑Valid Decision Rule (e‑process)

E‑value Definition
- Construct e_t such that E[e_t] ≤ 1 under null (no regime shift).
- Example: likelihood ratio between storm vs steady models.

Decision Rule
- Trigger storm mode if e_t ≥ 1/α (α = tolerated false‑positive rate).
- Safe under optional stopping (resize stream can end anytime).

Computation
- e_t = Π (p(x_t|storm) / p(x_t|steady)) with clipping to avoid underflow.

title: Render Pipeline: Atomic Reflow on Resize
description:
## Background

Resize is where TUIs go to die: partial paints, torn frames, and stale content (ghost rows) are the classic failure modes.

FrankenTUI's design philosophy (determinism, one-writer rule, RAII teardown) implies resize must be handled as a first-class *transaction*:
- a resize event results in exactly one coherent present
- any cleanup required by shrink happens in the same transaction
- presenter state is consistent after the transaction (no latent cursor/SGR state)

This task is the top-level "make resize reflow real" work item for the render pipeline.

## Goal

Implement **atomic reflow on resize** in both screen modes:
- Alt-screen: full-screen UI
- Inline: stable UI region with scrollback preserved

Atomic means: from the terminal's point of view, each resize produces a single, consistent frame without intermediate corrupted states.

## Scope

1) Replace placeholder resize behavior with continuous reflow.
- The runtime must produce a view at the new size (layout + widgets) and present it.

2) Define and enforce an **atomic present protocol** (see bd-1rz0.4.1).
- Clear/shrink cleanup happens before/with drawing.
- Output is one coherent write per frame (or as close as the writer can enforce).

3) Ensure **shrink cleanup** prevents ghosting.
- When height decreases, rows that were previously painted but are now out-of-bounds must be erased.
- When UI height changes (inline mode), stale chrome rows must be erased.

4) Presenter / terminal writer state correctness.
- Cursor position, SGR state, scroll region, and saved cursor semantics must not leak across the resize transaction.
- Any capability-dependent behavior (sync output, cursor save/restore) must follow deterministic fallback rules.

## Design Notes (Implementation Guidance)

- Treat resize handling as a transaction boundary:
  - compute new Frame/Buffer
  - compute Diff against previous Buffer
  - run shrink cleanup (if needed)
  - emit ANSI as one present

- Ghost row cleanup must be *dimension-aware*:
  - track previous terminal size
  - compute the "rows to erase" region as: [new_height .. prev_height)
  - clamp all erase operations to the actual terminal height

- Inline mode needs special care:
  - preserve scrollback above UI
  - only touch the reserved UI region + any ghost rows below it

## Tests / Validation

- Unit tests:
  - shrink: when height decreases, the presenter/terminal writer emits erases for ghost rows
  - grow: no unnecessary full clears
  - state reset: SGR/cursor assumptions after resize are correct

- Snapshot tests:
  - scripted resize sequences (grow -> shrink -> grow) with stable expected output

- PTY E2E:
  - resize storms at fixed seed and fixed schedule
  - verbose JSONL logs (env/caps/seed/timings/checksums)
  - checksum validation for final rendered frame

## Acceptance Criteria

- No ghosting after shrink in alt-screen and inline modes.
- Reflow is atomic: no visible intermediate corruption during resize sequences.
- Determinism: given the same input events and seed, produced output checksums match.
- Performance: resize handling stays within an explicit budget (capture p50/p95/p99 and add a regression gate in bd-1rz0.11).

## Alien Artifact Upgrades

- Explainability: when a capability fallback is used during resize present (e.g., no sync output), record a minimal evidence ledger entry (what capability, what evidence, what fallback).
- Guarantees: incorporate resize SLA monitoring (bd-1rz0.26) with anytime-valid alerts.

## Extreme Optimization

- Baseline the resize-storm PTY scenario (p50/p95/p99) before micro-optimizations.
- Only optimize after profiling; one lever per change; preserve behavior via golden frame checksums.
close_reason: Completed

title: Atomic Present Protocol + Shrink Cleanup
description:
## Background

This task defines the **atomic present protocol** used by the render pipeline to make resize safe:
- avoid partial paints during resize transactions
- ensure shrink cleanup happens immediately (no ghost rows)
- keep terminal writer / presenter state coherent after every present

This is the contract between runtime->render (BufferDiff) and output (TerminalWriter/Presenter).

## Protocol (Normative)

A resize-triggered present must behave like a transaction:

1) Determine current terminal size and update prev size tracking.
- Previous size is required for shrink cleanup.

2) If the terminal height shrank, erase any rows that were previously painted but are now out-of-bounds.
- Alt-screen: erase rows in the alt buffer beyond new height.
- Inline: erase ghost rows below the UI region, clamped to the real terminal height.

3) Ensure presenter state is safe for the new frame.
- Cursor position and SGR state should not leak across the transaction.

4) Present the diff as one coherent output batch.
- Prefer synchronized output when supported.
- Preserve one-writer invariants and avoid interleaving.

5) Restore any cursor-save invariants required by inline mode.

## Shrink Cleanup Rules

- Ghost rows are the set of rows that were previously inside the painted region but are now outside the new buffer height.
- Cleanup must be bounded and deterministic:
  - erase only the necessary region
  - clamp coordinates to current terminal size

## Tests / Validation

- Unit tests:
  - prev_term_width/prev_term_height tracking updates correctly
  - shrink cleanup erases the correct rows
  - inline mode clamps ghost-row cleanup to terminal height

- Snapshot tests:
  - shrink/grow sequences produce stable output

## Acceptance Criteria

- Protocol is documented and enforceable (module docs + tests).
- No residual artifacts after shrink in either screen mode.
- Determinism: stable behavior under fixed resize event sequences.

title: Double-Buffer Swap: O(1) Buffer Transition
close_reason: Completed: Added DoubleBuffer swap benchmark to buffer_bench.rs and E2E test script (scripts/test_double_buffer.sh). All 11 tests pass (6 unit + 5 property). Core implementation was already complete with present_ui_owned() zero-copy path.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Why This Matters for Zero-Flicker Reflow

During a resize storm, frames are rendered rapidly. Each frame currently incurs a buffer clone. With double-buffer swap:

1. **Latency Reduction**: 70μs saved per frame = tighter render loop
2. **Memory Bandwidth**: Less pressure on memory bus during resize
3. **Cache Efficiency**: No unnecessary copying means more cache available for actual rendering
4. **Determinism**: Swap is O(1) regardless of buffer size, making timing predictable

### Relationship to Other Beads
- **bd-1rz0.4.2 (Adaptive Buffer Allocation)**: DoubleBuffer is the allocation strategy
- **bd-4kq0.1 (Dirty-Rect Diff)**: Diff benefits from stable buffer addresses
- **bd-1rz0.3 (Resize Coalescer)**: Faster frames = more responsive coalescing

### Implementation Notes
The swap pattern is standard in graphics (GPU swap chains, SDL double buffering). It's battle-tested and well-understood.

Key insight: We don't need to preserve buffer contents across resize. The atomic reflow (bd-1rz0.4) ensures a full re-render on resize, so both buffers can be reallocated fresh.

title: Action Timeline: Alert Threshold Calibration (Conformal + e-process)
description:
## Goal
Set change-point alert thresholds with formal false-positive control and provide an explanation ledger per alert.

## Core Idea (Alien Artifact)
Conformal thresholding on residuals from the sketch baseline:
- Given calibration residuals R = {r_1..r_n}, threshold q = quantile_{1-alpha} using (n+1) rule.
- Alert when r_t > q.

Anytime-valid layer:
- Maintain an e-process on residuals to allow early alerts without inflating false positives.
- Example: e_t = exp(lambda * (r_t - mu) - (lambda^2 * sigma^2)/2), E_t = product e_t.
- Trigger if E_t > 1/alpha.

## Acceptance Criteria
- FPR <= alpha on synthetic and recorded traces.
- Alert carries evidence ledger: residual, q, conformal score, e-value, alpha.
- No alert spam under steady-state traffic.

## Tests (REQUIRED)
- unit_conformal_threshold: threshold equals (1-alpha) quantile of calibration set.
- unit_evalue_monotone: e-process nonnegative and grows with evidence.
- property_fpr_control: empirical FPR <= alpha + tolerance.

## E2E (REQUIRED)
- Replay trace with known change points; log alert timing and evidence.

## Alien Artifact Upgrades
- Model the core decision(s) with explicit state, priors/assumptions, and invariants; write down failure modes as first-class artifacts.
- Explainability: add an evidence ledger for any non-trivial decision (why this branch, why this fallback). Prefer Bayes factors / log-likelihood contributions over ad-hoc scoring.
- Guarantees: where prediction/thresholding exists, prefer distribution-free calibration (conformal prediction) or anytime-valid testing (e-process) so we can stop early without invalid inference.
- Graceful degradation: define capability tiers + deterministic fallbacks; never fail closed without a traceable reason.


## Extreme Optimization
- Baseline first: capture p50/p95/p99 for relevant command(s) with `hyperfine` (store raw output).
- Profile next: CPU flamegraph + allocation profile; identify top-5 hotspots.
- Opportunity matrix: implement only Score ≥ 2.0 (Impact×Confidence/Effort).
- Isomorphism proof per change: ordering, tie-breaking, RNG seeds, and golden checksums must match.
- Regression gates: add microbench + budgets; failures must print actionable deltas and include log artifacts.


## Testing Plan
- Unit tests: happy path + edge cases + regression fixtures.
- Property tests: invariants (idempotence, monotonicity, determinism) where applicable.
- Fuzz tests: parsers/state machines and any input-facing logic.
- Determinism: fixed seeds/time-freeze; snapshot fixtures must be stable.
close_reason:
Implemented conformal_alert.rs in ftui-runtime with:
- Conformal thresholding using (n+1) quantile rule
- E-process layer for anytime-valid FPR control
- Evidence ledger with full provenance (residual, q, e-value, alpha)
- 27 passing unit tests including FPR property tests
- GRAPA adaptive lambda support

## E2E Integration Test: Galaxy-Brain Transparency Demo (EV=killer)

### Scope
Full integration test rendering the galaxy-brain transparency demo screen. Validates that all Bayesian decision visualizations are present, progressive disclosure works, and card rendering is correct.

### Test Scenario
1. Initialize FrankenTUI with galaxy-brain demo screen active.
2. Verify initial render shows all active decision cards:
   - Posterior distribution sparklines for each decision point
   - Top evidence terms with Bayes factors
   - Chosen actions with expected loss
   - Confidence interval bars
3. Trigger drift: inject increasing frame times over 50 frames.
4. Verify automatic fallback visualization appears (decision switches from adaptive to conservative).
5. Test progressive disclosure: collapse/expand each decision card.
6. Verify card rendering at different terminal sizes (80x24, 120x40, 200x60).
7. Test keyboard navigation between decision cards.
8. Verify all 7 decision points from Evidence Ledger are represented.

### JSONL Structured Logging Specification
Each frame of the demo screen emits:
```json
{
  "event": "galaxy_brain_frame",
  "ts_ns": u64,
  "frame_id": u64,
  "cards_visible": u32,
  "cards_expanded": u32,
  "cards_collapsed": u32,
  "decision_points_shown": ["string"],
  "drift_detected": bool,
  "fallback_active": bool,
  "progressive_disclosure_state": {
    "card_id": "string",
    "expanded": bool,
    "sparkline_points": u32
  },
  "terminal_size": { "cols": u16, "rows": u16 },
  "render_time_ns": u64,

}
```

### Success Criteria
- All 7 decision points visible as cards on initial render.
- Drift injection triggers visible fallback indicator within 10 frames of detection.

title: Document Inline vs Alt-Screen mode trade-offs
description:
# Document Inline vs Alt-Screen Mode Trade-offs

## Background & Strategic Importance
The plan requires documentation that explains "inline vs alt-screen explanation (scrollback tradeoffs)". This is critical for users to understand which mode to use for their application. The wrong choice leads to frustrated users who either:
- Lose their log history (alt-screen for an agent harness)
- Get cursor corruption (inline without understanding constraints)

## Why This Documentation Is Critical
- ADR-001 (Inline Mode Strategy) is a cornerstone decision
- Users coming from other TUI frameworks assume alt-screen
- Agent harness users NEED inline mode but don't know it exists
- Common source of "why doesn't my app work" questions

---

## Content Structure

### What Is Inline Mode?

**Definition:** The UI renders in the normal terminal buffer, interleaved with the terminal's scrollback history.

**How it works:**
```
[Previous terminal output]
[Previous terminal output]
[Previous terminal output]
[Log line 1]                 <- These scroll up into scrollback
[Log line 2]
[Log line 3]
├──────────────────────────┤
│ Status: Running tool... │ <- This is the pinned UI region
│ > Enter command: _      │    (fixed height, redrawn in place)
├──────────────────────────┤
```

**Key behaviors:**
- Scrollback is preserved (native terminal feature)
- Logs become part of terminal history
- Can scroll back after program exits to see full history
- UI occupies a fixed region at the bottom
- Default mode for ftui

**Technical implementation:**
- Never issue full-screen clear (`\x1b[2J`)
- Only redraw the bounded UI region
- Use EL (erase line) for local clearing
- Cursor must be restored after every present()

---

### What Is Alt-Screen Mode?

**Definition:** The UI renders in the alternate screen buffer, a separate buffer from the primary terminal.

**How it works:**
```
┌──────────────────────────────────────┐
│                                      │
│         Full-screen TUI              │
│                                      │
│    No scrollback in this buffer      │
│                                      │
│                                      │
│   Status bar at bottom               │
└──────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Key behaviors:**
- Scrollback is NOT preserved (alt buffer is blank)
- When program exits, previous content is restored
- Classic TUI experience (vim, htop, less)
- Full-screen clears are safe
- Opt-in via `ScreenMode::AltScreen`

**Technical implementation:**
- Enter: `\x1b[?1049h` (smcup)
- Exit: `\x1b[?1049l` (rmcup)
- Previous screen automatically restored on exit

---

### Trade-off Matrix

| Feature | Inline Mode | Alt-Screen Mode |
|---------|-------------|-----------------|
| Scrollback preserved | ✓ | ✗ |
| Full-screen clear safe | ✗ | ✓ |
| Log history after exit | ✓ | ✗ |
| Cursor management | Complex | Simple |
| Classic TUI feel | ✗ | ✓ |
| Agent harness ideal | ✓ | ✗ |
| Resize handling | Requires anchor | Straightforward |
| Panic cleanup | Critical | Important |

---

### When to Use Inline Mode

**Use inline mode when:**
- Building agent harness UIs (Claude Code, Codex style)
- Log viewers where history matters after exit
- REPLs and interactive shells
- Any app where scrollback is valuable
- Applications that stream output the user may want to review

**Examples:**
- Claude Code's tool execution output
- `npm install` progress that you want to scroll back through
- Interactive database REPL with query history
- Build tool output (cargo, make)

**Configuration:**
```rust
App::new(model)
    .screen_mode(ScreenMode::Inline { ui_height: 4 })
    .run()
```

---

### When to Use Alt-Screen Mode

**Use alt-screen mode when:**
- Building full-screen dashboards (htop, btop)
- Traditional TUI applications (vim, nano)
- Modal dialogs and pickers that need full screen
- When you WANT content gone on exit (games, temporary views)
- Visual applications where scrollback is meaningless

**Examples:**
- System monitor dashboard
- Text editor
- File manager
- Interactive game
- Configuration wizard

**Configuration:**
```rust
App::new(model)
    .screen_mode(ScreenMode::AltScreen)
    .run()
```

---

### Mixed Strategy (Best of Both Worlds)

The plan supports a hybrid approach: Start in inline mode, temporarily switch to alt-screen for complex modals, then return to inline mode.

**When to use mixed mode:**
- Agent harness with occasional file picker
- REPL that needs an interactive editor
- Log viewer that spawns a detail modal

**Implementation:**
```rust
// Start in inline mode
App::new(model)
    .screen_mode(ScreenMode::Inline {
        ui_height: 6,
    })
    .run()

// In update(), when needing full-screen modal:
fn update(&mut self, msg: Msg) -> Cmd<Msg> {
    match msg {
        Msg::OpenFilePicker => {
            self.mode = Mode::FilePicker;
            Cmd::enter_alt_screen()
        }
        Msg::FilePickerClosed(path) => {
            self.mode = Mode::Normal;
            Cmd::batch(vec![
                Cmd::exit_alt_screen(),
                Cmd::msg(Msg::FileSelected(path)),
            ])
        }
        // ...
    }
}
```

**What happens:**
1. App runs in inline mode (scrollback preserved)
2. User triggers file picker
3. Switch to alt-screen (full-screen picker UI)
4. User makes selection
5. Switch back to inline mode
6. Scrollback still intact!

---

### Implementation Details

#### Inline Mode Contract

1. **Never clear full screen**
   - `\x1b[2J` destroys scrollback
   - Only clear the UI region

2. **Only clear bounded UI region**
   - Calculate UI region from bottom
   - Use EL (erase line) for clearing

3. **Cursor restored after every present()**
   - Frame::cursor_position specifies target
   - Presenter handles restoration

4. **Logs enter scrollback naturally**
   - Print log lines above UI region
   - Terminal scrolls them into history

#### Alt-Screen Contract

1. **Full-screen clears allowed**
   - Safe because alt buffer is isolated

2. **Simpler cursor policy**
   - No anchor calculation needed

3. **Exit restores previous content**
   - rmcup sequence handles this

4. **Cleanup on panic still required**
   - Must restore primary screen
   - RAII guard handles this

---

### Common Mistakes

#### Mistake 1: Full-screen clear in inline mode

```rust
// WRONG: Destroys scrollback!
write!(stdout, "\x1b[2J")?;

// WRONG: Also destroys scrollback!
frame.buffer.clear();  // If this issues ED 2

// RIGHT: Clear only the UI region
for y in ui_start..ui_end {
    frame.buffer.set_string(0, y, &" ".repeat(width), Style::default());
}
```

**Why it's wrong:** ESC[2J erases the entire screen, which in inline mode means destroying the scrollback history that makes inline mode valuable.

#### Mistake 2: Assuming scrollback in alt-screen

```rust
// WRONG assumption: "The user can scroll back to see logs"
// In alt-screen, there IS NO scrollback!
app.screen_mode(ScreenMode::AltScreen)
    .run()
// Logs are gone when app exits

// RIGHT: Use inline mode for log-heavy apps
app.screen_mode(ScreenMode::Inline { ui_height: 4 })
    .run()
// Logs preserved in scrollback
```

**Why it's wrong:** Alt-screen uses a separate buffer that has no scrollback. When the app exits, everything is gone.

#### Mistake 3: Not handling resize in inline mode

```rust
// WRONG: Fixed anchor that doesn't update
let anchor = 5;  // Assume UI starts at line 5

// RIGHT: Recalculate anchor on resize
fn on_resize(&mut self, size: Size) {
    self.anchor = size.height - self.ui_height;
}
```

**Why it's wrong:** In inline mode, the UI region anchor is relative to the bottom. When the terminal resizes, the anchor must be recalculated.

#### Mistake 4: Not testing with PTY tests

```rust
// Easy to miss cursor corruption in manual testing
// PTY tests catch it automatically

#[test]
fn test_inline_mode_cursor_contract() {
    let mut term = TerminalModel::new(80, 24);
    let app = TestApp::new();

    app.render(&mut term);

    // Cursor should be at input line, not corrupted
    assert_eq!(term.cursor_position(), (2, 23));
}
```

---

### Debugging Screen Mode Issues

#### Symptom: Scrollback lost on exit

**Cause:** Using alt-screen when inline mode was intended.
**Fix:** Change to `ScreenMode::Inline { ui_height: N }`.

#### Symptom: Cursor jumps around

**Cause:** Writing to terminal outside present() cycle.
**Fix:** Ensure all output goes through ftui runtime.

#### Symptom: UI region flickers

**Cause:** Clearing too much on each frame.
**Fix:** Only redraw changed cells (presenter handles this).

#### Symptom: Logs overwrite UI

**Cause:** UI height not properly configured.
**Fix:** Set `ui_height` to match your actual UI region height.

---

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Both modes clearly explained with diagrams
- [ ] Trade-off matrix complete and accurate
- [ ] Use cases documented with examples
- [ ] Mixed strategy explained with code
- [ ] Common mistakes listed with WRONG/RIGHT examples
- [ ] Debugging section for troubleshooting
- [ ] Links to related ADR (ADR-001)
- [ ] Code examples compile

---

## Location
`docs/concepts/screen-modes.md`

title: epic(graveyard-§7.7): Swiss Tables for Widget Lookup
description:
## Summary

Replace standard HashMap with SIMD-accelerated Swiss Tables (hashbrown crate with AHashMap). Score 12.0 — highest in the opportunity matrix, lowest effort. Expected 2x faster lookups for widget maps. Near drop-in replacement.

## Graveyard Entry

Section §7.7 — Swiss Tables for Widget Lookup  
Priority: 2  
EV Score: 12.0 — Ready (highest score, lowest effort)  

## Background & Math Foundations

Swiss Tables (Abseil, Google 2017) use SIMD instructions to probe multiple hash table slots simultaneously. The hashbrown crate is Rust's implementation (and is already used internally by std::collections::HashMap on many platforms, but using it directly with AHash gives better performance).

Key innovations:
- **SIMD probing**: Check 16 slots simultaneously using SSE2/AVX2
- **Metadata array**: 1-byte control tags per slot (7-bit hash + 1-bit empty/deleted)
- **Flat layout**: All metadata in contiguous array, enabling SIMD loads
- **Robin Hood removal**: No tombstones, no degradation under high load

Performance characteristics:
- Lookup: 1-2 SIMD probes for typical load factors (vs 3-5 scalar probes for std HashMap)
- Insert: Similar improvement
- Memory: Slightly lower due to no tombstone overhead

AHash (used with hashbrown) provides:
- Hardware-accelerated hashing via AES-NI
- ~3x faster than SipHash (std's default) for small keys
- Not cryptographic, but fine for widget ID hashing

## Why This Scores 12.0

- Effort: ~2 hours (change HashMap → AHashMap, update Cargo.toml)
- Impact: 2x faster widget lookups, which are on every frame's hot path
- Risk: Near zero (hashbrown is battle-tested, used by std internally)
- Reversibility: Trivial to revert

## Acceptance Criteria

1. All HashMap instances in widget registry replaced with AHashMap
2. Benchmark: 2x+ improvement on widget lookup microbenchmark
3. No behavioral changes (all existing tests pass unmodified)
4. No increase in compile time (hashbrown is already a transitive dependency)
close_reason: done

title: task(swiss-tables): Benchmark hashbrown vs std HashMap for widget lookups
description:
Quantitative benchmark comparing hashbrown/AHashMap vs std HashMap for widget registry operations to validate the expected 2x speedup.

## Detail

Benchmark scenarios:
1. Lookup by widget ID: 100, 1K, 10K widgets, random access pattern
2. Insert + lookup: Build registry from scratch, then random lookups
3. Mixed workload: 80% lookup, 10% insert, 10% remove (simulates frame-to-frame churn)

5. Hot key: Same widget looked up repeatedly (cache effects)

For each scenario, measure:
- p50/p95/p99 latency per operation
- Total throughput (ops/sec)
- Memory usage (RSS delta)
- Cache miss rate (via perf stat if available)

Implementation:

- Record results as CI artifacts for trend tracking

Expected results:
- 2x+ improvement on lookup operations
- Marginal improvement on sequential scan (dominated by memory bandwidth)
- Slight memory reduction (no tombstone overhead)

## Structured Logging

All benchmark results must be emitted as structured JSONL:
- op: bench_lookup, map_type, widget_count, p50_ns, p95_ns, p99_ns, ops_per_sec
- op: bench_mixed, map_type, widget_count, lookup_pct, insert_pct, remove_pct, throughput

- op: bench_summary, scenario, ahash_p50_ns, siphash_p50_ns, speedup_ratio

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Benchmark covers all 5 scenarios above
2. Results show statistically significant improvement (p < 0.05)
3. No regression on any operation
4. Results stored as CI artifacts with comparison visualization
5. Regression gate: future changes must not degrade by >5%

title: task(swiss-tables): Unit tests and integration validation with structured JSONL logging
description:
Comprehensive unit and integration test suite for the Swiss Tables (hashbrown/AHashMap) widget registry migration, with structured JSONL evidence logging. Validates correctness, performance parity, and no behavioral regression.

## Background

Swiss Tables (Abseil/Google 2017, hashbrown crate) use SIMD probing for 2x faster hash map lookups. Since the widget registry is on every frame hot path, replacing std HashMap with AHashMap must be validated exhaustively. Any subtle behavioral difference (iteration order change affecting determinism, hash collision pattern change) must be caught.

## Unit Tests

1. Insertion and retrieval: all widget types stored and retrieved correctly
2. Collision handling: verify correctness under high load factor (>0.9)
3. Deletion: remove widgets, verify no ghost entries or dangling references
4. Iteration order: document and test that iteration order differences do not affect frame output
5. Capacity and resize: verify automatic growth matches expected behavior
6. Empty map edge cases: operations on empty AHashMap produce correct results
7. Key types: test with WidgetId, String, and composite keys

## Integration Tests

1. Frame render parity: render 47+ golden frame scenarios with AHashMap, verify checksums match std HashMap baseline
2. Event dispatch: verify event routing through AHashMap-backed dispatch table matches baseline
3. Style cache: verify computed styles are identical with AHashMap-backed cache
4. Layout cache: verify cached layout results are identical
5. Concurrent access patterns: simulate multi-source widget updates

## Structured Logging

All tests emit JSONL records:
- test: test_name, phase: setup/execute/verify, map_type, entry_count, operation, result, timestamp_ns
- test: frame_parity, scenario, ahash_checksum, std_checksum, match: true/false
- test: collision_stress, load_factor, collision_count, max_probe_length

## Acceptance Criteria

1. 7+ unit tests covering all map operations and edge cases
2. 5+ integration tests verifying frame render and event dispatch parity
3. All tests emit structured JSONL logs
4. CI artifacts: JSONL logs, parity report, collision analysis
5. Deterministic: seeded keys for reproducible collision patterns
6. Zero tolerance: any frame checksum mismatch is a blocking failure

title: Document Terminal Compatibility Matrix
description:
# Terminal Compatibility Matrix Documentation

## Background
Plan Chapter 16 provides a detailed compatibility matrix. This needs to be documented for users to understand what features work where.

## Compatibility Matrix (from Plan)

| Feature | Kitty | WezTerm | Alacritty | Ghostty | iTerm2 | GNOME Term | Win Term |
|---------|-------|---------|-----------|---------|--------|------------|----------|
| True Color | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Sync Output | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| OSC 8 Links | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ |
| Kitty Keyboard | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| Kitty Graphics | ✓ | ✓ | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✗ |
| Sixel | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ | ✗ | ✗ |
| Focus Events | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Bracketed Paste | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |

## Feature Details

### True Color (24-bit RGB)
- Detection: COLORTERM=truecolor or COLORTERM=24bit
- Fallback: 256-color or 16-color palette
- Most modern terminals support this

### Synchronized Output (DEC 2026)
- Purpose: Atomic frame updates, flicker prevention
- Detection: Known terminal identification
- Fallback: Buffered writes still help
- ftui activates when detected

### OSC 8 Hyperlinks
- Purpose: Clickable links in terminal
- Format: `\x1b]8;;URL\x1b\\text\x1b]8;;\x1b\\`
- Windows Terminal: Not supported
- Most Linux/macOS terminals support

### Kitty Keyboard Protocol
- Purpose: Enhanced key event information
- Provides: press/repeat/release, modifiers
- Limited adoption outside Kitty ecosystem
- Feature-gated in ftui

### Scroll Region (DECSTBM)
- Purpose: Inline mode optimization
- Support: Nearly universal
- Quirks: tmux/screen passthrough issues
- ftui uses as optimization, not requirement

## Multiplexer Notes

### tmux
- Passthrough: Requires `\x1bPtmux;...\x1b\\`
- Sync output: Blocked by default
- OSC 8: Needs recent version + config
- Detection: TMUX env var

### screen
- Limited modern feature support
- No sync output passthrough
- Basic ANSI works fine
- Detection: STY env var

### Zellij
- Better passthrough than tmux/screen
- Native terminal support varies
- Detection: ZELLIJ env var

## Windows Considerations

### Windows Terminal
- True color: ✓
- Mouse: ✓
- OSC 8: ✗
- Sync output: ✗
- Raw mode: Via Crossterm

### ConEmu/Cmder
- Limited feature set
- True color: ✓ (newer versions)
- ANSI support varies by version

### cmd.exe / PowerShell (legacy)
- Very limited ANSI support
- Windows 10+ improved support
- Use Windows Terminal for best experience

## Inline Mode Notes
- Works everywhere (no special requirements)
- Cursor save/restore: Universal
- Scroll region: Nearly universal (optimization only)
- Sync output: Nice-to-have (not required)

## Recommended Test Matrix
For CI, test against:
1. Kitty (most features)
2. WezTerm (cross-platform)
3. Alacritty (popular, minimal)
4. Plain Linux VT (baseline)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Matrix table documented
- [ ] Feature descriptions complete
- [ ] Multiplexer notes included
- [ ] Windows section clear
- [ ] Inline mode notes present
- [ ] Test matrix recommended

title: Fix emoji-triggered border corruption in demo showcase (keep emojis)
description:
Problem
- Demo showcase has border misalignment/corruption in File Browser and Markdown screens when emojis are present. Emojis must remain.

Likely Causes
1) Several screens try to "clear" the full area using Paragraph::new("") + bg style, but Paragraph only paints style and does not clear cell content. With Flex gaps between panels, stale border characters from prior frames/screens can bleed into those gaps and appear as misaligned borders.
2) Buffer::print_text_clipped (ftui-render) advances by grapheme_width() but may only write the first char for multi-codepoint graphemes (e.g. VS16 sequences like "⚙️"), leaving holes that can preserve stale border chars.

Fix
- Clear demo screen root areas with actual space cells (bg=surface) so gaps are deterministically blank.
- Make Buffer::print_text_clipped fill any extra width when falling back to first char so no holes remain (and add a regression test).

Acceptance
- File Browser and Markdown screens render without stray/misaligned borders in gaps.
- Emojis remain enabled in file browser icons and unicode showcase.
- cargo fmt/check/clippy/test pass.

title: epic(graveyard-§7.1): Succinct Data Structures for Virtualized Lists
description:
## Summary

Compact representation of large virtualized lists using succinct bit-vectors (Elias-Fano encoding, LOUDS tree encoding). Expected 10x memory reduction for lists >100K rows. Profile first — only use where constants win (>100K element threshold).

## Graveyard Entry

Section §7.1 — Succinct Data Structures for Virtualized Lists  
Priority: 2  
EV Score: 4.0  

## Background & Math Foundations

Succinct data structures use space close to the information-theoretic minimum while supporting efficient queries. Two key structures:

**Elias-Fano encoding** for monotone integer sequences (height prefix sums):
- Stores n integers from universe [0, U) in n*ceil(log(U/n)) + 2n bits
- Supports rank/select in O(1) time with small constant
- For height prefix sums: U = total height, n = row count
- Example: 100K rows with total height 500K pixels → ~300KB vs 800KB for dense array

**LOUDS (Level-Order Unary Degree Sequence)** for tree structure:
- Encodes tree of n nodes in 2n + 1 bits
- Supports parent(), first_child(), next_sibling() in O(1) with rank/select
- For widget hierarchy: compact representation of tree structure for virtualized traversal

**When to use (threshold analysis):**
- Elias-Fano: beneficial when n > 100K (below this, dense array is faster due to cache effects)
- LOUDS: beneficial when tree depth > 10 AND n > 50K nodes
- Profile before committing: the constant factors in rank/select can dominate for small n

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Elias-Fano encoding for height prefix sums with O(1) rank/select
2. LOUDS encoding for widget hierarchy with O(1) tree navigation
3. 10x memory reduction demonstrated for lists >100K rows
4. Property tests: succinct query results match dense implementations exactly
5. Benchmark showing crossover point where succinct beats dense
6. Automatic fallback to dense when below threshold
close_reason: done

title: task(succinct): Implement Elias-Fano encoding for height prefix sums
description:
## Summary

Implement Elias-Fano encoding for monotone integer sequences, specifically targeting height prefix sums in virtualized lists. This enables O(1) lookup of "which row is at pixel offset Y?" with 10x less memory than a dense array.

## Detail

Elias-Fano encoding splits each integer into high bits and low bits:
- Low bits: stored explicitly in a dense array (ceil(log(U/n)) bits each)
- High bits: stored in unary encoding with a bit-vector supporting rank/select

Operations needed:
1. **encode(sorted_values: &[u64]) -> EliasFano**: Build the encoding from sorted height prefix sums
2. **access(index: usize) -> u64**: Get the prefix sum at a given row index
3. **rank(value: u64) -> usize**: Find how many prefix sums are <= value (which row is at pixel Y?)
4. **select(rank: usize) -> u64**: Get the rank-th prefix sum (pixel offset of row N)
5. **next_geq(value: u64) -> Option<(usize, u64)>**: Find the first prefix sum >= value

Implementation details:
- Use broadword programming for rank/select (Vigna 2008)
- Precompute rank superblocks every 512 bits for O(1) rank
- Select via binary search on rank superblocks + linear scan in block

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Correct encoding/decoding for all monotone sequences
2. O(1) rank and select operations (verified by benchmark)
3. Space usage within 10% of information-theoretic minimum
4. Property test: for any monotone sequence, all operations match naive implementation
5. Benchmark: memory comparison at 1K, 10K, 100K, 1M rows
6. Benchmark: query latency comparison vs dense array at same sizes
close_reason: done

title: task(succinct): Implement LOUDS tree encoding for widget hierarchy
description:
## Summary

Implement LOUDS (Level-Order Unary Degree Sequence) encoding for the widget tree hierarchy. This compacts the tree structure from O(n * ptr_size) to 2n+1 bits while supporting O(1) tree navigation.

## Detail

LOUDS encoding:
- Traverse tree in level order (BFS)
- For each node with d children, emit d ones followed by a zero
- Prepend a sentinel "10" for the super-root
- Total bits: 2n + 1 for n nodes

Navigation via rank/select on the bit-vector:
- parent(v): select0(rank1(v)) — jump to parent's degree sequence
- first_child(v): select1(rank0(v)) + 1 — jump to first child in next level
- next_sibling(v): v + 1 (if bit at v+1 is 1)
- is_leaf(v): bit at select1(rank0(v)) + 1 is 0

Use case in FrankenTUI:
- Virtualized tree views need to traverse large hierarchies for visible-range computation
- LOUDS allows traversal without materializing pointer-based tree in memory
- Combined with Elias-Fano for height sums, enables fully succinct virtualized tree views

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Correct LOUDS encoding from widget tree
2. O(1) parent, first_child, next_sibling, is_leaf operations
3. Property test: all navigation operations match pointer-based tree
4. Benchmark: memory comparison at 1K, 10K, 100K nodes
5. Integration test: virtualized tree view using LOUDS + Elias-Fano
close_reason: done

title: task(succinct): Benchmark succinct vs dense at various list sizes
description:
## Summary

Quantitative comparison of succinct data structures (Elias-Fano, LOUDS) vs dense arrays/pointer trees across a range of list sizes to identify the crossover point.

## Detail

Benchmark matrix:
- List sizes: 100, 1K, 10K, 100K, 1M rows
- Operations: random access, range query, sequential scan, insert (rebuild)
- Data structures: dense array, Elias-Fano, LOUDS (for tree), pointer tree
- Metrics: memory usage, query latency (p50/p95/p99), build time

Expected crossover points:
- Elias-Fano beats dense for memory at ~10K rows
- Elias-Fano beats dense for cache performance at ~100K rows (fits in L2 vs spills to L3)
- LOUDS beats pointer tree at ~50K nodes for memory
- Dense may beat succinct for query latency at <10K rows (simpler code, fewer cache misses)

The crossover analysis drives the automatic selection: use dense below threshold, succinct above.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Full benchmark matrix with memory and latency measurements
2. Clear identification of crossover points for each operation
3. Automatic fallback threshold derived from benchmarks
4. Results stored as CI artifacts
5. Recommendation: which data structure to use at each scale
close_reason: done

title: task(succinct): Property tests — succinct query results match dense
description:
## Summary

Property-based testing to verify that succinct data structures (Elias-Fano, LOUDS) produce identical query results to their dense counterparts for all operations.

## Detail

Property tests using proptest:

1. **Elias-Fano vs dense array:**
   - Generate random sorted sequences of length 1..10K
   - For each sequence, verify: access(i) matches dense[i] for all i
   - For each sequence, verify: rank(v) matches linear scan count for random v
   - For each sequence, verify: select(r) matches dense scan for random r
   - For each sequence, verify: next_geq(v) matches linear scan for random v

2. **LOUDS vs pointer tree:**
   - Generate random trees with 1..1K nodes and branching factor 1..10
   - For each tree, verify: parent(v) matches pointer-based parent for all v
   - For each tree, verify: first_child(v) matches pointer-based for all v
   - For each tree, verify: next_sibling(v) matches pointer-based for all v
   - For each tree, verify: is_leaf(v) matches pointer-based for all v
   - For each tree, verify: DFS traversal order is identical

3. **Round-trip tests:**
   - Build succinct from dense, query all elements, verify identity
   - Rebuild succinct from same data, verify bit-identical encoding

## Acceptance Criteria

1. All property tests pass with 10K+ cases each
2. Shrinking produces minimal failing cases when tests fail
3. Edge cases covered: empty sequence, single element, maximum size, all-same values
4. Tests run in CI with reproducible seeds
close_reason: done

title: task(succinct): E2E integration tests with structured JSONL logging
description:
## Summary

End-to-end integration tests for succinct data structures (Elias-Fano, LOUDS) verifying correct behavior within the virtualized list/tree widget pipeline, with structured JSONL evidence logging.

## Background

Succinct data structures operate at the bit level. Off-by-one errors in rank/select are silent and catastrophic — they cause the wrong row to render at the wrong pixel offset. E2E tests must verify the full pipeline from user scrolls to offset Y to correct row is visible.

## Detail

### E2E Tests

1. **Scroll-to-offset**: Build 100K-row list with Elias-Fano height sums, scroll to random offsets, verify correct visible rows
2. **Viewport resize**: Resize viewport during scroll, verify visible rows update correctly with succinct backing
3. **Dynamic insert/delete**: Insert/remove rows, rebuild succinct structure, verify scroll position preserved
4. **Threshold crossover**: Test at 99K rows (dense) and 101K rows (succinct), verify identical visible output
5. **LOUDS tree navigation**: Build 50K-node tree widget with LOUDS backing, verify expand/collapse/scroll
6. **Round-trip**: Dense -> succinct -> query all -> compare with dense queries, verify bitwise identical
7. **Degenerate inputs**: All same heights, zero heights, maximum heights, single row

### Structured Logging

```json
{"test":"scroll_to_offset","row_count":100000,"scroll_offset_px":452300,"expected_first_row":12045,"actual_first_row":12045,"query_ns":42,"encoding":"elias_fano"}
{"test":"threshold_crossover","row_count":101000,"encoding":"elias_fano","memory_bytes":31200,"dense_memory_bytes":808000,"ratio":0.039}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

1. 7+ E2E tests covering scroll, resize, dynamic mutation, threshold, tree, round-trip, and degenerate inputs
2. All tests emit structured JSONL with row counts, memory usage, query latency, and correctness status
3. Memory comparison report: succinct vs dense at each test size
4. Performance report: query latency percentiles at each test size
5. CI artifacts: JSONL logs, memory report, latency report
6. Zero tolerance: any incorrect visible row is a blocking failure
close_reason: done

title: Optional OpenTelemetry Audit Trail
description:
Add optional OTEL plumbing (via tracing) so apps can export runtime spans/decisions to a collector without default performance cost.

## Success Criteria
- Epic delivers a cohesive user-visible capability: Optional OpenTelemetry Audit Trail
- Child tasks are not just implemented; each has unit tests + E2E scripts with verbose JSONL logs and deterministic fixtures
- Graceful degradation tiers are specified (capabilities, fallbacks, safety) and validated in tests
- Epic includes a perf budget + regression suite (hyperfine + flamegraphs + CI gates) with explainable failures


## Alien Artifact Upgrades
- Model the core decision(s) with explicit state, priors/assumptions, and invariants; write down failure modes as first-class artifacts.
- Explainability: add an evidence ledger for any non-trivial decision (why this branch, why this fallback). Prefer Bayes factors / log-likelihood contributions over ad-hoc scoring.
- Guarantees: where prediction/thresholding exists, prefer distribution-free calibration (conformal prediction) or anytime-valid testing (e-process) so we can stop early without invalid inference.
- Graceful degradation: define capability tiers + deterministic fallbacks; never fail closed without a traceable reason.
- Drift/Regimes: if runtime metrics vary (resize storms, frame pacing), incorporate change-point detection and regime-specific policies.


## Extreme Optimization
- Baseline first: capture p50/p95/p99 for relevant command(s) with `hyperfine` (store raw output).
- Profile next: CPU flamegraph + allocation profile; identify top-5 hotspots.
- Opportunity matrix: implement only Score ≥ 2.0 (Impact×Confidence/Effort).
- Isomorphism proof per change: ordering, tie-breaking, RNG seeds, and golden checksums must match.
- Regression gates: add microbench + budgets; failures must print actionable deltas and include log artifacts.
- Add JSONL perf logs with schema: run_id, case, env, features, seed, metrics, budgets, pass/fail, and artifact paths.


## Testing Plan
- Unit tests: happy path + edge cases + regression fixtures.
- Property tests: invariants (idempotence, monotonicity, determinism) where applicable.
- Fuzz tests: parsers/state machines and any input-facing logic.
- Determinism: fixed seeds/time-freeze; snapshot fixtures must be stable.

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
Research summary (2026-02-03):

Recommended crates/versions (from opentelemetry-rust 0.31.0 release line):
- opentelemetry = "0.31"
- opentelemetry_sdk = "0.31"
- opentelemetry-otlp = "0.31"
- tracing-opentelemetry = "0.32.1" (note: tracing-opentelemetry versions are not synced; typically one ahead of opentelemetry crates)
- tracing = "0.1", tracing-subscriber = "0.3"

Integration pattern:
1) Build SdkTracerProvider with OTLP exporter; prefer batch processor for production. SimpleSpanProcessor is synchronous (debug). BatchSpanProcessor uses background thread and is higher throughput.
2) Install tracer provider and a tracing subscriber with OpenTelemetryLayer (tracing-opentelemetry).
3) Configure global propagator (TraceContext + Baggage) via TextMapCompositePropagator, or use OTEL_PROPAGATORS env var.
4) For explicit parent context, use OpenTelemetrySpanExt::set_parent and Context extraction/injection.

Env var contract to support (aligned to OTel spec):
- OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true => no-op SDK.
- OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES for Resource (service.name).
- OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER / OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER / OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER (default otlp).
- OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT (default gRPC 4317, HTTP 4318; HTTP appends /v1/traces etc).
- OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL (+ *_TRACES_PROTOCOL, *_METRICS_PROTOCOL) values: grpc | http/protobuf | http/json.
- OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS (+ per-signal) key=value list.

Note: opentelemetry-otlp 0.31 notes env vars do not override code config; if we want env-driven config, avoid hard-coded exporter settings.

title: Widget API Frame Integration Tests
description:
## Purpose

Create comprehensive integration tests for the Widget + Frame API to ensure all Frame features work correctly.

## Test Categories

### 1. Frame Feature Tests
- `frame.buffer` access from Widget::render
- `frame.hit_grid` registration and retrieval
- `frame.cursor_position` setting and clearing
- `frame.degradation` level checking

### 2. Widget Category Tests
Each category should have tests:

**Category A (buffer-only):**
- Block renders borders correctly
- Paragraph wraps text
- Rule draws lines

**Category B (hit testing):**
- List registers hit regions for each item
- Table registers hit regions for rows/cells
- Hit IDs are unique and retrievable

**Category C (cursor):**
- TextInput positions cursor correctly
- Cursor visibility toggles work

**Category D (degradation):**
- ProgressBar simplifies at EssentialOnly
- Spinner shows label-only at reduced levels

### 3. Edge Cases
- Empty area (0x0)
- Single cell area (1x1)
- Unicode content with Frame
- Widget nesting with Frame forwarding

## Test Template

```rust
#[test]
fn test_widget_frame_feature() {
    let mut pool = GraphemePool::new();
    let mut frame = Frame::new(80, 24, &mut pool);
    
    // Arrange
    let widget = TestWidget::new();
    let area = Rect::new(0, 0, 10, 5);
    
    // Act
    widget.render(area, &mut frame);
    
    // Assert
    assert!(frame.buffer.get(0, 0).symbol == "expected");
    // Add detailed assertions...
}
```

## Success Criteria
- All Frame features have dedicated tests
- Each widget category has test coverage
- Edge cases documented and tested
- Tests include logging for debugging

title: feature(pane-a11y): keyboard parity and accessibility semantics
description:
Goal

What this feature owns

Definition of done

design:

- Accessibility semantics are first-class pane operations, not post-hoc wrappers.

- Focus graph traversal is derived from split-tree topology for deterministic behavior under nested layouts.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Every pointer pane workflow has complete keyboard parity across terminal and web.
2) Focus, announcements, and adaptive modes are deterministic and validated.
3) Accessibility regressions are covered by repeatable scripted checks with rich logs.

title: task(pane-a11y): define canonical keyboard command model and focus graph semantics
description:
Background
- Full accessibility requires a first-class non-pointer interaction contract equivalent in power to pointer drag-resize.

Scope
- Define global pane commands (focus-next/prev, focus-edge, split, close, resize-step, move-pane, swap-pane, maximize/restore).
- Define focus graph traversal rules that are deterministic for any split-tree topology.
- Define conflict/precedence policy for app-level keymaps vs pane-manager keymaps.

Design notes
- Commands must map to semantic operations rather than host-specific key events.
- Repeat-key behavior and acceleration policy must be explicit and testable.

Acceptance
- A normative keyboard interaction spec exists with deterministic tie-break rules.
- Equivalent command streams yield identical pane state across terminal and web hosts.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Implement scoped accessibility behavior with deterministic keyboard/focus semantics.
2) Add unit/integration checks for affected focus traversal, command mapping, or announcement behavior.
3) Add or update scripted a11y regression scenarios covering impacted workflows.
4) Ensure diagnostics include focus state, command sequence, and host context for failures.
close_reason: Canonical PaneCommand model + deterministic focus graph + normative spec implemented (pane_command.rs 13 tests + docs/spec/pane-keyboard-interaction.md); --force past open parent epic bd-21pbi only; host bindings = bd-21pbi.2/.3.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Implemented the canonical keyboard command model + focus-graph semantics as a host-agnostic, executable contract.

Deliverables:
- crates/ftui-layout/src/pane_command.rs (new module, 13 tests): PaneCommand vocabulary (FocusNext/Previous, FocusDirectional, FocusEdge, ResizeStep, Split, Close, MovePane, SwapPane, Maximize, Restore); deterministic focus graph (topological in-order focus_order; cyclic focus_cyclic; edge-based spatial focus_directional with explicit tie-breaks [primary center distance -> perpendicular overlap -> focus-order index]; focus_edge); pure resolve() mapping each command to Focus | Structural(Vec<PaneOperation>) | Maximize/Restore | Noop(reason); PaneCommandAcceleration (repeat policy); PaneKeymapPrecedence (app vs pane-manager conflict resolution).
- docs/spec/pane-keyboard-interaction.md: the normative spec (RFC-2119), documenting the vocabulary, focus-graph tie-break rules, command->effect mapping, acceleration, precedence, no-op reasons, and the determinism + cross-host-equivalence guarantee.

Acceptance mapping:
1) Deterministic keyboard/focus semantics: resolve() is pure over (tree, layout, focus_context, command); commands map to semantic operations, never host key events.
2) Unit checks: focus order/cyclic/directional/edge, command mapping (incl. resize lowered through the SHARED PaneDragResizeMachine + operations_for_transition so keyboard resize uses the exact same nudge math as pointer/wheel), close survivor, maximize/restore, acceleration, precedence.
3) a11y regression scenario at the MODEL level: command_stream_is_deterministic_and_host_agnostic proves identical state_hash + active across runs (the cross-host parity property). HOST-level scripted a11y regression lands with the binding beads (bd-21pbi.2 terminal, bd-21pbi.3 web) which produce the commands.
4) Diagnostics: PaneCommandNoopReason gives machine-readable failure reasons; spec section 7 requires diagnostics to include active pane + command + reason (host context supplied by the binding layer).

Reuse (no duplication): SplitAxis, PaneResizeDirection, PanePlacement, PaneOperation/apply_operation, PaneSemanticInputEventKind::KeyboardResize + PaneDragResizeMachine, PaneLayout geometry, PANE_SNAP_DEFAULT_STEP_BPS. New: PaneCardinalDirection + the command/focus layer. Library code is panic-free (UBS criticals are the project's accepted test-code panic! pattern only).

Verification: 13/13 module tests pass; full ftui-layout lib suite 584 pass (no regression); cargo clippy --lib --tests -D warnings clean; fmt clean; cargo check --workspace --all-targets clean (additive public API breaks no downstream). Boundary: terminal/web key->command bindings + roving tabindex + ARIA are bd-21pbi.2/.3 (this bead defines the model they target).

comments.text:
Implemented the terminal keyboard binding layer over the canonical command model (bd-21pbi.1), as reusable, fully-tested library code in crates/ftui-runtime/src/pane_keymap.rs (8 tests).

Deliverables (all three bead sub-parts):

Modifier-qualified so it coexists with app shortcuts and never steals plain keys: Tab/Shift+Tab=focus next/prev; Ctrl+Arrows=focus directional; Ctrl+Shift+Arrows=focus edge; Alt+Arrows=move pane; Alt+'+'/'-'=grow/shrink; Alt+s/Alt+v=split H/V; Alt+w=close; Alt+[/]=swap prev/next; Alt+z/Alt+r=maximize/restore. Plus PaneKeyboardController: a reusable host helper that ties key->command->resolve->apply structural ops->track focus/maximize, with repeat-key resize acceleration. The controller_drives_pointer_free_workflow test proves a complete keyboard-only session (focus, split, directional focus, close, maximize/restore) mutating a real PaneTree deterministically — i.e. pointer-free workflows are operable; close updates focus to the deterministic survivor; unbound keys never touch state.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Implemented the web host binding over the canonical command model (bd-21pbi.1), the browser counterpart to the terminal binding (bd-21pbi.2). Reusable, fully-tested library code: crates/ftui-web/src/pane_keyboard.rs (7 tests).

Deliverables:
1) Browser key -> canonical pane command: key_to_pane_command(KeyEvent, resize_units) -> Option<PaneCommand>. BROWSER-SAFE: refuses any key carrying Ctrl or Super so it never steals browser/OS shortcuts (Ctrl+W close-tab, Ctrl++ zoom, Cmd+...). Binds plain + Shift keys (roving-tabindex pattern, host-gated to the focused pane container): Arrows=focus directional; Shift+Arrows=move; Home/End/PageUp/PageDown=focus edge; n/p=focus next/prev; =/-=grow/shrink; s/v=split H/V; x or Delete=close; [/]=swap prev/next; f/Escape=maximize/restore.
2) Roving tabindex + ARIA: pane_accessibility_tree(tree, focus) -> Vec<PaneAriaNode>. NORMATIVE roving invariant: exactly one leaf (effective-active; defaults to first in focus_order when unfocused) has tabindex=0, all other leaves -1 -> the pane manager is a single reachable Tab stop with internal arrow nav (no focus trap). Panes: role=group + aria-current on active. Splitters: role=separator + aria-orientation (horizontal split's divider is vertical, and vice-versa) + aria-valuenow/min(0)/max(100) = first-child share % -> AT can identify active pane, splitter orientation, and resize affordances.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Implemented accessible announcements for pane state transitions as a host-agnostic, deterministic, coalescing model.

Deliverables:
- Payload schema (ftui-layout pane_command): PaneAnnouncement { text, category: PaneAnnouncementCategory(Focus/Resize/Split/Close/Move/Swap/Maximize/Restore) } + announce_command(command, resolution, tree) -> Option<PaneAnnouncement>. No-ops emit nothing.

Acceptance: (1) deterministic announcement semantics; (2) unit tests for announcement text per transition + coalescing/dedupe + controller surfacing; (3) the coalescing + per-transition tests are the a11y regression scenarios; (4) diagnostics: announcements carry category + text, controllers expose pending/taken state. title: task(e2e): E2E test suite for Roaring Bitmap Dirty Tracking
description:
## E2E Integration Test: Roaring Bitmaps (EV=18)

### Scope
Full integration test rendering with Roaring bitmap-based dirty region tracking. Validates that diff output is identical to BitVec baseline and logs dirty set metrics per frame.

### Test Scenario
1. Initialize FrankenTUI with Roaring bitmap dirty tracking replacing BitVec.
2. Render all demo screens, performing incremental updates (text edits, scrolls, resizes).
3. On each frame, compute dirty regions using Roaring union/intersection.
4. Simultaneously compute dirty regions using BitVec (shadow comparison).
5. Verify diff output (escape sequences sent to terminal) is byte-identical.
6. Test edge cases: full-screen dirty, single-cell dirty, empty dirty, alternating rows.

### JSONL Structured Logging Specification
Each frame emits:
```json
{
  "event": "roaring_frame",
  "ts_ns": u64,
  "frame_id": u64,
  "screen": "string",
  "dirty_cells": u32,
  "dirty_rows": u32,
  "roaring_container_type": "array|bitmap|run",
  "set_size_bytes": u32,
  "union_time_ns": u64,
  "intersection_time_ns": u64,
  "diff_output_hash": "hex_string",
  "bitvec_diff_hash": "hex_string",
  "match": bool
}
```

### Success Criteria
- match == true for every frame (Roaring produces identical diff output to BitVec).
- Roaring set_size_bytes <= BitVec size for dense dirty patterns.
- Union/intersection times scale sublinearly with screen size.
- No panics, no unsafe code (#![forbid(unsafe_code)]).
- JSONL log is schema-compliant and parseable.
- Handles terminal sizes from 24x80 to 200x400.
close_reason: done

title: Parser: HTS/TBC/CBT tab stop sequences + DECKPAM/DECKPNM keypad modes + conformance fixtures
description:
## Gap Analysis

frankenterm-core cursor.rs has full tab stop logic (set_tab_stop, clear_tab_stop, clear_all_tab_stops, next_tab_stop, prev_tab_stop) but the parser has NO action variants for:
- HTS (ESC H) - Set Tab Stop at current column

- CBT (CSI Ps Z) - Cursor Backward Tabulation
- DECKPAM (ESC =) - Application Keypad Mode
- DECKPNM (ESC >) - Normal Keypad Mode

title: task(pane-perf): instrument allocation and retention telemetry for replay, checkpoint, and versioned paths
description:
Goal
- Turn pane-memory work into a measured discipline by capturing allocation volume, object retention, checkpoint/version residency, and state-hash overhead across competing execution strategies.

Why this exists
- The performance plan now includes checkpointing and possible persistence. That changes the memory problem from simple transient churn to total retained-state economics.

Deliverables
- Telemetry for transient allocations and retained memory.
- Comparable measurements for baseline, checkpointed, and persistent paths.
- Artifact format suitable for CI or local perf triage.
- Notes on the dominant memory drivers.

Acceptance
- Memory behavior is measurable and attributable by strategy.
- Future retention and pruning work has concrete baselines to optimize against.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Telemetry covers transient allocation counts, retained-state classes, checkpoint/version residency, state-hash overhead, and strategy-specific memory footprints.
2) The telemetry path is regression-tested and emits structured artifacts/manifests reusable by CI, local debugging, and later pruning-policy work.
3) Logs and reports make the dominant memory drivers understandable to humans, not just raw counters.
4) Measurements are deterministic enough to compare baseline, checkpointed, persistent, and policy-selected strategies meaningfully.
close_reason: Cross-strategy pane-memory telemetry (transient + retained) instrumented, regression-tested, deterministic, with JSON artifact + measured baselines. All 4 acceptance criteria met.

comments.author: AmberBadger
comments.text: Background: this bead exists so future sessions do not talk vaguely about memory again. The core question is not only how many allocations happen but what must remain resident to buy replay/undo performance and how much that costs. The telemetry should make that trade space explicit.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Implemented cross-strategy pane-memory telemetry. Deliverables: (lib) crates/ftui-layout/src/pane_memory.rs = PaneMemoryComparison/PaneMemoryStrategyFootprint/PaneMemoryDriver + pure deterministic pane_memory_comparison(baseline,checkpointed,persistent); (lib) PaneVersionStore::retention -> PaneVersionRetention byte model mirroring the canonical timeline methodology; (bench) crates/ftui-layout/benches/pane_memory_telemetry.rs emits a JSON manifest (schema_version-stamped) combining stats_alloc transient allocation counts + the modeled retained-state comparison across two workloads; (doc) docs/perf/pane_memory_telemetry.md with measured baselines.

Acceptance evidence:
(1) Telemetry covers transient alloc counts (stats_alloc Region per strategy), retained-state classes (node structs / leaf / extension / op-log / state-hash / container+metadata), version/checkpoint residency (retained_unit_count), state-hash overhead (dedicated class = entries x 2 x u64), and per-strategy footprints.
(2) Regression-tested (9 tests: 6 pane_memory + 3 pane_persistent::retention_*) and emits a structured JSON manifest reusable by CI/local triage and the pruning work.
(3) Dominant memory driver surfaced per strategy + one-line human summary + doc tables. Headline: node structs dominate ALL strategies (op-log+hashes are minor), so pruning must target retained nodes.
(4) Deterministic (comparison_is_deterministic): identical inputs -> byte-identical reports; baseline/checkpointed/persistent compared, and policy-selected is covered by passing a with_max_versions store.

Measured baselines (resize_storm 512 ops): baseline 15.7KB; checkpointed 575.6KB (36.6x baseline); persistent 1907.7KB (3.31x checkpointed). mixed_session: checkpointed/baseline 24.2x, persistent/checkpointed 2.98x. Modeled vs allocator-measured retained corroborate (576KB vs 604KB checkpointed).

title: task(pane-perf): design bounded retention and pruning policy for checkpoints, versions, and caches
description:
Goal
- Define and implement a deterministic retention policy that caps memory growth from checkpointing, persistent versions, and any pane perf caches without breaking replay or debugging requirements.

Why this exists
- Architectural replay-speed improvements are only operationally safe if they come with explicit memory ceilings and pruning behavior.

Scope
- Identify the retained-state classes that need caps.
- Define pruning rules and their invariants.
- Ensure debugging, replay, and state-hash guarantees remain understandable under retention pressure.
- Document fallback behavior when the budget is exhausted.

Deliverables
- Retention-policy specification.
- Implementation of caps and pruning behavior.
- Tests for pruning edge cases and deterministic fallback.
- Memory-before/after evidence.

Acceptance
- Memory usage is bounded by explicit policy rather than hope.
- Policy behavior is deterministic, observable, and regression-tested.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Unit and integration tests cover pruning edge cases, deterministic budget enforcement, replay/debug fallback behavior, and state-hash preservation under retention pressure.
2) The policy emits detailed telemetry and human-readable logs for retained-state classes, pruning decisions, budget exhaustion, and fallback events.
3) Operators and developers can force conservative behavior during debugging and understand exactly what data may be discarded by policy.
4) Memory ceilings are explicit, regression-tested, and tied to user-facing responsiveness and operational safety rather than hidden cache growth.
close_reason: Unified bounded-retention/pruning policy (byte+unit budget, conservative-debug, deterministic floor) implemented across persistent store + checkpointed timeline; 8 tests, telemetry decisions, before/after evidence, spec doc. All 4 acceptance criteria met.

comments.author: AmberBadger
comments.text: Reasoning: this bead is the operational guardrail for the whole asymptotic optimization effort. Bigger speedups are not worth much if they quietly turn pane interactions into an unbounded retained-memory system. The right output here is a policy future operators and developers can explain, not just a cache that seems fine.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Implemented unified bounded-retention & pruning policy. Deliverables: (lib) crates/ftui-layout/src/pane_retention.rs = PaneRetentionPolicy (byte + unit budget, 0=unbounded) + conservative-debug override + PaneRetentionDecision (serde telemetry + human log) + PaneRetentionOutcome {WithinBudget,PrunedToFit,ConservativeHold,FloorReached}; actuators apply_to_version_store + apply_to_timeline prune oldest history (newest unit always kept). (substrate hooks) PaneVersionStore::set_max_versions + PaneInteractionTimeline::set_max_entries = retroactive enforce. (bench) pane_memory_telemetry.rs now emits before/after policy decisions for both substrates. (doc) docs/perf/pane_retention_policy.md = spec + measured evidence.

Acceptance evidence:
(1) 8 tests cover pruning edge cases, deterministic budget enforcement (unit cap + byte budget), replay/debug fallback (conservative hold + floor), and state-hash preservation under retention pressure (head hash asserted unchanged across pruning on BOTH substrates).
(2) PaneRetentionDecision is serde-serializable telemetry (strategy, budget, units/bytes before-after, units pruned, outcome, preserved head hash) + a human-readable log line; the bench emits these as a CI artifact.
(3) Conservative-debug mode (PaneRetentionPolicy::conservative()) disables pruning and reports ConservativeHold so operators see what WOULD be discarded; the log names the retained-state class + counts.
(4) Memory ceilings are explicit (byte + unit), regression-tested, with a deterministic FloorReached safety stop (the live state is never sacrificed to a byte budget; the timeline floor = its baseline snapshot).

Measured before/after (cargo bench pane_memory_telemetry), head_hash IDENTICAL before/after = state preserved:
- resize_storm: persistent 513->125 versions, 1.91MB->475KB (budget 477KB, pruned_to_fit); timeline 512->240 entries, 576KB->278KB (budget 288KB).
- mixed_session: persistent 385->89, 879KB->209KB; timeline 384->160, 295KB->141KB.

title: task(pane-perf): reduce pane-core churn via structural sharing and small-object hot-path storage
description:
Goal
- Apply memory-focused hot-path changes such as structural sharing, compact touched-node storage, or other usually-small representations where the data justifies them.

Why this exists
- Once allocation/retention telemetry is available, this bead owns the concrete hot-path memory reductions that do not require a broader strategy shift on their own.

Deliverables
- One-lever memory reductions based on measured hotspots.
- Benchmarks and telemetry showing reduced churn or retained size.
- Proof notes showing semantics remain unchanged.

Acceptance
- Memory churn or retained state falls on the targeted path.
- No opaque or unbounded storage policy is introduced.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Any hot-path memory change is justified by measured churn or retained-state evidence, not aesthetic preference.
2) Unit and integration tests cover representation invariants, fallback behavior, and semantic equivalence where compact storage or sharing alters internal structure.
3) Detailed telemetry and logs explain what memory was saved, on which workloads, and with what trade-offs.
4) No optimization in this bead can bypass the bounded-retention policy or make rollback/debugging materially harder.
close_reason: Compact touched-node storage (SmallVec outcome + slice validators) makes the SetSplitRatio resize hot path allocation-free: measured 3.00->0.00 allocs/op. Equivalence-proven (differential oracle + 640 tests). Completes bd-25wj7 (3/3).

comments.author: AmberBadger
comments.text: Intent: keep this bead grounded. It should only absorb changes that clearly target measured pane-memory hotspots and that remain understandable in the presence of checkpointing or persistence. The existence of small-object techniques is not enough by itself; the profile must demand them.

comments.author: ubuntu
comments.text:
Reduced pane-core hot-path churn via compact touched-node storage — the resize fast path is now ALLOCATION-FREE. MEASURED (bench fast_path_resize, 512 SetSplitRatio ops on a plain tree): 1536 allocations (3.00/op, 61440 bytes) -> 0 allocations (0.00/op, 0 bytes).

The lever (both 'compact touched-node storage'):
1. validate_local_closure / validate_after_operation{,_with_mode} now take &[PaneId] instead of &BTreeSet<PaneId> (the validator only ITERATES touched). The fast path passes a stack slice &[split_id] — was BTreeSet::from([split_id]) (the B-tree alloc was 2 of the 3). The generic clone path collects its touched BTreeSet into the outcome SmallVec once and passes that (coerces to slice), reusing it for validation + outcome.
2. PaneOperationOutcome::touched_nodes and PaneOperationError::touched_nodes are now SmallVec<[PaneId; 4]> (inline for the common small case; resize touches 1 node) — was Vec, the outcome alloc. PaneOperationJournalEntry (serialized) keeps Vec; converted at that boundary via to_vec().

Out of scope (intentionally): the conservative path's whole-tree self.clone() (the ~20MB baseline churn) is a representation/strategy shift owned by bd-1k7ek.5 + gated by bd-25wj7.2, not a local lever.

Acceptance evidence:
(1) Justified by MEASURED churn (bench before/after 3.00->0.00 allocs/op), not aesthetics.
(2) Representation invariant test (touched_nodes_compact_storage_holds_correct_content: structural + fast + rejected paths) + the certified differential oracle pane_operation_family_equivalence (fast==conservative over 48x40 histories) + pane_persistent_equivalence, all green. 640 lib tests pass.
(3) docs/perf/pane_churn_reduction.md explains what was saved, on which workload, and the trade-off; the bench manifest carries fast_path_resize.
(4) SmallVec<[PaneId;4]> is bounded (4 inline + heap spill) — no opaque/unbounded policy, does NOT touch the bounded-retention policy, and the public field is still a contiguous PaneId sequence (rollback/debug unchanged).

title: Text Effects: Cursor/Caret Animation
description:
## Background
Typewriter and terminal effects need a blinking cursor. Currently no cursor support.

## Implementation

Add TextEffect variant:
```rust
TextEffect::Cursor {
    style: CursorStyle,
    blink_speed: f64,    // Blinks per second (0 = no blink)
    position: CursorPosition,
}

pub enum CursorStyle {
    Block,      // █
    Underline,  // _
    Bar,        // |
    Custom(char),
}

pub enum CursorPosition {
    End,                  // After last visible char
    AtIndex(usize),       // At specific index
    AfterReveal,          // After last revealed char (for Typewriter)
}
```

### Integration with Reveal Effects:
```rust
StyledText::new("Hello World")
    .effect(TextEffect::Reveal { mode: LeftToRight, progress: 0.5 })
    .effect(TextEffect::Cursor { 
        style: CursorStyle::Block,
        blink_speed: 2.0,
        position: CursorPosition::AfterReveal,
    })
// Cursor appears after 'Hello' (the revealed part)
```

crates/ftui-extras/src/text_effects.rs

- test_cursor_at_end: Cursor after last char
- test_cursor_blinks: Visible/invisible cycles
- test_cursor_after_reveal: Follows reveal progress
- test_cursor_custom_char: Uses specified character

title: epic(graveyard-§5.10): Per-Frame Arena Allocation for Render Path
description:
Region-based memory: per-frame arena eliminates allocator churn on hot render path. EV=24.0 (Tier S). CONSTRAINT: #![forbid(unsafe_code)] — MUST use bumpalo crate (safe bump allocator) instead of hand-rolled unsafe arena. bumpalo::Bump provides: alloc_with(), alloc_slice_copy(), reset(). Thread-local Bump per frame, reset at frame boundary. Apply to: Frame rendering temp allocations, widget layout scratch space, text segment construction. Fallback: standard allocator (no arena). Isomorphism: identical output (allocator is transparent). Risk: bumpalo lifetime ergonomics. Baseline: malloc/free per frame via heaptrack.

**User Value:** Eliminates per-frame allocation jitter, giving app developers smoother animation and reduced p99 tail latency.
