title: OpenTUI Core Systems (opentui_rust port)
description:
# OpenTUI Core Systems (reference extraction, not a blind port)

## Purpose
This epic exists for **traceability** to `opentui_rust`.

We are not doing a 1:1 port. Instead, we selectively extract ideas and components that strengthen FrankenTUI’s kernel or optional extras.

## Plan Alignment
The plan explicitly says:
- keep only kernel-strengthening primitives
- de-scope “the widget zoo” into feature-gated layers

This epic is a place to record what we *borrowed*, why, and where it lands in the ftui crate layout.

## Reference Source
- `legacy_reference_library_code/opentui_rust/src/`

## What We Intend To Reuse (High-level)
- Efficient terminal control sequence encoding (CSI/OSC/DEC modes)
- Buffer drawing helpers (lines/rects/borders) to implement widgets ergonomically
- Robust raw-mode / cleanup discipline patterns
- Optional text infrastructure (rope/editor/view) if/when we ship a richer editor
- Optional unicode utilities (normalization/search/bidi) if/when needed
- Optional tokenization infrastructure for syntax highlighting

## Tracked Issues (live elsewhere in the plan tree)
These issues are the concrete “extractions” and/or feature-gated extras derived from OpenTUI:
- `bd-3ky.1` ANSI sequence encoding helpers (feeds Presenter / TerminalWriter)
- `bd-3ky.2` Buffer drawing operations (feeds widget implementations)
- `bd-3ky.10` Raw mode handling + cleanup patterns (feeds TerminalSession / backend)
- `bd-3ky.3` Tokenizer engine (optional; feeds syntax highlighting)
- `bd-3ky.13` Language tokenizers (optional; feeds syntax highlighting)
- `bd-3ky.4` Highlight theme system (optional; feeds syntax highlighting)
- `bd-3ky.5` Rope (optional; feeds TextArea/editor)
- `bd-3ky.6` Editor core (optional; feeds TextArea/editor)
- `bd-3ky.14` Text View (optional; feeds Viewport/TextArea)
- `bd-3ky.7` BiDi (optional)
- `bd-3ky.8` Normalization (optional)
- `bd-3ky.9` Search (optional)

## Non-Goals
- A monolithic “OpenTUI port” that blocks ftui kernel shipping
- Shipping optional features before Gate 1–2 (inline stability + presenter correctness)

## Success Criteria

description:
# Implement ANSI sequence encoding helpers (CSI/OSC/DEC)

## Objective
Implement a small, well-tested set of helpers to encode the ANSI/VT control sequences that ftui emits.

This is **not** about terminal state tracking or diffing; it is only about producing correct bytes for known operations.

## Why This Exists
Presenter correctness depends on:
- emitting syntactically valid sequences
- emitting correctly terminated OSC strings
- using consistent conventions (1-indexed CUP, correct separators)

Isolating sequence encoding makes the Presenter easier to reason about and test.

## Reference (for ideas / completeness)
- `legacy_reference_library_code/opentui_rust/src/ansi/output.rs`
- `legacy_reference_library_code/opentui_rust/src/ansi/sequences.rs`

## Scope
Support encoding helpers for sequences we plan to use:

### CSI sequences
- SGR (reset, attributes, fg/bg: 16/256/truecolor)
- CUP cursor positioning (row/col, 1-indexed)
- relative cursor moves (optional; only if Presenter uses them)
- EL/ED erase variants used by Presenter
- DECSTBM scroll region (for inline mode optimizations)
- DECSET/DECRST toggles used by TerminalSession/TerminalWriter
- DEC 2026 synchronized output begin/end

### OSC sequences
- OSC 8 hyperlinks (start/end)
- (Optional) OSC 52 clipboard (Phase 7)
- (Optional) OSC title

### Modes
- bracketed paste enable/disable
- mouse tracking enable/disable (SGR encoding)

## Design Notes
- Keep this layer **pure**: it should generate bytes into a buffer, not own terminal state.
- Avoid per-call allocations where possible (reuse a scratch buffer).
- Prefer explicit, readable helpers over “clever” formatting.

## Integration Points
- `bd-10i.4.3` (Presenter) depends on this issue.
- TerminalSession / TerminalWriter may also reuse the same helpers for mode toggles.

## Tests Required
- Unit tests for exact bytes for each helper (table-driven).
- Unit tests for OSC termination correctness (ST vs BEL if supported).
- Property tests:
  - sequences are ASCII bytes
  - OSC sequences are always terminated

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Helper API exists for the sequences listed in Scope (or an explicit list of omissions is documented).
- [ ] Unit tests cover every helper and verify exact byte output.
- [ ] OSC 8 link sequences are always properly terminated.
- [ ] Presenter uses this layer (no ad-hoc string formatting for core sequences).
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

### Functional Requirements
- [ ] SGR sequences for all 16, 256, and RGB colors
- [ ] SGR sequences for all text attributes (bold, italic, underline, etc.)
- [ ] Cursor movement: absolute (CUP), relative (CUU/CUD/CUF/CUB)
- [ ] Cursor save/restore (DECSC/DECRC)
- [ ] Erase sequences: line (EL), screen (ED) with all modes
- [ ] Scroll region (DECSTBM) setup and restore
- [ ] Mode switching: DECSET/DECRST for alt screen, mouse, paste
- [ ] OSC sequences: hyperlinks (OSC 8), title (OSC 0/2), clipboard (OSC 52)
- [ ] Synchronized output (DEC 2026) with fallback
- [ ] All sequences batched to single write syscall per frame

### Correctness Requirements
- [ ] All sequences conform to ECMA-48 and xterm spec
- [ ] No malformed sequences emitted (valid ESC, CSI, OSC terminators)
- [ ] State tracking prevents redundant sequences
- [ ] Proper escaping of user content in OSC parameters

### Performance Requirements
- [ ] Sequence generation: < 100ns per sequence
- [ ] Frame buffer assembly: < 50µs for 80x24 terminal
- [ ] Zero allocation for common sequences (use stack buffers)

### Logging Requirements

- [ ] tracing::debug! for mode changes

title: Implement terminal raw mode handling
description:
# Implement terminal raw mode handling + cleanup discipline

## Objective
Implement the terminal backend glue needed for ftui to:
- enter raw mode
- enable/disable terminal modes (mouse, bracketed paste, focus, sync output)
- reliably restore the user’s terminal on exit and on panic

## Why This Matters
Most “TUI flakiness” is actually cleanup failure:
- cursor stays hidden
- raw mode persists
- bracketed paste remains enabled
- scroll region not reset

We must treat cleanup as a first-class invariant.

## Reference (for patterns)
- `legacy_reference_library_code/opentui_rust/src/` terminal/raw mode modules

## Scope
Implement (or wrap) backend operations:
- enter/exit raw mode (RAII)
- show/hide cursor
- enter/exit alt-screen (optional; inline mode is default)
- enable/disable:
  - bracketed paste
  - mouse (SGR)
  - focus events
  - sync output (DEC 2026) where supported
- ensure drop/cleanup executes even when unwinding (panic path)

## Design Notes
- This must integrate with the chosen backend (ADR-003).
- Cleanup must be idempotent (safe to call twice).
- Failures during cleanup should be logged but must not panic.

## Tests Required
- PTY integration tests (release mode where relevant) that assert after process exit:
  - raw mode is restored
  - cursor is visible
  - bracketed paste is disabled
  - mouse mode is disabled
  - alt-screen exited (if used)
  - scroll region reset (if used)

Scenarios:
- normal exit
- panic during render
- I/O error mid-write (best-effort cleanup)

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] RAII guard exists and is used by runtime/harness entrypoints.
- [ ] Cleanup is idempotent and does not panic.
- [ ] PTY tests cover normal + panic cleanup and pass reliably.
- [ ] Mode toggles are routed through the one-writer policy (no ad-hoc stdout writes).
acceptance_criteria:

### Functional Requirements
- [ ] Enter raw mode (disable line buffering, echo, signals)

- [ ] Signal handling: SIGWINCH, SIGTERM, SIGINT

### Safety Requirements
- [ ] Terminal always restored on normal exit
- [ ] Terminal always restored on panic
- [ ] Terminal restored even on SIGKILL (best effort)
- [ ] No undefined behavior on double-enter or double-exit
- [ ] Thread-safe (only one raw mode active at a time)

### Platform Requirements

### Logging Requirements

# Optional: runtime terminal capability probing (bounded timeouts)

## Background
Plan Section 0.4/9.1 + TerminalCapabilities contract: v1 detection should be conservative and environment-based.

However, the plan allows an optional *feature-gated* probing layer:
- device attribute queries (DA)
- OSC queries

Critical constraints:
- probing must be bounded with timeouts
- probing must fail-open (unknown => disable feature, never hang startup)
- probing must not compromise the one-writer rule

## Scope
Add an optional probing module that can refine `TerminalCapabilities`.

Examples (only if safe and supported):
- cursor position report (CPR)
- DA1/DA2 (device attributes)
- synchronized output support probing (if an unambiguous probe exists)
- background color query (for dark/light heuristics) if we decide to support it

## Design constraints
- Must run only when we have exclusive terminal ownership (TerminalSession active).
- Must be guarded by a feature flag (e.g., `caps-probe`).
- Must never block indefinitely; hard timeouts.

## Tests
- Unit tests for response parsing
- Integration tests (PTY) to ensure:
  - probe timeouts do not hang
  - capability results are conservative when probe fails

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Feature-gated probe module exists.
- [ ] All probes are bounded by timeouts and fail-open.
- [ ] Tests cover success + timeout + malformed responses.

title: Implement optional render/output thread (Mode B)
description:
# Implement optional render/output thread (Mode B)

## Background
Plan Sections 0.9.2 (Mode B) and 8.2 describe an optional dedicated render/output thread.

This exists to solve the real harness problem:
- logs can be produced by background tasks / subprocess capture
- UI needs tick-driven updates
- if output interleaves, inline mode breaks

Mode B keeps the **one-writer rule** by construction: the render thread is the only place bytes hit the terminal.

## Scope
- Feature-gated "Mode B" operation in addition to the default single-threaded mode.
- Render/output thread owns:
  - `TerminalSession` output handle
  - `Presenter`
  - `prev_buffer` (front buffer)
  - inline-mode policy state (ui rect/anchor/height)

## Design
### Messages
```rust
enum OutMsg {
    Log(Vec<u8>),
    Render(Buffer),
    Resize { w: u16, h: u16 },
    SetMode(ScreenMode),
    Shutdown,
}
```

### Coalescing rules
- Render messages are coalesced ("latest wins"):
  - drop intermediate renders if a newer one arrives
  - present at most one buffer per loop iteration
- Log messages are *not* dropped, but are:
  - newline-aware
  - chunked to avoid starving UI

### Error handling
- Render thread errors propagate back to the Program so we can:
  - restore terminal state
  - exit with a useful error

## Test Plan
- PTY tests must run in both modes:
  - default single-threaded mode
  - render/output thread enabled
- Stress tests:
  - heavy log spam + UI tick (spinner) + resize storms
  - ensure cursor invariants and scrollback preservation

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Mode B can be enabled via feature flag and/or App/Program option.
- [ ] All terminal writes are serialized in the render thread.
- [ ] Render coalescing works (latest buffer presented).
- [ ] Log chunking works and does not starve UI.
- [ ] PTY tests pass in both Mode A and Mode B.

## Location
Likely `ftui-core` (thread + terminal ownership) with integration hooks in `ftui-runtime`.
acceptance_criteria:
## Acceptance Criteria

### Functional Requirements
- [ ] Background thread for frame rendering
- [ ] Double buffering with atomic swap
- [ ] Frame rate limiting (configurable FPS cap)
- [ ] Frame skipping when behind schedule
- [ ] Graceful shutdown without hanging
- [ ] Error propagation to main thread
- [ ] Submit frame (non-blocking)
- [ ] Flush pending frames (blocking)

### Threading Requirements
- [ ] Main thread never blocked on I/O
- [ ] Channel-based command passing
- [ ] No data races on buffer swap
- [ ] Proper synchronization on shutdown

### Performance Requirements
- [ ] Submit latency: < 100µs
- [ ] Render latency: < 1ms for 80x24
- [ ] Memory: 2 buffers + channel overhead
- [ ] No allocation per frame (buffer reuse)

### Error Handling
- [ ] I/O errors propagated to main thread
- [ ] Panics in render thread caught
- [ ] Graceful degradation on slow I/O

### Logging Requirements
- [ ] tracing::debug! for frame submission
- [ ] tracing::debug! for frame skip
- [ ] tracing::trace! for render timing
- [ ] tracing::error! for I/O failures
- [ ] tracing::info! for shutdown

### Test Coverage
- [ ] Unit test: submit/flush cycle
- [ ] Unit test: frame rate limiting
- [ ] Stress test: high FPS submission
- [ ] Stress test: large frame buffers
- [ ] Error injection test: I/O failure

title: Implement Buffer drawing operations
description:
# Implement Buffer drawing operations

## Objective
Add ergonomic, well-tested drawing helpers on top of the core `Buffer` so widgets/renderables can be implemented without duplicating low-level cell loops.

## Why This Exists
The kernel is intentionally minimal, but widgets still need:
- borders/lines
- filling rects
- blitting
- text printing respecting clipping

If each widget reimplements these loops, we’ll get inconsistent behavior and bugs.

## Reference (for ideas)
- `legacy_reference_library_code/opentui_rust/src/` buffer/drawing modules

## Scope
Implement a `BufferDraw`-style API (name TBD) that operates on a `Buffer` and respects:
- scissor stack (no drawing outside clip)
- opacity stack (alpha compositing rules)

Operations to support (minimum):
- draw horizontal/vertical lines
- draw rectangle outline + filled rectangle
- draw borders using a provided border character set
- print text at position (ASCII + Unicode) without writing out-of-bounds
- blit/copy regions between buffers (opaque + alpha)

Optional (Phase 7 / nice-to-have):

title: epic(graveyard-§14.9): Seqlocks for Read-Heavy Config and Theme Data
description:
Seqlocks: optimistic reads without locking for theme, config, animation clock. EV=36.0 (Tier S). CONSTRAINT: #![forbid(unsafe_code)] — MUST use an existing safe crate (arc-swap, left-right, or seqlock crate) rather than hand-rolling UnsafeCell-based seqlock. - Theme reads are wait-free (no mutex contention)
- Correctness tests verify no stale reads under concurrent writes
- No unsafe code
- All existing tests pass

title: task(e2e): E2E test suite for Seqlocks/ArcSwap Concurrent Reads
description:
## E2E Integration Test: Seqlocks/ArcSwap (EV=36)

### Scope
Full integration test exercising rapid theme switching under concurrent reader threads using arc-swap/left-right for read-heavy config and theme data. Validates no torn reads occur and measures read latency.

### Test Scenario
1. Initialize FrankenTUI with ArcSwap-backed ResolvedTheme and TerminalCapabilities.
2. Spawn 8 reader threads continuously reading theme data while rendering.
3. Writer thread switches themes every 50ms (rapid cycling through 10 themes).
4. Run for 5 seconds (100 theme switches).
5. Each reader logs every read with latency and whether data was consistent.
6. Verify no reader ever observes a torn/partial theme (all fields from same generation).
7. Render frames during switching and verify visual consistency.

### JSONL Structured Logging Specification
Reader events:
```json
{
  "event": "seqlock_read",
  "ts_ns": u64,
  "reader_id": u8,
  "theme_generation": u64,
  "read_latency_ns": u64,
  "retry_count": u32,
  "consistent": bool,
  "fields_snapshot": "hash_string"
}
```
Writer events:
```json
{
  "event": "seqlock_write",
  "ts_ns": u64,
  "old_generation": u64,
  "new_generation": u64,
  "theme_name": "string",
  "write_latency_ns": u64
}
```

### Success Criteria
- Zero torn reads: consistent == true for every reader event.
- Read latency p99 < 1us (lock-free reads should be fast).
- All theme switches complete without blocking readers.
- retry_count is low (< 3 on average for seqlock-style reads).
- No panics, no unsafe code (#![forbid(unsafe_code)]).
- JSONL logs are schema-compliant and parseable.
- No deadlocks or livelocks under sustained concurrent access.

title: Headless Rendering Mode for CI Testing
description:
# Headless Rendering Mode for CI Testing

## Background & Motivation

The plan relies heavily on PTY tests for terminal verification (bd-10i.11.2). However, PTY tests are:
- Slow (process spawning overhead)
- Platform-dependent (different PTY behavior)
- Hard to run in some CI environments (Docker, restricted sandboxes)

**The solution:**
- Headless mode renders to in-memory buffer
- No terminal required - works anywhere
- Enables fast snapshot testing in CI
- Complements (not replaces) PTY tests

**Relationship to existing beads:**
- Extends bd-10i.11.1 (terminal-model test harness)
- Enhances bd-2u4 (snapshot/golden testing)

## Technical Design

```rust
pub struct HeadlessTerm {
    screen: Buffer,
    cursor: (u16, u16),
    captured_output: Vec<u8>,
    style_state: StyleState,
    capabilities: TerminalCapabilities,
}

impl HeadlessTerm {
    pub fn new(width: u16, height: u16) -> Self { ... }
    pub fn process(&mut self, output: &[u8]) { ... }
    pub fn screen_text(&self) -> Vec<String> { ... }
    pub fn assert_matches(&self, expected: &[&str]) { ... }
    pub fn export(&self, path: &Path) -> io::Result<()> { ... }
}
```

## Logging Requirements

All parse errors logged at WARN level with sequence bytes and position. Snapshot mismatches logged at DEBUG with line numbers and diff context.

## E2E Tests

```bash
cargo test --features headless -- --test-threads=1
REGENERATE_GOLDENS=1 cargo test --features headless
./scripts/ci-headless-test.sh --report
```

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] HeadlessTerm type implemented
- [ ] ANSI parsing matches real terminal behavior
- [ ] Snapshot comparison works with clear diff output
- [ ] CI tests run without PTY
- [ ] Integration with existing test framework
- [ ] All ANSI sequences from plan supported
- [ ] Export capability for debugging
notes:
## ANSI Sequences to Support

The headless terminal must support these sequences used by FrankenTUI:

### CSI (Control Sequence Introducer)
- Cursor movement: CUP (H), CUU (A), CUD (B), CUF (C), CUB (D)
- Erase: ED (J), EL (K)
- Scroll: SU, SD
- SGR (Select Graphic Rendition): colors, bold, italic, underline
- Private modes: ?25h/l (cursor visibility), ?1049h/l (alt screen)

### SGR Attributes
- Reset: 0
- Bold: 1, Dim: 2, Italic: 3, Underline: 4
- Foreground: 30-37, 90-97, 38;5;N, 38;2;R;G;B
- Background: 40-47, 100-107, 48;5;N, 48;2;R;G;B

### OSC (Operating System Command)
- OSC 8 (hyperlinks): parse but don't render as link
- OSC 0 (window title): capture but don't use

### Unsupported (should not crash)
- OSC 52 (clipboard)
- DCS/APC sequences
- Unknown CSI sequences

```rust
impl HeadlessTerm {
    fn process_csi(&mut self, params: &[u16], intermediate: &[u8], final_byte: u8) {
        match final_byte {
            b'H' => self.cursor_position(params),
            b'J' => self.erase_display(params),
            b'K' => self.erase_line(params),
            b'm' => self.sgr(params),
            b'A'..=b'D' => self.cursor_move(final_byte, params),
            _ => {
                tracing::warn!(
                    final_byte = final_byte as char,
                    params = ?params,
                    "Unknown CSI sequence"
                );
            }
        }
    }
}
```

This should be added to the implementation.
close_reason: HeadlessTerm implemented in ftui-render/src/headless.rs with 29 tests passing. Includes: screen_text(), assert_matches(), export(), diff output, presenter roundtrip verification.

title: task(e2e): E2E test suite for Recipe D Deterministic Debugging
description:
## E2E Integration Test: Recipe D Deterministic Debugging (EV=recipe)

### Scope
Full integration test recording event stream, replaying deterministically, verifying exact frame reproduction, and logging all nondeterminism sources captured.

### Test Scenario
1. Initialize FrankenTUI with Recipe D recording enabled.
2. Execute a scripted interaction sequence (60 seconds of realistic usage):
   a. Type text in editor widget (50 keystrokes).
   b. Navigate between tabs (10 tab switches).
   c. Scroll list widget (20 scroll events).
   d. Resize terminal twice.
   e. Trigger theme switch.
3. During recording, capture all nondeterminism sources:
   - System clock readings (monotonic and wall-clock)
   - Random seeds (if any)
   - Terminal size queries
   - Any async event ordering
4. Save recorded trace to file.
5. Replay trace from file with deterministic substitutions.
6. Capture frame-by-frame hashes during replay.
7. Verify EVERY frame hash matches the recording exactly.
8. Run HDD on a deliberately broken replay to minimize the divergence point.

### JSONL Structured Logging Specification
Recording events:
```json
{
  "event": "recipe_d_record",
  "ts_ns": u64,
  "frame_id": u64,
  "event_type": "key|mouse|resize|timer|async",
  "event_data": "serialized_string",
  "nondeterminism_sources": {
    "clock_monotonic_ns": u64,
    "clock_wall_ns": u64,
    "random_seed": "hex_string|null",
    "terminal_size": { "cols": u16, "rows": u16 }
  },
  "frame_hash": "hex_string"
}
```
Replay verification:
```json
{
  "event": "recipe_d_replay",
  "ts_ns": u64,
  "frame_id": u64,
  "recorded_hash": "hex_string",
  "replayed_hash": "hex_string",
  "match": bool,
  "divergence_point": "string|null"
}
```

### Success Criteria
- match == true for EVERY frame during replay (exact reproduction).
- All nondeterminism sources captured (no null random_seed if randomness used).
- Replay produces byte-identical terminal output sequence.
- HDD on broken replay identifies minimal divergence within 30 seconds.
- No panics, no unsafe code (#![forbid(unsafe_code)]).
- JSONL log is schema-compliant and parseable.
- Recording overhead < 5% of frame time.
- Trace file size < 1MB for 60-second interaction.
close_reason: done

title: Improved Crossing Minimization (Sifting Algorithm)
description:
## Goal
Augment or replace the barycenter heuristic in diagram_layout.rs with the sifting algorithm for better edge crossing reduction. The existing barycenter approach is correct but produces suboptimal layouts for dense graphs (10+ nodes per layer).

## Background
- Current: barycenter_sort does bidirectional sweeps using neighbor position averages. O(n*E) per sweep, good results for sparse graphs.
- Sifting: for each node in a layer, try inserting it at every position and pick the one with minimum crossings. O(n^2 * E) per layer but finds significantly better solutions.
- The layout quality metrics already measure crossings — improvement is directly measurable.

## Implementation
1. Add sifting_sort() alongside barycenter_sort() in diagram_layout.rs.
2. For each layer, for each node: remove from position, count crossings at each alternate position, insert at best position.
3. Use the optimized O(1) crossing counter (the ref_member boolean array) from the barycenter fix.
4. Run sifting after barycenter (as a refinement pass) rather than as a replacement.
5. Budget-gated: sifting is more expensive; respect the computation budget.

## Expected Improvement
- 15-30% fewer crossings on graphs with 20+ nodes (based on graph drawing literature).
- No change for simple graphs (barycenter already optimal for small inputs).

## Files
- crates/ftui-extras/src/diagram_layout.rs (add sifting_sort, integrate with minimize_crossings)

## Tests
- Unit: sifting produces <= crossings compared to barycenter alone
- Property: sifting output is a valid permutation of the layer
- Benchmark: measure crossing reduction on 10 test graphs
close_reason: done

title: epic(graveyard-§6.1): Incremental/Self-Adjusting Computation for Layout
description:
## Summary

Replace full layout recompute with Salsa-style incremental computation. Only recompute what changed. This is THE transformative optimization for FrankenTUI — layout is the dominant cost and most frames change <5% of widgets.

## Graveyard Entry

Section §6.1 — Incremental/Self-Adjusting Computation  
Priority: 1 (Tier A)  
EV Score: 6.7 — Transformative  

## Background & Math Foundations

Self-adjusting computation (Acar et al. 2002) maintains a dynamic dependency graph where nodes represent computations and edges represent data dependencies. When an input changes, only the transitive closure of affected nodes is re-evaluated. The Salsa framework (used in rust-analyzer) refines this with memoized queries and red-green trees for change propagation.

Key insight: Widget tree traversal order is identical between full and incremental (DFS pre-order). Incremental simply marks dirty nodes and re-evaluates the same subtrees. This preserves the isomorphism invariant — the output must be bit-identical regardless of computation path.

Complexity: Full layout is O(n) per frame where n = total widget count. Incremental layout is O(k) where k = dirty widget count. For typical UI interactions (typing, scrolling, hover), k/n < 0.05, yielding 20x+ speedup on the layout hot path.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Dependency graph correctly tracks all layout inputs (size constraints, content, style, children)
2. Dirty-node propagation is conservative (never misses a dependency) but minimal (no unnecessary recomputation)
3. Golden frame checksums for all 47+ test scenarios are pixel-identical between incremental and full layout
4. FRANKENTUI_FULL_LAYOUT=1 env var forces full recompute as fallback/debugging path
5. Benchmark shows measurable speedup on 1000-widget tree with <5% dirty nodes
6. No additional per-frame allocation beyond the dirty set tracking

## Risk Mitigation

- Isomorphism proof required before merge: demonstrate widget tree traversal order is identical
- Golden frame checksums gate the PR — any pixel difference is a blocking failure
- Fallback env var ensures production safety during rollout

title: task(incremental): Design dependency graph for incremental layout invalidation
description:
## Summary

Design the dependency graph data structure that tracks which layout computations depend on which inputs. This is the foundational design document and prototype for the entire incremental computation system.

## Detail

The dependency graph must track:
- Widget size constraints (min/max/preferred width and height)
- Widget content (text, children list, embedded content)
- Widget style properties (padding, margin, border, flex properties)
- Parent-child relationships in the widget tree
- Cross-widget dependencies (e.g., flex siblings that share remaining space)

Graph representation options:
1. Explicit adjacency list (simple, O(1) edge lookup, higher memory)
2. Implicit via query memoization (Salsa-style, lower memory, requires careful key design)
3. Hybrid: explicit for structural deps, implicit for value deps

Must support:
- O(1) dirty marking of a node
- O(k) propagation where k = dirty set size
- Cycle detection (layout cycles are bugs, must be caught)
- Deterministic traversal order (DFS pre-order, matching full layout)

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Design document with data structure choices and complexity analysis
2. Prototype implementation of the graph structure
3. Unit tests for dependency tracking, dirty propagation, and cycle detection
4. Benchmark: graph overhead per widget node (target: <64 bytes per node)

title: task(incremental): Implement dirty-node tracking with minimal overhead
description:
## Summary

Implement the dirty-node tracking mechanism that marks widgets as needing re-layout when their inputs change. Must have minimal per-frame overhead when nothing is dirty (the common case for static UIs).

## Detail

Dirty tracking approaches:
- Bitset per widget (cache-friendly, O(n/64) clear cost)
- Generation counter (O(1) clear by incrementing generation, O(1) check per node)
- Epoch-based (similar to generation but with overflow handling)

The generation counter approach is preferred: each widget stores a "last_computed_at" generation number. The frame counter serves as the global generation. A widget is dirty if last_computed_at < current_generation OR any of its inputs have changed since last_computed_at.

Input change detection:
- Content hash comparison (for text content)
- Structural equality (for constraint changes)
- Pointer equality where possible (for style objects)

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Zero overhead when no widgets are dirty (no per-frame allocation, no per-widget scan)
2. O(1) per widget to mark dirty
3. O(1) per widget to check if dirty
4. Dirty propagation to dependents is automatic and conservative
5. Unit tests: mark dirty, check propagation, verify clearing after recompute
6. Benchmark: overhead of dirty tracking vs no tracking on 10K widget tree

title: task(incremental): Implement incremental re-evaluation of dirty subtrees only
description:
## Summary

Core implementation: walk the widget tree and only re-evaluate layout for dirty subtrees. Clean subtrees return cached results. This is where the actual speedup materializes.

## Detail

The incremental layout algorithm:
1. Begin DFS pre-order traversal (same order as full layout)
2. At each node, check dirty flag
3. If clean AND all children clean: return cached layout result (O(1))
4. If dirty: recompute this node's layout using standard layout algorithm
5. After recomputing, update cached result and clear dirty flag
6. Propagate upward: if a child's layout result changed, parent must recompute

Key invariant: The output of incremental layout must be BIT-IDENTICAL to full layout. This is the isomorphism proof — same traversal order, same computation at dirty nodes, same results.

Edge cases:
- Widget added: entire subtree is dirty
- Widget removed: parent is dirty, removed widget's cache entry is evicted
- Constraint change from parent: child becomes dirty even if its own content didn't change
- Flex layout: all flex siblings may need recompute if one changes (conservative marking)

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Incremental layout produces bit-identical results to full layout for all 47+ golden frame scenarios
2. Property test: for any random widget tree and random dirty set, incremental == full
3. No regression in full-layout performance (the non-incremental path must not slow down)
4. Handles all edge cases: add/remove widgets, constraint changes, flex siblings
5. Benchmark: 20x+ speedup with <5% dirty nodes on 1000-widget tree
close_reason: done

title: task(incremental): Verify pixel-identical golden frame checksums (incremental vs full)
description:
## Summary

Verification gate: run all 47+ golden frame test scenarios in both full-layout and incremental-layout modes. Compare frame checksums. Any difference is a blocking failure.

## Detail

Golden frame checksums are the ultimate correctness oracle for incremental layout. The verification process:

1. For each of the 47+ test scenarios:
   a. Run scenario with FRANKENTUI_FULL_LAYOUT=1 (full recompute every frame)
   b. Capture frame buffer checksums (SHA-256 of cell grid)
   c. Run same scenario with incremental layout enabled
   d. Capture frame buffer checksums
   e. Assert: checksums are identical at every frame

2. Additionally, create "mutation scenarios" that exercise incremental paths:
   a. Start with stable layout, modify single widget, verify frame
   b. Start with stable layout, add/remove widgets, verify frame
   c. Start with stable layout, resize terminal, verify frame
   d. Rapid-fire mutations (10 changes per frame), verify frame

3. Store checksums as CI artifacts for regression detection

## Acceptance Criteria

1. All 47+ existing golden frame scenarios produce identical checksums in both modes
2. At least 20 new mutation-focused scenarios added
3. CI gate: any checksum mismatch fails the build
4. Checksums are stored as artifacts with scenario name, frame number, and hash
5. Human-readable diff output when checksums mismatch (show which cells differ)

title: task(incremental): FRANKENTUI_FULL_LAYOUT=1 env var fallback path
description:
## Summary

Implement the FRANKENTUI_FULL_LAYOUT=1 environment variable that forces full layout recompute on every frame, bypassing incremental computation. This serves as a debugging tool and production safety valve.

## Detail

When FRANKENTUI_FULL_LAYOUT=1 is set:
1. All dirty flags are ignored — every widget is treated as dirty
2. Layout traversal still uses the same code path (no separate "full" implementation)
3. Cache is still populated (so switching back to incremental mid-session works)
4. A log message is emitted at startup: "FRANKENTUI_FULL_LAYOUT=1: incremental layout disabled"

This is critical for:
- Debugging suspected incremental layout bugs (compare output with and without)
- Production rollback if incremental layout has a correctness bug
- Performance isolation: measure "is incremental the cause of this regression?"

The env var is checked once at startup and cached. No per-frame overhead for checking.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Setting FRANKENTUI_FULL_LAYOUT=1 produces identical output to not setting it (by definition, since full == incremental when correct)
2. Log message emitted at startup when env var is set
3. No per-frame overhead for the env var check
4. Integration test: run with and without env var, verify identical output
5. Documentation in TROUBLESHOOTING.md
close_reason: done

title: Text Effects: Scanline / CRT Effects
description:
## Background
CRT/scanline effects create strong nostalgic retro appeal, perfect for terminal UIs. Simulates the look of old monitors applied to text.

## Implementation

Add TextEffect variant:
```rust
TextEffect::Scanline {
    intensity: f64,      // 0.0-1.0, how dark the scan lines (0.3 typical)
    line_gap: u8,        // Every Nth row dimmed (2 = every other row)
    scroll: bool,        // Lines scroll slowly for CRT feel
    scroll_speed: f64,   // Rows per second if scrolling
    flicker: f64,        // 0.0-1.0, random brightness variation
}
```

### Rendering:
```rust
fn apply_scanline(&self, color: PackedRgba, row: u16, time: f64) -> PackedRgba {
    // Determine if this row is a scanline
    let scroll_offset = if self.scroll { 
        (time * self.scroll_speed) as u16 
    } else { 
        0 
    };
    let is_scanline = (row + scroll_offset) % self.line_gap as u16 == 0;
    
    // Apply dimming
    let dim_factor = if is_scanline { 1.0 - self.intensity } else { 1.0 };
    
    // Apply flicker (random per-frame variation)
    let flicker_factor = 1.0 - self.flicker * random_for_frame(time);
    
    apply_alpha(color, dim_factor * flicker_factor)
}
```

### Note on Screen Effects:
Screen-wide effects like curvature, vignette, and barrel distortion are out of scope for text effects. Those would be terminal/screen-level post-processing, not text styling.

### Phosphor Glow:
For authentic CRT look, combine Scanline with a subtle Glow effect:
```rust
StyledText::new("RETRO")
    .effect(TextEffect::Scanline { intensity: 0.3, line_gap: 2, ... })
    .effect(TextEffect::Glow { color: green, intensity: 0.2, ... })
```

## Files
crates/ftui-extras/src/text_effects.rs

## Unit Tests (REQUIRED)
- test_scanline_dims_every_nth: Correct rows affected
- test_scanline_intensity_applied: Color reduced by intensity
- test_scanline_scroll_moves_pattern: Pattern shifts with time
- test_scanline_flicker_varies: Different frames = different brightness
- test_scanline_gap_1_dims_all: Every row affected with gap=1
- test_scanline_gap_2_alternates: Every other row

## Visual Tests
- Snapshot multi-line text with scanlines, gap=2
- Snapshot same text at t=0 vs t=1 with scroll

## Acceptance Criteria
- Deliver the behavior implied by the title: Text Effects: Scanline / CRT Effects
- Alien Artifact: define invariants + failure modes; if heuristics exist, specify an explainable decision rule (evidence ledger / Bayes factors where applicable)
- Extreme Optimization: baseline -> profile -> opportunity matrix; for each perf change include an isomorphism proof + golden output checksums
- Unit tests: happy path + edge cases + regression fixtures; add property tests for core invariants where applicable
- E2E: scripts with verbose JSONL logging (env, capabilities, timings, seed, checksums) + deterministic mode

title: epic(graveyard-§5.2): Session Types for Terminal Mode Transitions
description:
## Summary

Compile-time terminal mode safety via session types / typestate pattern. Encode terminal states (Raw, Cooked, Alternate Screen, Mouse Capture) as types so that invalid mode transitions are compile errors, not runtime bugs.

## Graveyard Entry

Section §5.2 — Session Types for Terminal Mode Transitions  
Priority: 2  
EV Score: 4.0  

## Background & Math Foundations

Session types (Honda 1993, Honda/Vasconcelos/Kubo 1998) encode communication protocols as types. In Rust, the typestate pattern achieves similar guarantees: each protocol state is a distinct type, and methods consume one state and produce the next.

Terminal modes form a state machine:
- States: Cooked, Raw, AlternateScreen, MouseCapture, BracketedPaste
- Transitions: enter_raw(), exit_raw(), enter_alternate_screen(), enable_mouse(), etc.
- Invalid transitions: can't exit_raw() from Cooked, can't enable_mouse() without Raw

Current FrankenTUI uses runtime checks (assert/panic) for invalid transitions. This means:
- Bugs only caught at runtime, often in production
- Test coverage must explicitly test every invalid transition
- Error messages are opaque ("invalid terminal state" with no compile-time guidance)

With session types:
- Invalid transitions are COMPILE ERRORS with clear type mismatch messages
- IDE autocomplete shows only valid transitions from current state
- No runtime overhead (zero-cost abstraction — states are zero-sized types)

Ergonomics concern: deep typestate nesting creates verbose types. Mitigate with:
- Builder pattern for common transition sequences
- Type aliases for common states
- macro_rules! for transition method generation

## Acceptance Criteria

1. All terminal mode transitions encoded as typestate methods
2. Invalid transitions produce clear compile errors (verified with trybuild)
3. Zero runtime overhead (states are ZSTs)
4. Builder pattern for common sequences (e.g., enter_raw().alternate_screen().mouse_capture())
5. Migration guide for existing runtime-checked code
6. All existing tests adapted to use typestate API
close_reason: done

## E2E Integration Test: Expected-Loss Decision Layer (EV=unscored)

### Scope
Full integration test exercising all 4 states (stable/bursty/resize/degraded) through the unified expected-loss decision framework. Verifies optimal action selection and logs expected loss per state.

### Test Scenario
1. Initialize DecisionCore<State, Action> with calibrated loss matrix.
2. States: {stable, bursty, resize, degraded}.
3. Actions: {incremental_diff, full_diff, deferred}.
4. Exercise each state transition:
   a. stable: steady 60fps, verify a* = incremental_diff (lowest expected loss).
   b. bursty: inject 5ms spikes every 10 frames, verify a* adapts (may switch to full_diff).
   c. resize: send 10 rapid resize events, verify a* = deferred (coalescing).
   d. degraded: sustain p99 > 20ms, verify a* = full_diff with reduced fidelity.
5. Verify loss computation: a* = argmin_a SUM_s L(a,s) * P(s|evidence).
6. Test all state transitions: stable->bursty, bursty->resize, resize->stable, stable->degraded, degraded->stable.
7. Verify calibration: empirical frame-miss coverage matches predicted.

title: Demo Showcase: Snapshot/Time Travel Player
description:
## Background

FrankenTUI already embraces determinism (Buffer -> Diff -> Presenter). A natural superpower is "time travel":
- record frames / state snapshots
- replay deterministically
- inspect diffs and metadata

This screen turns the harness/snapshot infrastructure into a user-visible, jaw-dropping demo.

## UX / Core Interactions

- Timeline scrubber of recorded frames/snapshots.
- Playback controls: step back/forward, play/pause, jump to markers.
- Detail panel:
  - snapshot metadata (timestamp, terminal size, mode)
  - render stats (diff cell count, ANSI byte count)
  - optional: checksum/hash for integrity

Suggested keybindings:
- Space: play/pause
- Left/Right: step
- Home/End: first/last
- M: toggle markers

## Architecture Notes

- Use existing snapshot/time-travel capture mechanisms (ftui-harness / ftui-pty utilities).
- Store snapshots in a compact format:
  - buffer cells (or diffs)
  - metadata: size, mode, seed
- Optional integrity feature:
  - compute a hash chain over snapshots so replays are tamper-evident (useful for regression artifacts).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Can load a recorded snapshot set and scrub smoothly.
- Playback is deterministic under a fixed snapshot file.
- Displays at least one of:
  - per-frame diff cell count
  - per-frame ANSI byte count
  - checksum

Additionally (project-wide standards):
- Alien Artifact: define invariants + failure modes; if heuristics exist, specify an explainable decision rule (evidence ledger / Bayes factors where applicable)
- Extreme Optimization: baseline -> profile -> opportunity matrix; for each perf change include an isomorphism proof + golden output checksums
- Unit tests: happy path + edge cases + regression fixtures; add property tests for core invariants where applicable
- E2E: scripts with verbose JSONL logging (env, capabilities, timings, seed, checksums) + deterministic mode

## Alien Artifact Upgrades (Concrete)

- "Isomorphism proof" view:
  - show that replay output matches original via checksums
  - surface the exact invariants being asserted

## Extreme Optimization

- Scrubbing must be responsive:
  - pre-index snapshots
  - avoid per-step allocations
  - enforce a budget for 10k-frame scrubs

title: Bug: scroll operations ignore cursor bg color (BCE) for new blank lines
description: scroll_up() and scroll_down() in Grid always use Cell::default() for newly created blank lines. Per VT/xterm BCE (Background Color Erase) semantics, blank lines introduced by scrolling should inherit the cursor's current background color, just like erase operations already do correctly. Affected operations: SU (scroll up), SD (scroll down), IND (index at bottom), RI (reverse index at top), IL (insert lines), DL (delete lines), and newline-triggered scroll. Fix: add bg: Color parameter to scroll_up/scroll_down, propagate through scroll_up_into/scroll_down_from/insert_lines/delete_lines, and update the conformance test harness.
close_reason: Fixed in commits 34bc950c (wide char fixup + scroll BCE param in grid.rs) and ffecad22 (caller site updates + 8 scroll-with-bg-color conformance fixtures). All scroll operations now propagate cursor bg for BCE-correct blank fills.

title: Notification/Toast System with Queue Management
description:
## Background

Almost every application needs to show transient feedback:
- 'File saved successfully'
- 'Network error: connection refused'
- '3 items deleted'
- 'Copied to clipboard'

Currently, FrankenTUI has no built-in notification system. Developers must implement their own, leading to inconsistent UX.

## Unique Challenge: Inline Mode

In inline mode, notifications must not corrupt scrollback. This is a unique challenge that FrankenTUI is well-positioned to solve correctly.

## Solution: NotificationManager + NotificationStack Widget

```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum NotificationLevel {
    Info,
    Success,
    Warning,
    Error,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
pub struct Notification {
    pub id: NotificationId,
    pub level: NotificationLevel,
    pub title: Option<String>,
    pub message: String,
    pub duration: Option<Duration>,  // None = persistent
    pub dismissable: bool,
    pub action: Option<NotificationAction>,
    pub created_at: Instant,
}

pub struct NotificationAction {
    pub label: String,
    pub callback: Box<dyn FnOnce() + Send>,
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
pub enum NotificationPosition {
    TopRight,
    TopLeft,
    BottomRight,
    BottomLeft,
    TopCenter,
    BottomCenter,
}

pub struct NotificationManager {
    queue: VecDeque<Notification>,
    max_visible: usize,        // Default: 5
    position: NotificationPosition,
    default_duration: Duration, // Default: 5s
    stacking: StackDirection,   // Up or Down
}

impl NotificationManager {
    pub fn notify(&mut self, notification: Notification) -> NotificationId;
    pub fn info(&mut self, message: &str) -> NotificationId;
    pub fn success(&mut self, message: &str) -> NotificationId;
    pub fn warning(&mut self, message: &str) -> NotificationId;
    pub fn error(&mut self, message: &str) -> NotificationId;
    pub fn dismiss(&mut self, id: NotificationId);
    pub fn dismiss_all(&mut self);
    pub fn tick(&mut self, now: Instant) -> Vec<NotificationId>; // Expired
}

// Widget for rendering
pub struct NotificationStack<'a> {
    manager: &'a NotificationManager,
    theme: &'a NotificationTheme,
}

impl Widget for NotificationStack<'_> {
    fn render(&self, area: Rect, frame: &mut Frame);
}
```

## Visual Design

```
┌─ ✓ Success ─────────────────────┐
│ File saved successfully          │
│                          [Undo]  │
└──────────────────────────────────┘
┌─ ⚠ Warning ─────────────────────┐
│ Large file may take time to load │
└──────────────────────────────────┘
```

## Inline Mode Handling

- Notifications render in overlay region (not scrollback)
- Use cursor save/restore to preserve position
- Animate in from edge without flickering

## Files to Create

- crates/ftui-widgets/src/notification.rs
- crates/ftui-runtime/src/notification_manager.rs

## Success Criteria
- Epic delivers a cohesive user-visible capability: Notification/Toast System with Queue Management
- Child tasks are not just implemented; each has unit tests + E2E scripts with verbose JSONL logs and deterministic fixtures
- Graceful degradation tiers are specified (capabilities, fallbacks, safety) and validated in tests
- Formal invariants documented + enforced via property tests; any dynamic decisions have an evidence ledger and debug UI


## Alien Artifact Upgrades
- Model the core decision(s) with explicit state, priors/assumptions, and invariants; write down failure modes as first-class artifacts.
- Explainability: add an evidence ledger for any non-trivial decision (why this branch, why this fallback). Prefer Bayes factors / log-likelihood contributions over ad-hoc scoring.
- Guarantees: where prediction/thresholding exists, prefer distribution-free calibration (conformal prediction) or anytime-valid testing (e-process) so we can stop early without invalid inference.
- Graceful degradation: define capability tiers + deterministic fallbacks; never fail closed without a traceable reason.


## Extreme Optimization
- Baseline first: capture p50/p95/p99 for relevant command(s) with `hyperfine` (store raw output).
- Profile next: CPU flamegraph + allocation profile; identify top-5 hotspots.
- Opportunity matrix: implement only Score ≥ 2.0 (Impact×Confidence/Effort).
- Isomorphism proof per change: ordering, tie-breaking, RNG seeds, and golden checksums must match.
- Regression gates: add microbench + budgets; failures must print actionable deltas and include log artifacts.


## Testing Plan
- Unit tests: happy path + edge cases + regression fixtures.
- Property tests: invariants (idempotence, monotonicity, determinism) where applicable.
- Fuzz tests: parsers/state machines and any input-facing logic.
- Determinism: fixed seeds/time-freeze; snapshot fixtures must be stable.
- Metamorphic tests: shrink/grow, reorder non-semantic inputs, and ensure invariants still hold.

```rust
pub struct Toast {
    id: ToastId,
    content: ToastContent,
    config: ToastConfig,
    state: ToastState,
}

    pub message: String,
    pub icon: Option<ToastIcon>,

    Success, Error, Warning, Info, Custom(char),

    TopLeft, TopCenter, TopRight,
```

title: task(e2e): E2E test suite for Recipe B Tail-Safe Adaptive
description:
## E2E Integration Test: Recipe B Tail-Safe Adaptive Controller (EV=recipe)

### Scope
Full integration test inducing drift, verifying fallback triggers, and logging conformal/e-process/BOCPD convergence. Validates p99 stays bounded under all conditions.

### Test Scenario
1. Initialize FrankenTUI with Recipe B controller active (expected-loss + conformal + e-process + BOCPD).
2. Phase 1 - Steady state (frames 0-100): stable 60fps, verify adaptive behavior.
3. Phase 2 - Gradual drift (frames 100-200): slowly increase frame times from 8ms to 18ms.
4. Verify BOCPD detects changepoint within 20 frames of drift onset.
5. Verify e-process crossing triggers sequential test alarm.
6. Verify conformal prediction intervals widen to accommodate drift.
7. Phase 3 - Fallback (frames 200-250): verify safe-mode activates (deterministic conservative policy: full diff, no coalescing, no degradation).
8. Phase 4 - Recovery (frames 250-350): drift reverses, verify controller re-adapts.
9. Throughout all phases: verify p99 frame time stays < 20ms (tail-safe guarantee).

### JSONL Structured Logging Specification
Each frame emits:
```json
{
  "event": "recipe_b_frame",
  "ts_ns": u64,
  "frame_id": u64,
  "phase": "steady|drift|fallback|recovery",
  "conformal_interval": { "lower": f64, "upper": f64 },
  "conformal_coverage": f64,
  "e_process_value": f64,
  "e_process_crossed": bool,
  "bocpd_run_length": u32,
  "bocpd_changepoint_prob": f64,
  "expected_loss_action": "string",
  "safe_mode_active": bool,
  "frame_time_ms": f64,
  "p99_frame_time_ms": f64,
  "p99_bounded": bool
}
```

### Success Criteria
- BOCPD detects drift within 20 frames of onset (changepoint_prob > 0.8).
- E-process crosses threshold during drift phase.
- Safe mode activates before p99 exceeds 20ms.
- p99_bounded == true for ALL frames (the tail-safe guarantee).
- Recovery phase re-enables adaptive behavior within 50 frames.
- No panics, no unsafe code (#![forbid(unsafe_code)]).
- JSONL log is schema-compliant and parseable.
- Conformal coverage maintains >= 95% throughout test.

title: Design System: Semantic Color Palette with Status/Priority/Type Colors
description:
## Background

The beads_viewer achieves its polished look through a sophisticated color system where **every color conveys meaning**:
- Status colors: OPEN (green), IN_PROGRESS (blue), BLOCKED (red), CLOSED (muted)
- Priority colors: P0/CRITICAL (hot red), P1/HIGH (orange), P2/MEDIUM (yellow), P3/LOW (cyan)
- Type colors: Bug (red), Feature (purple), Task (blue), Epic (gold)

Each semantic color has:
- Primary foreground color
- Background tint for badges/highlights
- Contrast-validated text color for backgrounds
- Pre-computed Style objects for performance

Currently FrankenTUI's theme.rs has basic colors but lacks semantic meaning.

## Implementation

1. Add semantic color modules to theme.rs:
```rust
pub mod status {
    pub const OPEN: PackedRgba = PackedRgba::rgb(80, 220, 140);
    pub const OPEN_BG: PackedRgba = PackedRgba::rgba(80, 220, 140, 40);
    pub const IN_PROGRESS: PackedRgba = PackedRgba::rgb(100, 180, 255);
    pub const BLOCKED: PackedRgba = PackedRgba::rgb(255, 100, 100);
    pub const CLOSED: PackedRgba = PackedRgba::rgb(120, 120, 140);
}

    pub const HIGH: PackedRgba = PackedRgba::rgb(255, 150, 50);
    pub const MEDIUM: PackedRgba = PackedRgba::rgb(255, 220, 80);

}
```

4. Document color meanings

## Justification

Colors are the foundation of visual design. Semantic colors:
- Reduce cognitive load (users learn color meanings)
- Create visual hierarchy
- Enable instant recognition of status/priority
- Make the UI feel professional and intentional

title: Data Viz: Add Sparklines Widget for Trend Visualization
description:
## Background

beads_viewer uses sparklines extensively for showing trends:
- 8-level Unicode block characters: ▁▂▃▄▅▆▇█
- Auto-scaling with min/max detection
- Color gradients from cold to hot
- Compact visualization in tight spaces

Sparklines are essential for data-rich dashboards.

## Current State

charts.rs has chart implementations but sparklines may not be fully featured.
charmed_rust has sparkline support that could be referenced.

## Implementation

1. Sparkline widget in ftui-widgets or ftui-extras:
```rust
pub struct Sparkline<'a> {
    data: &'a [f64],
    min: Option<f64>,
    max: Option<f64>,
    color: PackedRgba,
    gradient: Option<(PackedRgba, PackedRgba)>,
}

impl Sparkline<'_> {
    const CHARS: &'static [char] = &[' ', '▁', '▂', '▃', '▄', '▅', '▆', '▇', '█'];
    
    pub fn render_string(&self) -> String {
        let min = self.min.unwrap_or_else(|| self.data.iter().copied().fold(f64::INFINITY, f64::min));
        let max = self.max.unwrap_or_else(|| self.data.iter().copied().fold(f64::NEG_INFINITY, f64::max));
        let range = max - min;
        
        self.data.iter().map(|&v| {
            let normalized = if range > 0.0 { (v - min) / range } else { 0.5 };
            let idx = (normalized * 8.0).round() as usize;
            Self::CHARS[idx.min(8)]
        }).collect()
    }
}
```

title: Data Viz: Mini-Bars and Progress Indicators
description:
## Background

beads_viewer uses mini-bars for compact metric visualization:
- Fills using █ (full) and ░ (empty) blocks
- Color-coded by value threshold:
  - Green (>75%): Healthy
  - Orange (50-75%): Warning
  - Cyan (25-50%): Low
  - Muted (<25%): Critical
- Perfect for dashboards with many metrics

## Implementation

```rust
pub struct MiniBar {
    value: f64,      // 0.0 to 1.0
    width: u16,
    show_percent: bool,
}

impl MiniBar {
    pub fn color_for_value(value: f64) -> PackedRgba {
        match value {
            v if v > 0.75 => status::SUCCESS,
            v if v > 0.50 => status::WARNING,
            v if v > 0.25 => accent::INFO,
            _ => fg::MUTED,
        }
    }
    
    pub fn render(&self) -> Line {
        let filled = (self.value * self.width as f64).round() as usize;
        let empty = self.width as usize - filled;
        let color = Self::color_for_value(self.value);
        
        let bar = format!(
            "{}{}",
            "█".repeat(filled),
            "░".repeat(empty)
        );
        
        if self.show_percent {
            Line::from_spans([
                Span::styled(bar, Style::new().fg(color)),
                Span::raw(format!(" {:3.0}%", self.value * 100.0)),
            ])
        } else {
            Line::styled(bar, Style::new().fg(color))
        }
    }
}
```

title: Widget: Status and Priority Badge Rendering
description:
## Background

beads_viewer renders polished status/priority badges with:
- Foreground + background color combinations
- Bold text for emphasis
- Consistent padding
- Semantic meaning at a glance

Examples:
- Status: [OPEN] green bg, [PROG] blue bg, [BLKD] red bg
- Priority: [P0] hot red, [P1] orange, [P2] yellow, [P3] cyan

Badges are used throughout the UI for instant recognition.

## Implementation

```rust
pub fn render_status_badge(status: Status) -> Span {
    let (label, fg, bg) = match status {
        Status::Open => ("OPEN", fg::PRIMARY, status::OPEN_BG),
        Status::InProgress => ("PROG", fg::PRIMARY, status::PROGRESS_BG),
        Status::Blocked => ("BLKD", fg::PRIMARY, status::BLOCKED_BG),
        Status::Closed => ("DONE", fg::MUTED, status::CLOSED_BG),
    };
    
    Span::styled(
        format!(" {} ", label),
        Style::new().fg(fg).bg(bg).bold()
    )
}

pub fn render_priority_badge(priority: Priority) -> Span {
    let (label, color) = match priority {
        Priority::Critical => ("P0", priority::CRITICAL),
        Priority::High => ("P1", priority::HIGH),
        Priority::Medium => ("P2", priority::MEDIUM),
        Priority::Low => ("P3", priority::LOW),
    };
    
    Span::styled(
        format!(" {} ", label),
        Style::new().fg(bg::BASE).bg(color).bold()
    )
}
```

title: Data Viz: Heatmap Gradient Color Function
description:
## Background

beads_viewer uses heatmap gradients for density visualization:
- 8-color gradient from cold to hot
- Cold: Navy → Blue → Teal
- Mid: Green → Gold → Orange  
- Hot: Red → Hot Pink

Used for:
- Dependency density
- Activity heatmaps
- Risk visualization
- Any metric requiring attention hierarchy

## Implementation

```rust
/// Get heatmap color for normalized value (0.0 to 1.0)
pub fn heatmap_gradient(value: f64) -> PackedRgba {
    // 8-color gradient
    const COLORS: &[(f64, (u8, u8, u8))] = &[
        (0.000, (30, 30, 80)),     // Navy
        (0.143, (50, 50, 180)),    // Blue
        (0.286, (50, 150, 150)),   // Teal
        (0.429, (80, 180, 80)),    // Green
        (0.571, (220, 180, 50)),   // Gold
        (0.714, (255, 140, 50)),   // Orange
        (0.857, (255, 80, 80)),    // Red
        (1.000, (255, 100, 180)),  // Hot Pink
    ];
    
    // Interpolate between colors
    let clamped = value.clamp(0.0, 1.0);
    for i in 1..COLORS.len() {
        if clamped <= COLORS[i].0 {
            let (t0, c0) = COLORS[i - 1];
            let (t1, c1) = COLORS[i];
            let t = (clamped - t0) / (t1 - t0);
            return PackedRgba::rgb(
                lerp(c0.0, c1.0, t),
                lerp(c0.1, c1.1, t),
                lerp(c0.2, c1.2, t),
            );
        }
    }
    PackedRgba::rgb(255, 100, 180)
}

fn lerp(a: u8, b: u8, t: f64) -> u8 {
    (a as f64 + (b as f64 - a as f64) * t).round() as u8
}
```

title: Animation: Spring Physics System from charmed_rust/harmonica
description:
## Background

charmed_rust's harmonica crate provides spring physics for smooth, natural animations:
- **Spring**: Damped harmonic oscillator for realistic motion
- **Projectile**: Particle simulator with gravity

This could power smooth UI transitions, hover effects, and micro-interactions.

## Current State

FrankenTUI animations are time-based (sine waves) but lack spring physics.
charmed_rust has this already implemented.

## Implementation Options

1. **Port harmonica to ftui-extras**: Add animation module
2. **Depend on charmed_rust/harmonica**: If it's a separate crate
3. **Simplified spring for demo**: Just the core algorithm

Core spring algorithm:
```rust
pub struct Spring {
    position: f64,
    velocity: f64,
    target: f64,
    stiffness: f64,   // Higher = faster response
    damping: f64,     // Higher = less oscillation
}

impl Spring {
    pub fn update(&mut self, dt: f64) {
        let force = -self.stiffness * (self.position - self.target);
        let damping = -self.damping * self.velocity;
        let acceleration = force + damping;
        
        self.velocity += acceleration * dt;
        self.position += self.velocity * dt;
    }
    
    pub fn value(&self) -> f64 {
        self.position
    }
    
    pub fn set_target(&mut self, target: f64) {
        self.target = target;
    }
}
```

description:
## Background

File browser should feel like a native file manager with:

## Implementation

### File Type Icons

```rust
fn file_icon(name: &str, is_dir: bool) -> &'static str {
    if is_dir {
        return "📁";
    }
    
    match name.rsplit('.').next() {
        Some("rs") => "🦀",
        Some("py") => "🐍",
        Some("js" | "ts") => "📜",
        Some("md") => "📝",
        Some("json" | "toml" | "yaml") => "⚙️",
        Some("png" | "jpg" | "gif") => "🖼️",
        Some("mp3" | "wav") => "🎵",
        Some("mp4" | "mov") => "🎬",
        _ => "📄",
    }
}
```

### Size Formatting

Use ftui-extras/filesize module or create:
```rust
fn format_size(bytes: u64) -> String {
    const UNITS: &[&str] = &["B", "KB", "MB", "GB", "TB"];
    let mut size = bytes as f64;
    let mut unit_idx = 0;
    
    while size >= 1024.0 && unit_idx < UNITS.len() - 1 {
        size /= 1024.0;
        unit_idx += 1;
    }
    
    if unit_idx == 0 {
        format!("{} B", bytes)
    } else {
        format!("{:.1} {}", size, UNITS[unit_idx])
    }
}
```

title: Keyboard Navigation: Vim-Style Keys Throughout
description:
## Background

beads_viewer uses Vim-style navigation (h/j/k/l) throughout, which power users expect:
- j/k for up/down in lists
- h/l for left/right or prev/next
- g/G for top/bottom
- / for search
- n/N for next/prev match

Consistent keyboard shortcuts make the app feel professional.

## Implementation

### Navigation Keys

```rust
fn handle_navigation(code: KeyCode, modifiers: Modifiers) -> Option<NavAction> {
    match code {
        // Arrow keys (always work)
        KeyCode::Up | KeyCode::Char('k') => Some(NavAction::Up),
        KeyCode::Down | KeyCode::Char('j') => Some(NavAction::Down),
        KeyCode::Left | KeyCode::Char('h') => Some(NavAction::Left),
        KeyCode::Right | KeyCode::Char('l') => Some(NavAction::Right),
        
        // Jump
        KeyCode::Char('g') if \!modifiers.contains(Modifiers::SHIFT) => Some(NavAction::Top),
        KeyCode::Char('G') => Some(NavAction::Bottom),
        KeyCode::Home => Some(NavAction::Top),
        KeyCode::End => Some(NavAction::Bottom),
        
        // Page
        KeyCode::PageUp | KeyCode::Char('b') if modifiers.contains(Modifiers::CONTROL) => Some(NavAction::PageUp),
        KeyCode::PageDown | KeyCode::Char('f') if modifiers.contains(Modifiers::CONTROL) => Some(NavAction::PageDown),
        
        // Search
        KeyCode::Char('/') => Some(NavAction::StartSearch),
        KeyCode::Char('n') => Some(NavAction::NextMatch),
        KeyCode::Char('N') => Some(NavAction::PrevMatch),
        
        _ => None,
    }
}
```

Update help overlay to show Vim keys:
- 'j/k or ↑/↓' for vertical navigation

description:
## Background

beads_viewer pre-computes style objects at startup rather than creating them per-frame:
```go

    StatusOpen      lipgloss.Style
    StatusOpenBadge lipgloss.Style  // fg + bg combo
    PriorityP0      lipgloss.Style
    PriorityP0Badge lipgloss.Style
    MutedText       lipgloss.Style
    InfoBold        lipgloss.Style
    // ...
}
```

This provides:
1. **Performance**: No per-frame style allocation
2. **Consistency**: Single source of truth for each semantic style

```rust
    // Status styles
    pub status_open: Style,
    pub status_open_badge: Style,
    pub status_progress: Style,
    pub status_progress_badge: Style,
    pub status_blocked: Style,

    pub priority_high: Style,
    pub priority_high_badge: Style,
    pub priority_medium: Style,
    pub priority_low: Style,

    pub success: Style,
```

title: Chrome: Professional Status Bar with Dynamic Info
description:
## Background

The status bar is the bottom anchor of the UI. beads_viewer's status bar includes:
- Left: Screen title + position indicator
- Center: Live metrics (frame count, tick count)
- Right: Terminal dimensions + elapsed time
- Dynamic coloring based on state

A polished status bar makes the whole app feel professional.

## Current State

chrome.rs has basic status bar but could be improved with:
- Better visual segmentation
- More dynamic information
- Consistent styling
- Screen-specific accent colors

## Implementation

1. Three-segment layout with clear visual separation:
```rust
fn render_status_bar(state: &StatusState, frame: &mut Frame, area: Rect) {
    let chunks = Layout::horizontal([
        Constraint::Percentage(35),  // Left: title + position
        Constraint::Percentage(30),  // Center: metrics
        Constraint::Percentage(35),  // Right: dimensions + time
    ]).split(area);
    
    // Left segment
    let left = format!("  {} [{}/{}]", 
        state.title, 
        state.screen_index + 1, 
        state.total_screens
    );
    
    // Center: tick and frame counts
    let center = format!("tick:{} frm:{}", state.tick, state.frame);
    
    // Right: terminal size + uptime
    let right = format!("{}×{} {:02}:{:02}", 
        state.width, state.height,
        state.elapsed_mins, state.elapsed_secs
    );
}
```

title: task(render-perf): build render equivalence, replay, and tail-latency gauntlets
description:
Background:
Render performance changes will only be safe if they are continuously checked against visible equivalence and tail-latency regressions. A dedicated gauntlet is the place where certificate work, presenter minimization, and layout reuse are forced to prove themselves under the canonical fixtures.

Goal:
Create the render-specific validation suite that turns optimization claims into durable evidence.
design:
Work packages:
- Define the render gauntlet scenarios, including sparse updates, large invalidations, resize storms, style-heavy screens, and adversarial challenge cases that stress the limits of certificate and cache assumptions.
- Require focused unit/property tests for certificate logic and invalidation rules before full-system gauntlets run.
- Require replay and snapshot evidence plus scripted E2E scenarios that prove visible equivalence under each scenario.
- Capture tail-latency metrics and identify which optimization levers improve or degrade p95/p99.
- Ensure failure artifacts make it easy to see whether the problem was stale certificates, presenter divergence, cache invalidation, challenge-fixture fragility, or missing log coverage.
- Make the gauntlet reusable for future render changes, not just the first wave.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Render changes cannot be considered complete without unit/property coverage, visible-equivalence checks, and scripted E2E/replay tail-latency gates.
2. Failure artifacts are diagnostic, not merely binary, and include detailed mismatch logs and replay pointers.
3. The gauntlet becomes the standing safety net for future render optimization work.
4. The gauntlet explicitly includes challenge fixtures and negative-control cases so a win on curated render workloads is not enough by itself.
notes: This bead is where the render lane proves it is an engineering program rather than a benchmark-chasing exercise.

title: task(runtime-perf): instrument executor, subscription, queue, and shutdown dynamics
description:
Background:
Runtime optimization decisions should be driven by a detailed picture of queue growth, executor latency, subscription churn, process waits, and shutdown behavior. Without that, it is too easy to ship a scheduler tweak that looks clever but mainly moves pain around.

Goal:
Create the measurement layer that exposes the runtime's real load dynamics and lifecycle costs.
design:
Work packages:
- Define the runtime metric vocabulary: queue depth, enqueue/dequeue timing, task/service latency, cancellation timing, shutdown drain behavior, and subscription/process transition reasons.
- Reuse the shared observability schema and replay-friendly logging contracts instead of inventing a runtime-only telemetry dialect.
- Tie runtime metrics back to fixture IDs and baseline IDs.
- Call out which runtime metrics are leading indicators of user pain versus implementation detail noise.
- Make it explicit how later control-policy beads should interpret these signals.
- Ensure the instrumentation plan remains compatible with deterministic replay and does not become an opaque logging firehose.
- Require the instrumentation surface to support both focused test assertions and scripted stress/E2E evidence generation.
acceptance_criteria:
1. Future runtime work can reason about load and lifecycle behavior using a stable measurement contract.
2. The bead distinguishes operationally meaningful metrics from low-value telemetry.
3. The task text is sufficient to guide both implementation and review of runtime instrumentation work.
4. The instrumentation work is incomplete without unit/integration checks for metric semantics, scripted stress/E2E collection paths, and detailed machine-readable logs that later policy, comparator, and rollout beads can consume directly.
notes: This bead is foundational because queueing/control ideas are only useful if the observed state is trustworthy and interpretable.

title: Render Diff Overhaul: Dirty-Rect + SIMD
description:
## Goal
Make diff computation asymptotically faster and deterministically correct by combining dirty‑rect tracking with blockwise SIMD comparisons.

## Background
Current diff scans every row each frame and only short‑circuits when entire rows are equal. This is correct but leaves performance on the table when only small regions change.

## Core Idea
1. **Dirty‑Rect Tracking**: Track mutated regions during rendering (per‑row bitset + bounding boxes). Diff uses dirty metadata to skip untouched rows without relying on probabilistic hashes.
2. **Blockwise SIMD**: For dirty rows, compare cells in vectorized blocks (portable SIMD) to produce a change mask quickly.

## Correctness Invariants
- No change may be missed: dirty tracking must be updated on every buffer mutation path.
- SIMD comparison must match `Cell::bits_eq` semantics for every lane.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Diff time reduces by >= 3× on sparse updates (measured).\n- Correctness proven via property tests that compare against full scan for random buffers.\n- No unsafe code introduced.

## Subtasks
- Dirty‑rect invariants + integration points
- SIMD block compare implementation
- Diff correctness + perf harness + golden outputs
close_reason: done

title: Diff Dirty-Rect Spec + Mutation Audit
description:
## Goal
Define the exact dirty‑rect invariants and audit all buffer mutation paths to guarantee correctness.

## Math/Spec
Let D be the set of dirty rows. Invariant: For any frame, if cell (x,y) changes, then y ∈ D. Formally, for all y: if ∃x with old(x,y) ≠ new(x,y), then y ∈ D. This makes dirty‑row skipping **sound**.

## Implementation Notes
- Enumerate all write paths (`Buffer::set`, `Frame` rendering helpers, widget rendering).
- Add a single, centralized mutation API that marks dirty rows.

title: Presenter Optimization: Cost-Optimal ANSI + SGR Delta
description:
## Goal
Reduce terminal output size and latency by computing a cost‑optimal emission plan and minimizing style escape sequences.

## Background
Current presenter uses "reset + apply" for each style change and emits cursor moves per run. This is robust but not minimal in bytes.

## Core Idea
- **SGR Delta Engine**: Emit only the necessary style toggles (bitmask diff) instead of full reset.\n- **Cost-Optimal Emission**: Model ANSI ops as a weighted graph and compute minimal cost path per row (or per run set) using dynamic programming.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Output byte count reduced by >= 25% on style‑heavy screens.\n- Equivalent visual output proven with golden snapshots and checksum diff.\n- Deterministic under fixed seed and inputs.

## Subtasks
- SGR delta algorithm + invariants
- DP cost model for ANSI ops
- Presenter perf + golden outputs

## Tests / Validation
- Unit tests for SGR delta correctness (style diffs, reset handling).
- Golden snapshot + checksum parity vs baseline presenter.
- Microbench with JSONL perf logs (bytes emitted, render time, allocations).
- E2E PTY run on style-heavy screens with verbose logging of byte counts.

title: Presenter SGR Delta Engine + Evidence Ledger
description:
## Goal
Replace reset‑and‑apply with a minimal SGR delta engine that emits only necessary toggles, with explainable decisions.

## Math/Spec
Let style state be a bitmask over attrs + fg/bg colors. Define a cost for each SGR operation (bytes). Compute the minimal sequence to transform state A→B. This is a shortest‑path problem on a small state graph; precompute optimal transitions for the 2^k attr space and finite color ops.

## Acceptance Criteria
- For every style transition, emitted bytes ≤ reset+apply.
- No incorrect style leakage across runs.
- Deterministic evidence ledger: emitted ops + cost comparison.

## Tests (REQUIRED)

- unit_cost_dominance: byte cost never exceeds baseline.
- e2e_style_stress: scripted style churn with byte metrics.

## E2E Logging

title: Presenter DP Cost Model (ANSI Shortest Path)
description:
## Goal
Compute a minimal‑byte emission plan by modeling ANSI ops and cursor moves as a shortest‑path problem.

## Model
Define a state as (cursor position, style state). Operations include CUP, HPA, relative moves, erase‑to‑EOL, and literal writes. Each op has a byte cost. For each row, compute optimal action sequence to realize the target cells and minimize total cost.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Cost model chooses full‑row rewrite when it is cheaper than sparse runs.
- Verified minimal or near‑minimal byte cost on canonical fixtures.
- Stable output ordering (deterministic).

## Tests (REQUIRED)
- unit_cost_model_edge_cases: empty row, full row, single cell.
- property_emit_equivalence: DP output renders same buffer as baseline.
- perf_cost_model_overhead: DP planning cost stays within budget.

## E2E Coverage

title: Budget Controller Spec (PID + e-process)
description:
## Goal
Define the exact control equations and formal guarantees for budget adaptation.

## Math Spec
Let e_t = frame_time_t − target. PID control:
- u_t = Kp*e_t + Ki*sum(e) + Kd*(e_t − e_{t-1})
Map u_t to degradation level changes with hysteresis.
Anytime-valid gate:
- E_t = product exp(lambda * r_t − (lambda^2 * sigma^2)/2) on residuals r_t
- Allow degrade only when E_t > 1/alpha (evidence strong).

## Acceptance Criteria
- Controller gains chosen with stability margins.
- Hysteresis thresholds documented and justified.

## Tests (REQUIRED)

- unit_eprocess_gate: degrade only after evidence threshold.

title: Layout Temporal Coherence + Stable Rounding
description:
## Goal
Reduce layout jitter across frames by using mathematically optimal rounding and temporal coherence constraints.

## Core Idea
Given fractional sizes from constraint solving, allocate integer cells to minimize displacement from previous frame while respecting constraints. Formulate as:
minimize sum_i |x_i^t − x_i^{t-1}| + lambda * slack
subject to sum x_i = total and x_i ∈ Z, with bounds.
Solve via min‑cost flow or balanced rounding (Huntington‑Hill) with temporal tie‑breakers.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Layout positions change minimally under small terminal size changes.\n- No constraint violations; stable deterministic rounding.\n- Property tests validate invariants and minimal displacement.

## Subtasks
- Formal rounding spec + proof sketch\n- Implementation + integration into Flex/Grid\n- Property tests + regression snapshots

title: Layout Rounding Spec (Min-Displacement Optimization)
description:
## Goal
Define the precise optimization objective and rounding algorithm for stable layout.

## Math Spec
Let r_i be the real-valued target size. Solve integer allocation x_i:
minimize sum_i w_i * |x_i − r_i| + mu * |x_i − x_i_prev|
subject to sum x_i = total, and bounds (min/max/ratio).

Use either:
- Min‑cost flow on a bipartite graph of extra cells, or
- Huntington‑Hill apportionment with temporal tie‑breakers.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Proof sketch of optimality / bounded suboptimality.
- Deterministic tie‑break rules.

## Tests (REQUIRED)

- unit_temporal_tie_break: stable when r_i unchanged.

## E2E Coverage

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## Mathematical Foundation

Layout computation is a pure function:
```
layout(area, constraints, intrinsics?) → chunks
```

Memoization is valid when:
1. The function is pure (same inputs → same outputs)
2. Inputs are hashable/comparable
3. Output is cloneable or shareable

All three conditions hold for layout:
1. Constraint solving is deterministic
2. Rect, Constraint, Size are all hashable
3. Vec<Rect> is cheaply cloneable

### Cache Size Bounds
Worst case: Every frame has unique (area, constraints) pair.
- Mitigation: LRU eviction with capacity limit (e.g., 64 entries)
- Typical case: 3-5 unique layouts per screen, cache is tiny

### Consistency with Intrinsic Sizing
When using FitContent constraints, the layout depends on widget measurements. The cache key must include intrinsic sizes, which adds complexity:

1. **Eager hashing**: Hash all intrinsics upfront (always computed)
2. **Lazy hashing**: Only hash when FitContent present (saves work for static layouts)
3. **Invalidation on content change**: Bump generation when model changes

Recommendation: Lazy hashing with generation-based invalidation.

## Relationship to Other Beads
- **bd-2dow.5 (Measure Cache)**: Layout cache sits ABOVE measure cache; layout uses cached measures
- **bd-1rz0.4 (Atomic Reflow)**: Layout cache survives resize if constraints unchanged
- **bd-4kq0.4 (Layout Temporal Coherence)**: This IS the temporal coherence mechanism

### Integration Order
1. Implement measure cache (bd-2dow.5)
2. Implement layout cache (this task)
3. Wire together: layout cache keys include measure cache fingerprints

title: Text Wrap: Knuth-Plass DP (Optimal Raggedness)
description:
## Goal
Upgrade existing greedy wrap to an optional Knuth‑Plass dynamic programming line‑breaking algorithm for optimal raggedness and stability.

## Core Idea
Minimize total badness: sum (slack^3 + penalty) across lines, while respecting Unicode grapheme boundaries. Use DP with breakpoints; complexity O(n^2) with pruning.

## Acceptance Criteria
- Produces more stable and visually balanced line breaks.\n- Deterministic output given input and width.\n- Fallback to greedy mode for performance‑critical paths.

## Subtasks
- Knuth‑Plass math spec + penalties\n- Implementation with pruning\n- Tests + perf regression gates

title: Knuth-Plass Spec (Badness + Penalties)
description:
## Goal
Define the exact badness function and DP formulation for line breaking.

## Math Spec
For line i with slack s_i = width − line_width:
- badness_i = (s_i / width)^3 * 1000
- Add penalties for hyphenation or forced breaks.
Objective: minimize total badness.
Use DP: cost[j] = min_i (cost[i] + badness(i→j) + penalty(i→j)).

## Tests (REQUIRED)
- unit_badness_monotone: larger slack => higher badness.
- unit_penalty_applied: explicit penalties affect breaks.

## Acceptance Criteria
